articles.title: Nicholas Ty takes oath as new Deputy Ombudsman
articles.summary: Lawyer Nicholas Felix Ty took his oath on Thursday, November 26, 2026, as the new deputy ombudsman for Luzon.

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 9:47pm
Lawyer Nicholas Felix Ty took his oath on Thursday, November 26, 2026, as the new deputy ombudsman for Luzon.

Before his appointment, he served as an undersecretary at the Department of Justice (DOJ), overseeing legal and inter-agency initiatives, including efforts to address human trafficking and transnational crimes.
Upon taking his oath, Ty expressed gratitude to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for giving him the continued opportunity to serve in public office.
In his new role, Ty said one of his priorities is to serve as a loyal soldier to Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla to help fulfill the latter’s goal of eradicating corruption in the country.
“Ang mga priorities natin bilang Deputy Ombudsman ng Luzon ay siyempre tulungan ang kasalukuyang nakaupong Ombudsman si Ombudsman Boying Remulla,” Ty said.
(Our priorities as Deputy Ombudsman for Luzon are, of course, to assist the sitting Ombudsman, Ombudsman Boying Remulla.)
“At ako naman ay magiging isang tapat na sundalo dito kay Ombudsman Remulla upang matuloy talaga ang kaniyang hangad na masugpo ang korapsyon dito sa bansa natin,” he added.
(And for my part, to be a loyal soldier to Ombudsman Remulla so that his goal of stamping out corruption in our country can truly be achieved.)
Ty said he believes the experience and insights he gained during his stint at the DOJ will prove useful in his new position at the Office of the Ombudsman.
He vowed to remain faithful to the Constitution and his sworn duties to hold violators accountable.

“Maging tapat talaga sa Konstitusyon, maging tapat sa mga batas, maging tapat sa mga tungkulin ng isang public servant at talagang maging ehemplo sa ibang mga public servant at siyempre tulungan ang ating Ombudsman para panagutin ang mga taong lumalabag sa kanilang mga obligasyon,” the new deputy ombudsman said.

(To truly be faithful to the Constitution, faithful to the laws, faithful to the duties of a public servant, to truly serve as an example to other public servants, and of course, to help our Ombudsman hold accountable those who violate their obligations.)
Ty graduated from the University of the Philippines College of Law.
He earned his Master of Laws in International Economics and Business Law from Kyushu University in Japan.
He has practiced law for more than 20 years and has also taught as an assistant professor at the UP College of Law. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Muni Network: Newsrooms unite against AI disruption
articles.summary: Facing the threats of AI-induced disruption and declining web traffic, Southeast Asian newsrooms unite through the Muni Network for the future of news

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – As artificial intelligence continues to squeeze traffic and revenue from independent media, the question of what path newsrooms need to take to survive the disruption has been at the forefront of many conversations within the industry.

Some independent newsrooms in the Philippines and other Southeast Asian countries are going a step beyond talking. From November 19 to 22, editors, technology leads, and newsroom strategists from these news groups gathered at the Rappler headquarters to confront the issue and explore approaches to addressing the AI enigma that capitalize on their collective strengths and communities.

Organized and hosted by Rappler, the event, Future of News (FON) Laboratory, aimed to build a collective approach to AI disruption, declining website traffic, and unfair policies by tech platforms, striving to secure, as its name suggests, the future of news.

“Since the launch of AI overview, we have seen a 50% to 70% drop in our organic traffic coming from the search engine,” said Wahyu Dhyatmika, CEO of Indonesia’s Tempo Digital. “We have to find other ways to ensure that we still can reach our audience, can still be impactful, and also build a new business model.”Rappler CEO Maria Ressa stressed the need for a shared solution. “It doesn’t matter if one news group is moving ahead because we cannot fight these forces alone,” she said.

Ressa emphasized the need for newsrooms to find new business models and build audiences together. “That’s the other reason I wrote The Fight Back. The fight back literally is building our communities. It is bottom up with our communities, and then we have to work with our governments,” she explained.

“The November 2026 sessions follow many preliminary meetings and one-on-one sessions where we confronted difficult questions that usually got in the way of collaboration,” said Gemma Mendoza, head of strategic programs at Rappler.

blocks.caption: FORGING ALLIANCE. Editorial leaders and representatives from Kiripost (Cambodia), Katadata and Tempo (Indonesia), Malaysiakini (Malaysia), Mizzima (Myanmar), Mountain Beacon and Palawan News (Luzon), Daily Guardian and Sunstar Cebu (Visayas), and MindaNews (Mindanao) pose for a group photo during…

blocks.text: Newsrooms that sent participants to the Future of News Laboratory included Kiripost (Cambodia), Katadata and Tempo (Indonesia), Malaysiakini (Malaysia), and Mizzima (Myanmar), alongside Philippine community newsrooms Mountain Beacon and Palawan News (Luzon), Daily Guardian and SunStar Cebu (Visayas), and MindaNews (Mindanao).

Among matters discussed in preliminary sessions was Meta’s aborted effort to implement a clause in its commercial terms, which treated presence on its platforms as permission for the tech giant to scrape publisher content and use the same as training data for its AI products.

blocks.caption: MUNI-MAXXING. Some representatives from Southeast Asian newsrooms engage in a workshop on how to set up, configure, and maximize MUNI in their workflows. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: “Meta’s recent decision to withdraw the planned website-crawling clause in its updated commercial terms proves that collective pushback works,” said Mendoza, who also leads Rappler’s Future of News initiative.
Representatives of participating newsrooms agreed that they cannot afford to lower their guard.
“They (platforms) steal data, they use data. And the irony is we buy data back from them,” said Redempto Anda, editor-in-chief of Palawan News.

Aryo Widhy Wicaksono from Indonesia’s Katadata also noted that because people now read news straight from social media and AI summaries instead of visiting news websites, fewer brands are buying ads from publishers.
“All the news that we produce, we took effort, we took time, we took a lot of work to do that. And then the AI just took an overview [of] it without really doing anything,” Wicaksono added.

While calling out unfair practices by AI companies, the FON participants also explored ways by which newsrooms can use AI safely to improve and enrich their daily work, as long as human editors stay in control.
At Cambodia’s Kiripost, AI is already helping small teams work faster.
“Recently, our data team, without any coding experience, started a few months ago with vibe coding,” shared Tharum Bun, its co-founder and managing editor.

blocks.caption: THOUGHTS ON AI. Cambodian media company Kiripost managing editor Tharum Bun discusses his newsroom’s unique strengths and the impact of AI in their journalism. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: “Small web tool apps that we have never had before, now we can build in a few months, and we can produce more visual data and stories in a very effective way,” Bun added.
For Mildred Galarpe, editor-in-chief of SunStar Cebu, AI initially felt like a “shining, shimmering tool” that tempted newsrooms to adopt it without enough caution.

blocks.caption: COLLABORATION. SunStar Cebu editor-in-chief Mildred Galarpe suggests community engagement efforts that newsrooms should implement, during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: Galarpe noted, however, that moving too quickly led to early mistakes, such as accidentally swapping the family names of the new and old governors in their coverage due to AI use. That experience taught them that while AI is an effective tool to fast-track work, it is not the editor.

“The human eye should always be there. Nothing should be published without your thumbprint,” Galarpe said.Rappler’s Ressa further stressed that AI cannot replace humans because its models operate on probability instead of facts, meaning what many refer to as “hallucination” is actually just the system working as designed.“You will always need a human in the loop…because news is anchored in facts, but the tech that is ruling our lives, they’re anchored in profit, so it’s corrupted the entire world,” Ressa added.

To turn their stand into action, the participating newsrooms are joining forces through the Muni Network, inspired by the MUNI tab on the Rappler app.The Muni Network will officially launch on December 10, coinciding with Human Rights Day, with plans to expand across the region soon.For Anda, this network is essential for small newsrooms like theirs.

“I look at it as a startup venture, because this is something that is pioneering. You have newsrooms gathering together and figuring out a way to go around this problem of AI using our data [and] how we deal with social media platforms inundating and taking over newsrooms,” Anda added.
By combining their audiences and reach, smaller and independent newsrooms hope to achieve greater impact together, if not match the strength of global tech giants.
“AI doesn’t know boundaries,” Wicaksono said. “If we have a collaboration, we add those small sounds or small voices [to] become one.”

blocks.caption: STATUS CHECK. Some Southeast Asian newsroom representatives put their ideas, capabilities, and ways to respond to AI threats on a whiteboard during the first day of the Future of News Laboratory on November 19, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

blocks.text: The federation wants to change how newsrooms work together across Southeast Asia.
Dhyatmika added that publishers won’t stand a chance if they act individually in the era of AI. For him, newsrooms should not see each other as competitors but collaborators.
He emphasized that acting collectively would enable them to get a fairer share of the value created by their products in the digital ecosystem.

Alongside the workshop, the Future of News Laboratory participants also attended Rappler’s Social Good Summit centered on the theme “We, The Humans” — a timely reminder that humans (the journalists in this situation) must remain in control of technology and use its potential to drive meaningful action instead of being driven by it.
Before the November sessions, the group had also issued a joint statement to sound the alarm on the negative effects of AI on journalism, facts, and democracy.

Released last May for World Press Freedom Day, the joint statement highlighted issues such as algorithmic suppression of news, the economic challenges posed by Big Tech monopolies, and the rise of disinformation, which collectively threaten the survival of independent media.

Early collaborators have already launched public chat channels to strengthen local journalism and held community chats around newsroom-initiated investigations. Among those who participated were Daily Guardian and Sunstar Cebu. Both newsrooms have their branded chat channels embedded on their respective websites.

In September 2025, in time for World News Day, the collaboration also released an experimental video simulating Replica, an “AI-powered journalist.” The video aimed to send a dire warning about what could happen if independent newsrooms die and the only source of news would be AI, ending with a call for citizens to support real journalism. – Rappler.com

articles.title: EU-Indonesia trade deal opens new markets, but challenges remain
articles.summary: The agreement eyes new export and investment opportunities for Jakarta and Brussels. But can Indonesia turn Europe's growing interest in its markets and critical minerals into sustainable gains at…

image.caption: Economy minister Airlangga Hartarto (2-L) hailed a 'new chapter' in EU-Indonesia tiesImage: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: As the European Union seeks to deepen its presence in Asia and diversify its trade relationships, Indonesia is emerging as an increasingly important partner.

At a signing ceremony in Brussels last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the bloc's trade agreement with Jakarta as one of its "most ambitious deals" in the region, linking markets of 730 million people.

The deal, the culmination of nearly a decade of negotiations, reflects the EU's efforts to diversify its trade partnerships, secure access to critical raw materials and reduce strategic dependencies on China.
For Indonesia, it offers opportunities to attract investment, expand exports and strengthen its position in global supply chains.
The agreement will gradually scrap tariffs on more than 98% of product categories, covering almost the entire value of bilateral trade over 15 years.
Indonesia and EU finally seal landmark trade deal
Indonesia's strategic importance to Europe

For the EU, gaining better access to critical raw materials, particularly nickel, and diversifying its supply chains are central to its strategic partnership with Indonesia, said Philip Schleifer, an associate professor of political science at the University of Amsterdam.

"The main strategic interests are opening up a large and growing market for European companies, diversifying and deepening its economic partnerships, reducing strategic dependencies on China, and securing access to critical raw materials," Schleifer told DW.
Indonesia's mineral resources are particularly important for Europe's green and digital transitions. Nickel, for instance, is a key material for batteries and electric vehicles.
The agreement also creates opportunities for European investment in strategic sectors, including electric vehicles, electronics and pharmaceuticals.

But Indonesia has its own industrial ambitions. The government wants to move beyond exporting raw materials by developing domestic processing industries and retaining more value from its natural resources.

"The challenge for the EU is to reconcile its own interest in securing raw material supply with Indonesia's industrial development objectives," said Eline Blot, a senior policy analyst at the Institute for European Environmental Policy (IEEP).
Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US
Export opportunities and challenges for Indonesia
For Jakarta, the agreement offers opportunities to expand exports, attract investment and strengthen its position in global supply chains.

Yose Rizal Damuri, an economist at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said his institution's study estimates Indonesian exports could increase by around 60% in the coming years.
"Not only can Indonesia increase exports to Europe, but it can also become more strongly integrated into the global supply chains of European companies," Yose told DW.
Potential beneficiaries include labor-intensive manufacturing sectors such as textiles, garments, footwear and furniture, alongside other Indonesian commodities and manufactured products.

The agreement could also encourage European investment and create employment opportunities. However, Yose stressed that access to the European market does not automatically translate into higher exports.
He identified three priorities for Indonesia: raising awareness of the agreement among domestic businesses, strengthening production capacity and improving the country's business climate.

"Various trade agreements signed by Indonesia have relatively low utilization rates. The value of exports using these facilities remains limited compared with overall export values," he said, emphasizing the need for better information and outreach to producers.

Syafruddin Karimi, an economist at Andalas University, also highlighted the opportunity to diversify Indonesia's export markets and reduce dependence on major trading partners such as China, the United States and regional Asian economies.
However, he warned that Indonesian producers must improve their compliance with European standards.
"Products must be traceable, including whether their production involves environmental damage or labor practices that undermine human dignity," Karimi said.
He added that smaller businesses would need greater government support to meet requirements concerning raw materials, production processes and workers' rights.
Is Europe still a global power? The brutal free trade debate
Environmental costs of economic integration
The expansion of trade and investment could also increase environmental pressures, particularly in nickel mining, palm oil production and manufacturing.

IEEP analyst Blot warned that increased production without stronger environmental safeguards could worsen pollution, ecosystem degradation and industrial emissions. "Nickel mining and processing can contribute to pollution and ecosystem degradation, while palm oil remains closely associated with deforestation," she said.
The growing importance of Indonesian iron and steel exports also raises concerns about emissions from energy-intensive production.

The EU's Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) presents another challenge for Indonesian producers, particularly small-scale farmers who may lack the resources, technical capacity and documentation needed to demonstrate compliance.
Blot acknowledged that these requirements could create disproportionate costs for smaller producers and potentially favor larger companies.
However, she cautioned against using smallholders' livelihoods as an argument to weaken environmental regulations.
Some Indonesian smallholder organisations, she noted, have supported the EUDR as an opportunity to improve accountability in the palm oil industry.
"Rather than weakening environmental requirements, the priority should be to ensure that smallholders receive adequate financial and technical support to meet them," she said.

Professor Schleifer at the University of Amsterdam also warned that growing global demand for Indonesian natural resources could create environmental and social problems previously associated with commodities such as timber, palm oil and coal.

While Indonesia has considerable bargaining power because of its mineral wealth, the challenge is ensuring that increased demand translates into domestic industrial development rather than simply expanding resource extraction.
How a leading EV supplier covered up toxic pollution
Can Indonesia turn market access into sustainable growth?

The agreement includes a dedicated Trade and Sustainable Development chapter covering climate change, biodiversity conservation, sustainable forest management and labor rights. It also provides mechanisms for cooperation and civil society participation.

However, there is no guarantee these commitments will be implemented. "Experience with other EU trade agreements suggests that there is often a big gap between sustainability commitments on paper and outcomes on the ground," Schleifer said.
Blot similarly called for a time-bound roadmap with measurable objectives, stronger monitoring and meaningful participation from civil society and local communities.

For Indonesia, the challenge also lies in preparing domestic industries to compete. Karimi stressed that the government, both at national and regional levels, must work with businesses to improve production standards, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises.
Yose also emphasized the importance of a predictable business environment, warning that frequent policy changes and regulatory uncertainty could discourage investors.
"Without improvements in the domestic business climate, this will not become a reality. Everything will remain good on paper but will not turn into real momentum for change," he said.
Ultimately, the trade agreement offers Indonesia an opportunity to strengthen its position in international trade and attract investment from Europe.

But whether the agreement delivers broader economic benefits will depend on the country's ability to develop competitive industries, move into higher-value production, and ensure that environmental protection and workers' rights are not overlooked.
DW's Muhammad Athif Aiman contributed to this article.

articles.title: CHR maintains stance vs. abortion except in extreme cases
articles.summary: CHR maintains stance vs abortion except in extreme cases

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 9:32pm

The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) on Thursday stood firm on its pro-life position, saying it opposes abortion except for when a woman's life is at risk, or if she is a rape victim, or there are medical grounds for the procedure.
This was brought up during the Senate plenary deliberations into the proposed P1.285-billion budget of the CHR for fiscal year 2027.
During the session, Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III asked the CHR of its current stand regarding abortion, considering that there have been efforts seeking to decriminalize it.

“The official stand of the Commission on Human Rights is pro-life. They are anti-abortion, except in extreme circumstances, for example, life-threatening, second, victims of rape, and medical reasons,” budget sponsor Senator JV Ejercito answered.
Sotto said he would no longer propound any more questions if the CHR is maintaining its position against abortion.

“Thank you for that because there is an ongoing hearing. I understand that they are trying to revise the Revised Penal Code. So, hearing that from the CHR, I have no more questions and I have no problem with the budget, Mr. President. I fully support the submission,” he said.
Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri, meanwhile, also welcomed CHR’s take.
Describing himself as a "Republican" conservative lawmaker, Zubiri said he is "pro-life."

“We appreciate the fact that you came out stating that you will not support legislation to that effect to decriminalize abortion because ayaw po nating mangyari katulad ng Estados Unidos na ano lang, parang pwede kang pumunta ng mall at magpa-abortion [we don’t want to be like the United States where people could just go to a mall and get an abortion],” he said.
“Over my dead body will I allow legislation to that effect, which shall allow decriminalizing of abortion while I’m here in the Senate,” he added.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) earlier maintained that abortion is a crime, but admitted that it was open to proposing exemptions with proposed amendments to the Revised Penal Code (RPC) pending before the House of Representatives.

A DOJ committee reportedly prepared a draft Criminal Code of the Philippines which aims to amend the RPC. A DOJ official also said there were efforts by some progressive lawmakers to decriminalize abortion. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Ex-Cale88 co-owner, BOC official to testify in Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada, who is also the Vice President's dentist, is expected to testify on Cale88's organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, ownership, and…

blocks.text: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte talks to supporters as she prepares to leave the Quezon City Regional Trial Court after the postponement of the arraignment for her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.
Noel Celis/Reuters

Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada, who is also the Vice President's dentist, is expected to testify on Cale88's organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, ownership, and financial affairs

MANILA, Philippines – A former co-owner of Cale88 Foods Corporation, who is also Vice President Sara Duterte‘s dentist, is expected to testify before the Senate impeachment court when her trial resumes on December 1.

The defense counsel submitted a manifestation dated November 25 asking the Senate impeachment court to issue subpoenas ad testificandum et duces tecum to Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada and direct her to participate during the proceedings scheduled from December 1 to 4.
Lebosada was also directed to bring certified true copies of the following documents:

items: Registration documents of Cale88 Foods Corporation, including relevant government records;
Documents relating to Cale88’s operations;
Documents relating to the company’s finances and business transactions; and
Other documents relevant to the foregoing.

blocks.text: Cale88, a banana chips production company co-owned by Lebosada and Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, came under scrutiny during the impeachment trial after Anti-Money Laundering Council records showed that it received P776 million in cash inflows despite having only P125,000 in paid-up capital and declaring P208 million in sales.

Lawyer Alex Cabrera, who prepared a forensic financial report on Duterte’s bank and financial records, described Cale88’s business model as “implausible” and likened its operations to a “revolving door,” which he said was indicative of money laundering.
Lebosada is expected to testify on Cale88’s organizational structure, government registrations, business operations, ownership, and financial affairs.

The defense also sought a subpoena for Agaton Teodoro Uvero, deputy commissioner of the Assessment and Operations Coordinating Group of the Bureau of Customs. Uvero is expected to testify on Cale88’s exportation records under the custody of the BOC.
The impeachment court confirmed the issuance of subpoenas to both witnesses.

“As of this morning, Thursday, November 26, 2026, the Office of the Clerk of Court has completed service of both subpoenas — serving the Office of Bureau of Customs Deputy Commissioner Atty. Agaton Teodoro O. Uvero personally at 9:05 am, and serving Dr. Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada in Davao City via electronic mail at 9:54 am pursuant to the Court’s electronic service directive,” said impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol.
The impeachment trial is currently on hold to give way to Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget. Proceedings are scheduled to resume on December 1. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Flood watch in place on Vancouver Island as king tide impact continues
articles.summary: A flood watch is in place for eastern Vancouver Island as the B.C. coast continues to deal with a series of storms that are combining with unusually high tides on Thursday.

image.caption: A person is seen near a rushing river in the Nanaimo area of Vancouver Island on Wednesday. A flood watch has been maintained for eastern Vancouver Island as king tides combine with a storm to continue to create hazards for coastal B.C. (Claire Palmer/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A flood watch is in place for eastern Vancouver Island as the B.C. coast continues to deal with a series of storms that are combining with unusually high tides on Thursday.
Swath of high streamflow advisories in place for the rest of Vancouver Island and the South Coast

The B.C. River Forecast Centre issued the flood watch on Wednesday, along with a swath of high streamflow advisories for the South Coast and the rest of Vancouver Island, as between 50 and 100 millimetres of rain were predicted to fall on the island.

Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) said in an orange coastal flooding warning for Metro Vancouver that "moderate to significant flooding" was expected along coastlines and low-lying areas due to storm surge and very high tides.

A number of evacuation alerts were issued by the regional districts of Nanaimo and Comox Valley on Wednesday, adding to previous alerts from the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation and Parksville, with residents told to be ready to leave at a moment's notice.
A warning to stay away from the river, posted by the Regional District of Nanaimo, is seen on Wednesday. (Claire Palmer/CBC)
The B.C. River Forecast Centre said in its flood watch that residents should stay clear of running rivers and never drive across flooded roads.

"Significant storms earlier in the month have contributed to saturated soils and higher flows, increasing the potential for rapid runoff and flow response during this next storm," the Wednesday flood watch reads.

items: How king tides happen, and what that means amid flood warnings in B.C.
Ahousaht declares state of emergency as storm and king tides batter west coast of Vancouver Island

blocks.text: The king tides currently hitting B.C.'s coast — referring to a phenomenon where cosmic alignments can mean dramatic tides which can be about 0.3 to 0.6 metres higher than the average — are expected to end on Thursday.
ECCC said the water levels could elevate by as much as 0.7 metres during high tide on Wednesday and Thursday.
Grouse Grind closed
While the coastal flooding warnings covered nearly the entire B.C. coastline on Wednesday, high winds and rainfall were also an issue for many areas.
B.C. Ferries cancelled a number of evening sailings between Metro Vancouver and Vancouver Island, citing high winds in the Strait of Georgia, on Wednesday.
3 forces are raising the risk of coastal flooding in B.C.

The Metro Vancouver Regional District said that the Grouse Mountain Regional Park in North Vancouver — which houses the popular Grouse Grind trail — would be closed on Thursday due to the heavy rain in the forecast.

"Park staff will assess and determine if trails are safe to reopen once weather conditions allow. Please stay out of the park for your safety, that of park staff, and first responders," the regional district said on Wednesday.

articles.title: Joshua Kimmich critcizes Bayern bosses over Musiala health comments
articles.summary: Joshua Kimmich has slammed Bayern Munich's leadership over comments about Jamal Musiala's health issues. The bosses have questioned whether the player can return to previous form – and is still worth…

image.caption: Joshua Kimmich feels that Musiala's situation should be dealt with behind closed doorsImage: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bayern Munich's disappointing 2-1 Champions League defeat at Lille on Wednesday night – in which Jamal Musiala came on for the last quarter of an hour – was overshadowed by comments the club's captain made afterwards.

"It must never happen that something like this is played out at a player's expense. Of course, the club always comes first and is bigger than the player, but it's not bigger than the person," Kimmich told reporters in the mixed zone.
"That's an absolute no-go and not Bayern-like," he added.
Kimmich was responding to recent comments made by Bayern supervisory board members Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge.

"If he (Musiala) doesn't return to being the Jamal of old, then we need to have a conversation with his family, with the player, and, above all, with his agency – because, frankly, the current financial figures would no longer be justifiable," Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told Sky on Friday.
Honorary President Uli Hoeness has described the situation as a "dilemma" for the club, while CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen raised the prospect of talks with Musiala's management and family.
Neurological condition

While theGermany player has struggled with a number of injuries over the past couple of seasons, his health came into sharper focus in August, after he collapsed on the pitch in a couple of preseason matches. He subsequently revealed that he had been diagnosed with a neurological condition which causes him to suffer from occasional "absence seizures."
Kimmich added that criticism of a players' performances was legitimate, but that concerns about Musiala's situation should have been dealt with behind closed doors.
"That's something you should sort out internally, around a table, rather than trying to resolve it publicly," he said.
"It's not that he has problems because he's unprofessional. He's there every day trying to get the maximum out of himself."
Talks between two sides ongoing

Meanwhile, Bayern bosses met with Musiala's agents on Tuesday, and clarified the timeline of events, dismissing speculation that the player could have concealed the condition when he signed his last contract extension.

Bayern said the two sides agreed that he was first examined for seizure symptoms in April 2025, two months after he had signed his contract extension, which makes him one of the club's top earners and is to keep him in Munich until 2030. Discussions between Bayern management and Musiala's representatives are reportedly ongoing.

articles.title: Crew member dies after diesel tanker sinks off Ibiza coast
articles.summary: Authorities rescued 17 crew members but one later died in hospital after a diesel tanker sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza. A contingency plan against possible pollution damage is now in place.

image.caption: The chemical tanker Med Emre was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona [FILE: June 8, 2024]Image: Manuel Hernández Lafuente/VesselFinder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities said on Thursday.

The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, said in a statement.
According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.
The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it sank about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.

blocks.caption: The last known position of the tankerImage: Vesselfinder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the sinking was not immediately clear.
Authorities monitor pollution risk

The Transport Ministry said the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.
Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.
Spain's merchant marine authority ​has activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest.
The Balearic regional government said it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.
The importance of Ibiza for biodiversity
The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.
The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.
Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable."

blocks.caption: Any pollution entering the sea could potentially harm Mediterranean seagrass ecosystems [FILE: February 8, 2020]Image: Dietmar Hasenpusch/Hasenpusch-Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: But he said the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood."
"It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he said.

Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.

articles.title: Police identify suspect vehicle tied to Toronto home invasion that killed musician Michael Eckert
articles.summary: Toronto police have identified a suspect vehicle tied to a fatal shooting and attempted home invasion that took place early Wednesday in midtown Toronto.

image.caption: Toronto police have shared a photo of a vehicle that may have been used by suspects in a fatal shooting and attempted home invasion on Nov. 25, 2026. (Toronto Police Service)

blocks.text: Toronto
Toronto police have identified a suspect vehicle tied to a fatal shooting and attempted home invasion that took place early Wednesday in midtown Toronto.
Toronto musician Michael Eckert, 39, identified as the victim after he was shot by a suspect Wednesday
The vehicle is believed to be a four-door sedan that could potentially be a Honda with dark winter metal rims, Toronto police said in a news release.
Emergency crews responded to reports of a shooting at a residence in the St. Clair Avenue West and Poplar Plains Road area at around 2:40 a.m., according to police.
An unknown number of suspects forced entry into the residence, police said. One of the suspects was confronted by a resident of the home, shot him, and then fled, police said.
The resident was taken to hospital, where he was pronounced dead. That man has been identified as Toronto musician Michael Eckert, 39.
Toronto musician Michael Eckert killed in attempted home invasion, police say
Tributes continue to roll in for beloved musician
Eckert is being remembered as a talented musician who "always led with his heart," according to his longtime friend Galen Pelley.
"He spoke louder through his music than he ever would off stage or in person," he said, adding Eckert's instrument of choice was the pedal steel guitar.

Eckert was a "true pillar" of the music community and played directly from the heart, said Grammy-winning artist Justin Gray in a post on Facebook. He said the sudden loss is "beyond comprehension" and that the two worked together for over 20 years.
"He meant a lot to our community and our city and the world are dimmer places without him. Soar high, Neon Eagle. You will be dearly missed and fondly remembered," he said.
Michael Eckert was a beloved artist in Toronto's music scene and was expected to play a show on Saturday night, according to tributes rolling in on social media. (Alberta Davis/Facebook)
Eckert performed at the 113th Grey Cup in Calgary as back up for Blue Rodeo this month, Pelley said, adding: "He's gone too soon and that was a real moment for him to flourish."
Blue Rodeo expressed its condolences to Eckert's family and friends and called him "a kind, supportive and sweet person who was loved by so many in our music community."

"He was an absolute wizard on his instrument, deeply accomplished and fearlessly adventurous," the band said in a social media post. "It's always sad when we lose someone in our community, but a senseless, tragic loss of this sort is especially painful."

items: Man, 39, ID'd as victim of fatal shooting in midtown Toronto home invasion: police

blocks.text: MP Melissa Lantsman posted on social media platform X that the country needs to have stricter laws against home invasions and harsher penalties.

She also said Eckert was a familiar face in Toronto's music scene and known to many "from the stage, the crowd and the bar after the show." Lantsman said he was expected to play a show on Saturday with The Lizards.
"Michael's loved ones deserve more than condolences. They deserve action. RIP and come see the show Saturday to honour a brilliant musician," she said.

articles.title: Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes sinks near Ibiza, killing one
articles.summary: The possible environmental damage is still being assessed by Spain's sea rescue service.

blocks.text: An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has sunk off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.

The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
The Med Emre sank 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.
The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.
The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline. It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

articles.title: What is the US permitting bill and would it actually help the climate?
articles.summary: A sweeping US bill to speed up energy projects has rare bipartisan support. Supporters say it would unlock clean energy and lower bills, but critics say it's a gift to fossil fuels.

image.caption: Will the permitting bill boost renewables or fossil fuels?Image: Caleb Jones/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: While the dust has barely settled on the Democrats' big midterm showing, lawmakers still have business to get done before a new US Congress takes office in 2027: namely, a permitting reform bill with rare cross-party support that could accelerate clean energy or fossil fuels — or both, depending on who's asked.

Permitting reform might sound like a snooze. But the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) could have far-reaching consequences for the country's energy mix, household utility bills and climate goals.

BAAJA, which is backed by US President Donald Trump, has already cleared the Senate and now faces a vote in the House of Representatives. DW breaks down what's in the bill, the political fight playing out on the sidelines and what it could mean for consumers' pockets and the US energy transition.
What does the bill do?
Before many new solar farms, wind projects or power plants can connect to the electricity grid, they must first pass through an arduous and complex permitting process.

Getting the green light for an energy project can often take years and requires permits from multiple government agencies. If it manages to overcome those hurdles, a legal challenge can easily stop new infrastructure in its tracks.

blocks.caption: It can take years until projects get the greenlight due to a complex permitting processImage: Getty Images via AFP

blocks.text: The nearly 500-page bill aims to overhaul that process. It would speed up environmental reviews, simplify the planning and construction of power transmission lines, make permits harder to revoke and require the growing number of data centers to pay for grid upgrades they need.

The bill is mostly technology-agnostic. So, the same reforms that would make it easier to build a lot of green energy infrastructure quickly could, in theory, be used to speed up oil and gas projects whose carbon emissions are warming the planet.

That's what's made BAAJA controversial, with some Democrats saying permitting reform is needed to get energy bills down and others saying they support provisions, like building more transmission lines required for transporting green energy, but not the whole package.
Would the bill cut emissions or raise them?
It's hard to estimate, and there's a lot of contradictory information out there.

The Rhodium Group, an independent research firm, found the bill would lower US greenhouse gas emissions in every scenario it ran, by up to 4% in 2040 compared with no bill. This is a fraction of the emissions reductions targets the US dropped when it withdrew from Paris climate accord this year.

Purdue University engineer Kevin Kircher reached the opposite conclusion. His analysis, which has not been peer-reviewed, estimates that domestic emissions would rise by about 2%, mostly because he assumes the bill would boost US fossil fuel production.
How LA is plugging hidden oil wells

The difference comes down to a bet about what the bill ends up speeding up more: renewables and the power lines to carry them, or fossil fuels. That depends on which administration is issuing the permits.

Under Joe Biden's administration, for instance, renewables got a boost but since Trump took office, his administration has favored fossil fuels and spent billions paying developers to give up their offshore wind leases.
What would it mean for US household energy bills?

The White House Council of Economic Advisers, a team of economists that advises the president, estimates it would eventually cut the average household's electricity bill by $178 to $251 (€162 to €229) a year.

The logic is that long permitting delays discourage investment in infrastructure, which drives up prices. But that estimate considers only one part of the bill, faster environmental reviews, and doesn't say when the savings would arrive.

Independent analyses also found a drop in electricity prices for consumers, though a more modest one. The Rhodium Group estimates the bill's passage would save the average household $41 to $66 a year by 2035. That's largely because new transmission lines would let cheaper power reach customers and the costs of expanding the grid for data centers would no longer be passed on to households.

Critics point to the fact that those savings are relative. Electricity demand from data centers is expected to push up prices regardless, and permitting reform would only slow that rise rather than reverse it.
Data centers face backlash from US communities

Oil Change International, an advocacy group that opposes the bill, argues households will still end up paying more for energy than they do now, especially if the bill mainly speeds up gas projects, since US gas prices are expected to rise sharply over the next decade.
What do environmentalists say about it?

Most major US environmental groups oppose the bill as written, including the Natural Resources Defense Council, League of Conservation Voters and Earthjustice. The Sierra Club called it "fundamentally flawed."
Much of the criticism focuses on provisions making federal permits harder to revoke.

"It would prevent a future administration from reconsidering a prior administration's flawed decisions to authorize activities such as Arctic drilling, deep seabed mining, or development of data centers on public lands," Earthjustice wrote in a critique.
The reverse is also true. That provision also makes it harder for an administration to come in and halt clean energy projects, as Trump did with offshore wind.

Opponents warn the bill could weaken protection for water and habitats, and limit environmental lawsuits. One area that environmental groups praised is the overhaul of how transmission lines are planned and approved.
That matters because the windiest and sunniest places in the US are often far from the cities that need power, and building long-distance power lines to connect them can take a decade or more.

Still, many critics say they would rather wait until Democrats control Congress in January and pass a version more focused on clean energy. Though that approach is risky, any bill would still require Trump's signature to become law.

articles.summary: Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as officials urged residents to leave the area.

blocks.text: A alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.

The city-run Erawan Emergency Medical Centre said it was treating four "red" cases and three "yellow" - less severe - cases.

On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.
He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.
Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.

It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.
An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

articles.title: Data breaches are coming fast and furious. Are businesses doing enough to protect your data?
articles.summary: Recent data breaches at Bell and Staples are the latest in a swath of incidents where consumers' personal data was accessed by bad actors. As AI tools make it easier to carry out hacks, many…

image.caption: As AI makes cyber incidents more likely, experts say some businesses are taking the threat seriously, but many are still leaving their customers' personal data exposed. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

blocks.text: First it was a data breach at Staples, with the company alerting staplesprint.ca customers Friday that some personal information was accessed in a recent security incident.

Then came a notice from Bell, saying an "agentic threat actor" had accessed personal information like names, phone numbers and email addresses, impacting customers of Bell, Bell Aliant, Bell MTS, Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile. Agentic usually refers to AI tools that can act independently.

The incidents are just the latest examples of breaches — Loblaws, Save-on-Foods, Montreal car-sharing company Communauto and telecomm provider Eastlink have all made headlines for data incidents in the past few months.
For Bell customers like Anna Stephenson, who received an email this week saying her data might have been compromised, news of another hack doesn't feel all that surprising anymore.
"It's kind of the world we live in now where we have to sort of deal with these things," she said.

items: Bell says cybersecurity incident affected customers at Virgin Plus, Lucky Mobile
AI-powered Bell hack a sign of things to come, cybersecurity firm says

blocks.text: Though she understands Bell's challenge in staying one step ahead of criminals, Stephenson wants to see companies do more to protect the valuable data they keep about customers.
"In my opinion, companies need to invest more in that security, and hopefully that's something that Bell's looking into," Stephenson said.
Bell cyberattack raises fear AI is making data breaches easier

The experts agree. As AI tools make it easier to carry out hacks, lots of businesses are trying to keep up with the onslaught of attacks — but security and data experts say poor data management and security practices often leave consumer information more vulnerable than it should be.

As AI tools make it easier to carry out hacks, lots of businesses are trying to keep up with the onslaught of attacks — but security and data experts say poor data management and security practices often leave consumer information more vulnerable than it should be.
Too much data, not enough protection

Canadian privacy laws require companies to follow 10 principles when collecting, using and safeguarding personal information. When a breach happens that creates a real risk of harm, businesses have to report it to the privacy commissioner, notify individuals as soon as possible and keep records about the breach.
Those rules put the onus on businesses to manage and protect consumer data, according to Sharon Bauer, a lawyer and founder of Bamboo Data Consulting.

items: More criminals are using AI for ransomware attacks, cybersecurity centre warns
AI agents tried to hack Library and Archives Canada website, research firm says

blocks.text: "It is their responsibility to make sure that the data is secure," said Bauer.

While federal courts can fine businesses up to $100,000 if they fail to take certain steps, like report a breach, the federal privacy commissioner can't hand out fines itself. Bauer says that means the existing rules don't always have enough teeth to make companies feel like they need to comply.

Sharon Bauer is a Toronto-based privacy lawyer and founder of Bamboo Data Consulting. Often, businesses are keeping too much customer data they don't need, making it vulnerable to potential breaches, Bauer says. (Submitted by Sharon Bauer)
And best practices for keeping data aren't always followed. While lots of businesses have to keep some personal info on file, Bauer says many keep too much information that they simply don't need.
"It's probably one of the biggest risks that we find in almost every company that we work with," Bauer said.

She says companies might keep dates of birth that aren't being used, for example. Not storing data is the best way to prevent it from being stolen, according to Bauer, so keeping old or out of date customer information creates an unnecessary risk.

Terry Cutler, CEO of Cyology Labs, which provides cybersecurity services to small and medium-sized businesses, says many companies are often simply unaware of how vulnerable they are. He says some businesses he's worked with will use software that keeps part of their systems safe, thinking it covers their bases, while other parts of their network are exposed.

Cutler says a lot of companies currently "don't have the proper detection technology to know there's a hacker in their system, and they don't have a good response plan to get the hacker out once he's been detected."
And with AI making it easier for hackers to steal valuable data, the importance of taking cyber issues seriously is growing, too.

items: Welcome to the 'patchpocalypse' — a new AI era of hacking
PHP flaw: How AI just hacked an unhackable part of the internet | About That

blocks.text: Brent Arnold, founder of cybersecurity and privacy law firm Capstan Legal, says hackers can essentially automate attacks using AI, as agentic tools can work on their own to solve a problem once they're given an end goal — like hacking into software.
He says he's seen a deluge of attacks by hackers moving at hyper speed in recent months, something likely being driven by AI.
"It all happens a lot faster before it can be detected," he said.
One in four malicious data breaches are now powered by AI, according to IBM's 2026 data breach report — a 56 per cent increase compared to the year before.
Arnold points out that the standard for protecting data isn't perfection, but that companies should take reasonable steps to prevent data theft.
Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database
However, as threats become more sophisticated, he says businesses will need to raise their prevention measures to match.
"The standard is always reasonable measures, but what that looks like is getting more and more sophisticated as the attacks get more and more sophisticated."
Some firms stepping up
While some companies might not be keeping up with cyber risks, Bob Gordon, strategy advisor for the Canadian Cyber Threat Exchange, says others are taking the issue very seriously.

The cyber exchange is made up of big and small businesses that share information about cyber threats, including how hackers might attack and what evidence they may leave. Sharing this intelligence is a big help to smaller companies, Gordon says, because they often have fewer resources to pour into security.

Gordon says the exchange has attracted new members in recent months. He says it's a sign that businesses are starting to realize cyber security isn't just a tech concern, but rather a major risk that can impact consumer trust or even temporarily shut down operations in a worst-case scenario.
Cutler says calls to his cybersecurity firm are up by about 40 per cent — mostly from companies wanting to know how hackable they are and how they can prevent breaches.
Communauto was hit by a data breach — here’s what you need to know
Some companies have also stepped up prevention measures after breaches.

Communauto, for example, experienced a security incident earlier this year when it said an employee accessed customers' personal information. While a spokesperson said in an email that there's no evidence the stolen data was leaked, the company is still monitoring the dark web for it. Certain personal information will now be deleted or anonymized sooner, and access to customer data is now further restricted internally, the spokesperson said.
After its breach, Bell said it was investigating and had reached out to the RCMP's cyber crime unit. Staples said it was taking its breach "very seriously," and had also launched an investigation.
Cracking down with new rules
On top of those efforts, a new federal bill making its way through Parliament could bring tougher privacy rules.

Bill C-36 isn't yet law, but it would introduce stricter requirements about deleting customer data after it's been used — or whenever a person requests deletion — more measures about how it's stored and the ability to impose major fines in the millions of dollars if organizations don't follow the rules.

54:36The Value of Your Data and How to Protect It
Arnold says he's not sure stronger laws will have much impact.
"The big problem is, companies often just don't even think about this," he said.

If the issue isn't on their radar, the threat of greater fines won't move the needle according to Arnold, meaning education about some of the free or cheap resources available to businesses could be a better place to start.

items: AI's 'warning shot': Tech companies, experts raise fears of more rogue swarms after alarming Hugging Face hack

blocks.text: While Bauer says the new rules might not be perfect, they would up the ante for businesses to comply.
"I think that this is a wake up call for all businesses to start to think about how they handle … personal information and how they protect it."

articles.summary: ‘Ang mga tinanggal ng Senado sa ngalan ng paglaban sa korupsiyon ay hindi dapat palihim na ibalik sa bicam sa ngalan ng kompromiso,’ says Social Watch Philippines co-convenor Maria Victoria Raquiza

blocks.text: BUDGET WATCH. Social Watch Philippines holds a press conference as the Senate conducts plenary deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget on November 26, 2026.
Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring/Rappler
‘Ang mga tinanggal ng Senado sa ngalan ng paglaban sa korupsiyon ay hindi dapat palihim na ibalik sa bicam sa ngalan ng kompromiso,’ says Social Watch Philippines co-convenor Maria Victoria Raquiza

items: Social Watch Philippines wants civil society groups to attend the bicameral conference committee meeting in person to monitor the 2027 national budget discussions.
The group emphasizes the need for transparency, saying that major decisions were previously made off-camera despite livestreaming.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Budget watchdog Social Watch Philippines wants civil society groups to be present in person when the bicameral conference committee convenes to tackle the proposed 2027 national budget.

“Panawagan talaga natin…ay nando’n tayo mismo, on-site sa bicameral conference committee meeting para namo-monitor natin ang aktuwal na nangyayari,” Social Watch Philippines co-convenor Maria Victoria Raquiza said in a press conference on Thursday, November 26.
“Hindi ‘yong sa nangyari last year na livestreaming nga, open bicam nga, pero sa totoo lang, ang major decisions ay ginawa off-camera,” she added.

(Our appeal is for us to be allowed on-site at the bicameral conference committee meeting so we can monitor what’s actually happening. We don’t want a repeat of last year where there was livestreaming, it was supposedly an open bicam, but in reality, the major decisions were made off-camera.)
Raquiza also said advocates want to have a voice during the proceedings.

Following the Senate’s briefing with civil society organizations in October, Senator Ping Lacson invited them to join the 2027 budget bicam. He also floated the idea of keeping the meeting open even if bicam members ask for session suspensions.
Raquiza said the Senate must publicize 2027 budget amendments so that civil society groups can scrutinize these changes before the bicam meeting.

Among the changes introduced by the Senate finance committee is the realignment of P19.8 billion from government assistance programs, including the Medical Assistance Program and the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations, to augment funding for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth).
This boosted PhilHealth’s budget from P73 billion in the House version of the general appropriations bill (GAB) to P94.2 billion in the Senate committee report.
Social Watch Philippines noted that the updated figure still falls short of the P244-billion funding requirement of the state health insurer next year.

The group added that while the budget for health promotion went up from P485 million in the House GAB to P1.55 billion in the Senate version, it is still lower than the minimum 1% of the total Department of Health budget of P273 billion, supposedly violating the Universal Health Care Act.

The Senate also introduced a P97-billion reduction in the allocation for over 3,400 “non-compliant” projects of the Department of Public Works and Highways. The funding would be realigned to foreign-assisted infrastructure projects.
“Ang mga tinanggal ng Senado sa ngalan ng paglaban sa korupsiyon ay hindi dapat palihim na ibalik sa bicam sa ngalan ng kompromiso,” Raquiza said.
(What the Senate removed in the name of fighting corruption must not be stealthily returned during the bicam in the name of compromise.) – Rappler.com

articles.title: Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa
articles.summary: Lenacapavir, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection.

blocks.text: Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.
The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.
The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (£30) per person annually.
Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.
The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.
The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.
Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.
In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.
Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025.
The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection.

"These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday.
More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.
The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, plans to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.
It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.
South Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.
Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.

The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.
The UN aims to end Aids as a public health threat by 2030.

articles.title: Kilmar Ábrego García leaves for Spain. But the Trump administration got what it wanted
articles.summary: His departure ends a high-profile legal battle over due process and deportation, but leaves the Trump administration facing little accountability for its actions

blocks.text: Kilmar Ábrego García, the man illegally deported to his native El Salvador last year and whose immigration case spurred a 20-month-long battle with the Trump administration, arrived in Spain on Wednesday.
Trump administration officials and Ábrego García supporters are both claiming voluntary departure from the US to avoid deportation is a victory for their respective sides.
And they’re both sort of right, if such an ugly immigration spectacle can even be associated with concepts of victory.

On the one hand, Ábrego García has the relief of leaving the country seemingly his own accord, given that he was not going to be allowed to remain legally in the US. By going to Spain he avoids the pitfalls he had been facing. These were: being indefinitely detained inside a horrific prison in El Salvador, being sent to an unfamiliar African country where, if some other examples are anything to go by, he could end up in a prison or detained under harsh conditions in a secured hotel, indefinitely, or detained indefinitely in a US cell. His attorneys hope that, under a different president in the future, he may be allowed to return to the US.
And on the other hand, the Trump administration has won by getting rid of a high-profile immigrant they were determined not to let rest.

Ábrego García first arrived in the spotlight in March 2025, after the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador despite a US court order protecting him from being deported there, for his own safety. His case led to a nearly two-year-long “David and Goliath” type battle between him and the Trump administration, raising concerns about due process and constitutional rights, the separation of powers and accountability, the US government’s deals with countries for deportations and questionable federal prosecutions.

The entire case transcends the complicated character of Ábrego García himself. It has shown the world the lengths the Trump administration will go to when carrying out its anti-immigrant crackdown, and was an early example of the emboldened returning president defying federal court orders, to say nothing of fairness.

Ábrego García arrived in the US in 2011 from El Salvador without proper authorization and lived in Maryland for years, regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He married a US citizen and had a child with her.

In 2019, he was arrested outside a hardware store in Maryland after local police, relying on an informant and what his lawyers called “no evidence”, accused him of being a gang member. He was turned over to ICE, but a judge ruled he should not be deported to his country of origin due to danger in that country. He continued with his life with a valid work permit.

Then in March 2025, ICE officials arrested him while driving home with his five-year-old son. And after the Trump administration had struck a deal with the Salvadorian government, run by the rightwing and self-proclaimed “world’s coolest dictator”, Nayib Bukele, ICE quickly deported Ábrego García to El Salvador along with dozens of Venezuelan men in one of the most infamous immigration actions of the second Trump administration. As the flights were midair, a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to turn them back, due to accusations of due process violations. The administration defied the federal judge. The men arrived in El Salvador and were violently taken to a notorious anti-terrorism prison called Cecot, ostensibly to be detained indefinitely. Many claimed they were tortured, assaulted, raped and traumatized by the ordeal.

In court filings, the Trump administration admitted they had mistakenly deported Ábrego García due to an “administrative error”. After a lengthy legal battle, including input from the US supreme court, the administration was ordered to return him to the US. They initially refused, but eventually he was brought back in June 2025.

The Trump administration then quickly charged him with crimes relating to human smuggling, based on a traffic stop in Tennessee dating from 2022, and he was detained again. In parallel with the criminal case, this allowed ICE to begin attempts to remove him to a series of African countries. Ábrego García and his legal team resisted. Then, presumably concluding he had no future as a free man in the US, he offered to be removed to Costa Rica. The administration refused to send him to the Central American country and pushed to deport him to Africa.

The government denigrated him publicly as a “gang member”, “human trafficker”, “wife beater” and “child predator”. They pointed to accusations that he had allegedly abused his wife. He had never committed any of those crimes.
However, his human smuggling case was dismissed in May of this year, with the federal judge saying it was a “vindictive prosecution”.

Negotiations continued behind closed doors. A court order unsealed on Wednesday shows that the federal judge presiding over his case had ordered the Trump administration to effectuate Ábrego García’s voluntary departure from the US. The judge ordered the administration not to intervene in his departure. On Tuesday, it was announced he was leaving the US voluntarily, but to Europe, not Central America. He duly arrived in Spain’s capital, Madrid, on Wednesday morning with his wife. Competing claims of victory broke out from Ábrego García’s supporters and the Trump administration.

“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this administration’s constant persecution,” said Senator Chris Van Hollen, who visited Ábrego García in El Salvador and pushed for his return.

“We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Ábrego García has self-deported from the United States to Spain,” said homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin, using a favored Trump administration phrase when people leave the country specifically to avoid deportation.

The years-long and tired narrative of the “good” immigrant versus “bad” immigrant has only helped immigration hardliners justify the propping up of an aggressive enforcement system that targets all and tramples on due process rights, regardless of criminal history.

One of Ábrego García’s attorneys said he is leaving the US because he thought he was “never going to get a fair shake” under the Trump administration. They aren’t wrong. But this is purely by design. And his is one case of thousands in which people are not getting a fair shake under an immigration system that resembles more closely punishment than merely civil immigration proceedings.

Ábrego García “humiliated” the Trump administration “because he exposed their failures and beat them in court; even all the way to the Supreme Court”, immigration policy analyst Aaron Reichlin-Melnick said on social media. “For that, they tried everything to punish him. And they lost, again and again. Now, they lose a final time: he leaves as a free man.”

But the Trump administration does have reason to feel smug. No one in the administration has been held responsible, in any significant way, for the catastrophic Cecot ordeal, its violation of court orders and the alleged torture they helped facilitate. And no one is being held responsible for wielding an immigration enforcement system targeting thousands – although the midterms “blue wave” for the Democrats was certainly a signal of increasing voter opposition.
Ábrego García’s departure to Spain means perhaps no more than the closing of a very disturbing chapter in an ongoing horror story.

articles.title: Ministers ‘fail to make case’ for Heathrow third runway, MPs report says
articles.summary:
Transport committee says policy papers show expanding airport would fall short of pledges on economy and climate

Ministers have “failed to make the case” for

blocks.text: Ministers have “failed to make the case” for a third runway at Heathrow, according to a damning report by MPs.

The Commons transport committee said on Thursday that the detailed policy papers laid out by the government showed that expanding the London airport would fall short of pledges on the economy and climate.
The chair of the committee, Ruth Cadbury, said plans for the third runway “should be grounded” and the government needed to “go back to the drawing board”.
Heathrow is seeking to build a third runway and expand its terminals at a cost of about £33bn to almost double passenger numbers, adding up to 276,000 flights a year.

The committee was tasked with examining the government’s Heathrow expansion national policy statement (HENPS) – but Cadbury there was a “complete disjoint” between the plans and a lack of wider aviation strategy.

The report found that the case was not made across the four tests ministers had set for expansion – that it deliver growth across the country, without harmful impacts on climate, noise and air quality.

The report said that while the government was designating the runway as a critical national project, the economic growth projections in modelling commissioned by the Department for Transport were a fraction of previous estimates – a 0.05% boost to GDP rather than o.5% – and did not justify the designation.

It said that expansion was “not currently compatible with the UK’s legally binding climate targets, and it seems impossible for the additional carbon dioxide emissions it will generate to be offset elsewhere in the economy”.
MPs said that the case for “potential compatibility rests too heavily on delivery of technologies” such as greener fuel and carbon capture which was “nowhere near the necessary trajectories”.

The committee said it “did not agree that reversing hard-won improvements in local air quality is an acceptable consequence” and the statement did not take account of World Health Organization guidelines or emerging pollutants.
It added that the government still needed to set out how commitments relating to noise mitigation were “secured and delivered”.

The report also said it was “highly concerning that there are no clear, committed, funded plans in place to improve surface public transport to an expanded Heathrow”, concluding: “Expansion should not go ahead at any price, or at any cost to society or the environment.”

Cadbury said: “Our report should be a wake-up call for ministers. We found that the government should have set out its overall strategy for aviation before publishing the draft HENPS. It did not do so and now it has failed to make the case for Heathrow expansion.
“Plans for a third runway should be grounded for now and the government should go back to the drawing board before proceeding any further.”

The government under Keir Starmer had strongly backed a third runway, particularly the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves. However, Andy Burnham has historically opposed the third runway and the scheme appears in doubt.
Responding to the committee’s report, Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, said the third runway still had strong support.

“The overwhelming weight of evidence and support remains strongly behind Heathrow expansion. Trade unions, business groups, airlines, regional airports, senior cabinet ministers and the majority of MPs back expansion because they recognise it is vital to creating quality jobs and supporting long-term economic growth across the UK,” Woldbye said.
Heathrow on Wednesday released polling showing three-quarters of Labour MPs backed the expansion plan.
