articles.title: [OPINION] Slowly but surely, Washington drifts away from Asia
articles.summary: The US security relationship with the region has also come under stress

blocks.text: What a difference a year makes!

When he made his whirlwind trip to Kuala Lumpur to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in late October 2025, Donald Trump had Asian leaders bowing and scraping before him like feudal vassals. He had imposed punitive tariffs on all the countries of East Asia, and none of their leaders dared to complain lest he take umbrage and raise the tariffs several notches higher.

Cambodian President Hun Manet told Trump he would nominate him for the Nobel Peace Prize for “ending” his country’s border war with Thailand, and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, who had done the heavy lifting to bring Cambodia and Thailand to the table, graciously let him to take center stage and take all the glory for the fragile success of the negotiations.
Returning a year later, Trump was a significantly diminished figure.

He met briefly with ASEAN heads of state in Manila last week, the most significant news out of which were his announcing the conclusion of a controversial bilateral trade agreement with Thailand that was, in fact, still being negotiated — as well as his praise for the late president Ferdinand Marcos, the father and namesake of the incumbent president and the dictator who ruled the country from 1966 to 1986, saying the contemporary Marcos had “good genetics.”

Instead of cheers, Trump’s coming evoked jeers, with student-led mass demonstrations against the plan to include the Philippines in the US State Department initiative Pax Silica, which would incorporate the country into an artificial intelligence global supply chain aimed at countering a parallel initiative by Beijing.

There was no bowing and scraping this time. The assembled leaders probably smiled with secret satisfaction that the US Supreme Court had ruled in February of this year that Trump’s punitive tariffs against ASEAN and other countries were illegal; that he was trapped in a “forever war” with Iran; and that he had been dealt a massive blow by the results of the November elections, which saw the Democrats gain control of the Senate and House by very large margins, effectively rendering him a lame-duck president.

As in previous years, China was a massive but unseen presence at the ASEAN summit. China has long been the number one trading partner of the Southeast Asian countries, its trade with ASEAN surpassing $1 trillion in 2025, with ASEAN being in deficit by $244 billion.
It has, however, trailed the US in terms of investments. Cumulative investment from the US in ASEAN hit $557 billion in 2025, while that of China was $199 billion.

However, while China’s economic relations with the region have remained relatively stable, things have been very rocky between ASEAN and the US under Trump. There is, for one, the administration’s push to impose punitive tariffs, motivated partly by strong suspicion that China has been using some countries, like Vietnam, as platforms to export Chinese goods to the US. Then, there is Washington’s drive to get information technology firms such as Taiwan’s TSMC and Korea’s Samsung to invest in facilities in the US owing to their being currently located in geopolitically vulnerable areas.

The pressure on IT companies to locate away from East Asia can only increase with the fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ‘s marital scandal, with the claim of US intelligence agencies that the Singapore-based cloud computing provider Megaspeed, of which Alice Huang was the CEO, has been a source of unauthorized shipments of advanced Nvidia chips to Beijing that had been banned by the US.

The US security relationship with the region has also come under stress. The Philippines has been the US’s main ally in the region, yet Filipino officials have been dissatisfied with what they consider Washington’s purely rhetorical denunciations of clashes between the Chinese and Philippine coast guard vessels in the South China Sea. Southeast Asian governments have also noticed how the Trump administration has not given clear signs of coming to Taiwan’s defense in the event of a China-Taiwan clash, in contrast to the Biden administration’s explicit commitment.

Also noted was Trump’s failure to back Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi when she asserted Japan would be involved in defending Taiwan in event of hostilities breaking out between Taipei and Beijing. In fact, there’s been a sharp decline in US warships transiting through the Taiwan Straits, with the number falling by some 56% from transits during the Biden administration, leading the rightwing Heritage Foundation to anxiously assert that “there is a real risk that American allies and partners — let alone Beijing — could misinterpret the Trump administration’s strategy as a retreat on American commitments. Perceptions of that kind, once formed, can become difficult to reverse.”

It has also not escaped Southeast Asia’s governments that Trump has been eager to have a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un to lower tensions on the Korean peninsula, and that, despite the geoeconomic rivalry between Washington and Beijing, Trump wants to establish a friendly personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jin Ping. During Xi’s visit to Washington last September, Trump pulled out all the stops to butter up the Chinese leader, just as Xi gave him full honors during his visit to Shenzen to attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ last week.

Many commentators have said that unlike his predecessors, Trump’s attitude towards ASEAN and other Asian states has been “transactional” instead of being anchored on longstanding ideological and security considerations, pointing to his levying punitive tariffs on friends and foes alike as well as to his hectoring countries hosting US bases to raise their contribution to their defense to five per cent of GDP.

What many observers fail to note is that rather than just stemming from a businessman’s whims, Trump’s attitude is rooted in the reality that the American economic and military presence in the Asia Pacific is becoming structurally unsustainable for the US.

A legacy of the US drive to defeat Japan during the Second World War, the US bases from Korea to the Philippines were repurposed during the Cold War to contain China and the Soviet Union. In return for their political loyalty in the struggle against Communism, the US not only provided security but also gave Japan first and later South Korea and Taiwan, very liberal entry for their goods into the US market while allowing them to maintain high levels of tariff and non-tariff protection against US products, allowing all three to achieve high-speed industrial growth.

In the late eighties and early nineties, the so-called “tiger cubs” of Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Singapore took advantage of the same liberal access to the US market while maintaining tariff walls against US products. From the early nineties on, China took the same route, eventually displacing its Asian neighbors as the source of cheap manufactures for the US market.

But China took the so-called Asian export-industrialization model one step further: it encouraged US manufacturers to relocate to China to take advantage of labor that was five per cent of its price in the US. It was an offer that many of America’s big name corporations could not resist, with Apple leading the way, contracting most it manufacturing operations to Foxconn and other firms based in Shenzen. By 2017, Apple admitted to creating 4.8 million jobs in China, or double the number it had created in the US.
Thus, before Trump’s first term in office, the US was suffering a triple whammy in its relations with East Asia.

First, it was running massive trade deficits with almost all the East Asian countries. Second, it was being deindustrialized as US firms moved their labor-intensive operations to China, even as cheap Chinese-made goods flooded the US market and rendered those firms that had not relocated non-competitive. And, third, it was spending over $11 billion a year to maintain its massive base structure in Japan, Korea, the Philippines, and Singapore. It was largely this unsustainable economic and military deficit that lay behind the radical reorientation of US strategic policy represented by the National Security Strategy 2025 that was released late last year.

In the 80 years prior to NSS 2025, Washington’s “Grand Strategy” was to meet challenges anywhere in the world that posed a threat to the national interest of the United States, and towards this end, it built a formidable military machine and system of forward bases, most of which were in the Asia Pacific. In the four decades between the late forties and late eighties, the strategy was justified by the ideology of containing Communism and supposedly promoting democracy in Washington’s client states.

The fall of the Soviet Union, followed by the dynamic ascent of East Asia, the rapid deindustrialization of the US economy, and the 2008 Global Financial Crisis made the old Cold War image of the US being Atlas carrying the world on his shoulders increasingly anachronistic to many Americans. Even as the Republicans and Democratic party elites remained stuck in a time warp, committed to the old Containment strategy in post-Containment times, Trump was able to seize on a large section of the population’s feeling that the US could no longer shoulder the costs of a dated strategy and wield it as a militant slogan that had popular resonance: that US allies in Asia and Europe had “taken advantage of US generosity” to build robust economies and saw the US military umbrella as a great excuse to spend very little for their own security.

blocks.caption: [OPINION] US National Security Strategy 2025: An iconoclastic document

blocks.text: The trenchant introduction of NSS 2025 was definitely one-sided, but it also contained a great deal of truth:

After the end of the Cold War, American foreign policy elites convinced themselves that permanent American domination of the entire world was in the best interests of our country. Yet the affairs of other countries are our concern only if their activities directly threaten our interests…Our elites badly miscalculated America’s willingness to shoulder forever global burdens to which the American people saw no connection to the national interest. They overestimated America’s ability to fund, simultaneously, a massive welfare-regulatory-administrative state alongside a massive military, diplomatic, intelligence, and foreign aid complex. They placed hugely misguided and destructive bets on globalism and so-called “free trade” that hollowed out the very middle class and industrial base on which American economic and military preeminence depend. They allowed allies and partners to offload the cost of their defense onto the American people, and sometimes to suck us into conflicts and controversies central to their interests but peripheral or irrelevant to our own. And they lashed American policy to a network of international institutions, some of which are driven by outright anti-Americanism and many by a transnationalism that explicitly seeks to dissolve individual state sovereignty. In sum, not only did our elites pursue a fundamentally undesirable and impossible goal, in doing so they undermined the very means necessary to achieve that goal: the character of our nation upon which its power, wealth, and decency were built.

NSS 2025 made it clear that under Trump, building a bastion of economic and military power in the western hemisphere would be Washington’s priority, and this was underlined by his brazen words about annexing Greenland, his implicit threat to take over the Panama Canal, and his kidnaping in broad daylight of Venezuelan President Francisco Maduro early this year.

While the NSS did say the US had a strong stake in the Asia Pacific, the stress was on reversing past policies towards China that were based on wrong economic assumptions by four successive administrations — assumptions that led to policies that has turned China into a “near peer competitor” of the United States. The priority was to “rebalance America’s economic relationship with China, prioritizing reciprocity and fairness to restore American economic independence.” Keeping the status quo on Taiwan is mentioned as is keeping the sea lanes in the South China Sea open, but it is formulaic. As for Southeast Asia, there is no mention at all of mainland and island Southeast Asia as a specific area of interest.
Will the Legions Sail Home?

Most Southeast Asian elites have taken very seriously NSS 2025’s message that their region is now of secondary, if not marginal, interest to Washington, and the Japanese and Korean establishments now have very serious doubts about the solidity of the US commitment to their defense if they are not seen as making progress in meeting Washington’s demand that they spend at least five per cent of their GDP on their defense and defray most of the costs of maintaining the US bases they host.

The realization is seeping in among the elites of the region that relying on the naval power and offshore bases of a power some 7000 miles away to provide protection is unsustainable in the long run, if not in the medium term. That the legions of America will eventually go home, as did Rome’s legions in Britain in the third century CE, is no longer dismissed as improbable.

Contributing to the apprehensions of the Asian elites has been Washington’s failure to subdue Iran after nine months of warfare. If a small country like Iran could successfully resist a massive joint US-Israeli to overthrow the their government, would not a bigger power be much more difficult for the US to take on? Also, the Asian elites know that the war has hardened the opposition of the American right, middle, and left to armed US intervention anywhere in the world. In other words, their staying power is no longer guaranteed by American military power.

In contrast, Asian elites have seen how simply by standing aloof from the Iran conflict, and allowing the US to expend its military resources and legitimacy in a war that has served mainly Israel’s interests, China has seen its status grow throughout the region. Winning the battle for influence without a fight might be an exaggerated way of putting it, but that is essentially what China has derived out of Trump’s ill-advised adventure in Iran. For Asia’s elites, the lesson is clear: China, not the US, is here to stay, so it is best to come to terms with this reality.

Here, it might be useful for Asian governments to look three decades back. There was a time, the 1990’s, when the governments of ASEAN, led by Malaysia’s Mohammad Mahathir, promoted the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) as a site where conflicts among countries in the region could be settled via diplomacy and not by force. It had its flaws, but the ARF was a step in the direction of a collective security system.

Yet the US boycotted the founding meeting of the ARF in Bangkok in July 1994 to register Washington’s disapproval of ASEAN’s ambitions. Then President Bill Clinton, in fact, explicitly denigrated the ARF and other multilateral security initiatives, saying they “are a way to supplement our alliances and forward military presence, not supplant them.” When the Asian Financial Crisis hit the region in 1997, Washington used it not only to try to resubordinate the ASEAN economies but also to delegitimize the ARF.

Today, with the US’s retreat from Asia, the ASEAN Regional Forum might be an idea whose time has finally come. The question is, does the current crop of ASEAN leaders have the courage and imagination to seize this opportunity to create what could eventually become a collective security order where governments from all over East Asia can come together to settle their differences?

And the US? For all his contradictions, haphazard behavior, and narcissistic tendencies, Donald Trump’s influence on the direction of the relationship between East Asia and the US must not be underestimated. His retreat from the region, justified and promoted by NSS 2025, may one day lead historians to compare him to Richard Nixon, the unlikely Cold Warrior who made peace with China and brought it into the mainstream of global politics and eventually into the global economy.

Trump dumped an obsolete Grand Strategy of global hegemony that the US could no longer sustain but which continued to command the adherence of both the fossilized Republican and Democratic Party elites, like Dick Cheney and Joe Biden, who knew what toll it was taking but lacked the nerve to abandon it. Indeed, the interminable war on Iran to which Trump was maneuvered by Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu simply confirmed for his MAGA base the correctness of the isolationist thrust of NSS 2025.

But what if a Democrat is elected president in 2028? Would they not bring back the old Grand Strategy? I’m very sure they won’t. In fact, the Cold War Democrats owe Trump the favor of doing the dirty work of cutting off a diseased organ that they did not have the guts to hack off. – Rappler.com
Walden Bello is co-chair of the Board of the Bangkok-based Focus on the Global South and co-editor, with Don Kalb, of Backlash: The Global Rise of the Radical Right (Pluto: 2026).

articles.title: Duterte defense cites 'bugalbugal' for 'I-will-kill-you' rhetoric
articles.summary: Former President Rodrigo Duterte"s lawyers are asking the International Criminal Court (ICC) to consider Visayan culture and language in assessing the profanity and alleged threats he made amid his…

blocks.text: Former President Rodrigo Duterte’s lawyers are asking the International Criminal Court (ICC) to consider Visayan culture and language in assessing the profanity and alleged threats he made amid his drug war.
These statements attributed to Duterte during the war on drugs include “Papatayin kita," or "I will kill you" in English.

In an expanded section in its pre-trial brief, the defense cited “bugalbugal”, which it described as “a familiar Cebuano practice of verbal play involving teasing, mockery and deliberately irreverent humor.”

Lead defense counsel Peter Haynes said bugalbugal’s meaning depends on shared cultural understanding and the relationship between the speaker and audience, where words that may appear hostile in isolation could instead be understood as playful ridicule.
It also cited studies of Cebuano humor which, according to the filing, identify “hyperbole, ambiguity, and departures from literal meaning” as common features.

“These linguistic insights, and contemporary commentary applying bugalbugal to Mr Duterte’s speeches, provide grounds for examining whether apparently literal threats conveyed exaggeration, ridicule, or theatrical intimidation to their intended audience,” Haynes said.
'I will kill you' not literal
The defense’s filing argued that Duterte’s language must be assessed within its linguistic and cultural setting rather than a literal reading of individual statements.

“To Western ears, and indeed to listeners outside of Davao, Mr Duterte’s rhetoric directed towards those involved in producing, trafficking or even using drugs, may be objectively shocking,” Haynes said.
The defense said the question for the judges is whether those statements carried the same meaning for the audiences Duterte was addressing.

The defense specifically raised whether phrases such as “I will kill you” or “Papatayin kita” are used in Visayan and Cebuano speech as an emphatic expression without necessarily showing an intent to murder.
Haynes also said Duterte used “jocular ridicule” in public speeches to connect with crowds, “particularly those familiar with his Visayan manner of speaking”.
Other studies cited by the defense examined the use of swearing for solidarity and emphasis and Duterte’s multilingual style of political speech.
Official transcripts, Haynes added, “document audience laughter in response to his threatening language.”

“These reactions are relevant to whether particular passages were understood as familiar theatrical exaggeration rather than instructions to kill, particularly when considered alongside his stated use of threats to frighten offenders into abandoning illegal activities.”
'Bugoy' hard talk
Duterte’s lawyers also argued that the former president cultivated a “deliberate bugoy,” or “tough guy,” image to deter or scare offenders into reform.
Citing academic literature, lead counsel Peter Haynes highlighted “paternalistic cussing”, or language that expresses authority, concern, or reprimand abrasively.
“These studies identify the meanings and purposes of his ‘hard talk’, distinct from any intention to commit the charged crimes,” the filing stated.

Haynes claimed that prosecutors are selectively quoting inflammatory portions of presidential speeches while leaving out statements that qualified the use of force or warned police officers against abuse.
For the defense, “neutralization” does not mean an indiscriminate order to kill but rather “a standard measure subject to legal constraints.”

“The Prosecution invites the Trial Chamber to interpret the term as synonymous with killing, thereby suggesting that it gave officers on the ground carte blanche to eliminate their targets during police operations,” the defense stated.
Reiterating the defense

Haynes’ arguments on Duterte’s manner of speech reiterated what the former president’s previous counsel, Nicholas Kaufman, said amid the charges confirmation hearing: “neutralization” denotes “lawful restraint”.
On the sidelines of that hearing, former presidential spokesperson Salvador Panelo insisted that many of the former president’s drug war statements were hyperbole or exaggeration.
Filipino law experts have weighed in on that aspect, with some emphasizing the importance of insider witnesses who could explain how “neutralize” was interpreted among police ranks.
The Office of the Prosecutor has told Trial Chamber III that insider witnesses are on its List of Witnesses.
The first five prosecution witnesses are expected to testify before the court once the prosecution and the Common Legal Representatives of the Victims (CLRV) finish their opening statements.
Duterte’s charges of crimes against humanity will be heard by Trial Chamber III from November 30 onwards. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Health issues delay trial of Berlin woman accused of spying for Russia
articles.summary: Prosecutors say the defendant used her political and military contacts to provide information on German defense and aid deliveries to Ukraine. Her arrest in January sparked a diplomatic row between…

image.caption: The espionage suspect, whose face is pixelated, was seen in a Ukraine conference in Berlin in December 2025Image: Ukraine presidency

blocks.text: The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman on charges of spying for Russia due to start Thursday was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.
The arrest of the 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman triggered a diplomatic clash between Berlin and Moscow.
Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power.
Her full name has not been released due to German privacy laws.
She was arrested on January 21 and put in pretrial detention.
What is Ilona W. accused of?

She is accused of having contacts with current and former German defense ministry officials to provide information about defense industry locations, drone tests and planned drone deliveries to Ukraine.
She was also said to have been in contact with a man, her alleged handler, working for Russian intelligence at the Russian Embassy in Berlin since at least November 2023, prosecutors say.

On several occasions, she allegedly helped her contact at the embassy attend political events in Berlin under a false identity in order to establish contacts there. She is also suspected of having compiled background information on participants in high-level political events.
German spy chief warns of rising Russia threat
Berlin summoned the alleged handler, who was identified by Der Spiegel magazine as the embassy's deputy military attache, over the incident and expelled him from Germany.
Ilona W. led an advocacy group for years that called for international cooperation, focusing particularly oon German, Russian, Ukrainian relations.
In addition to her advocacy work, she also ran a small marketing agency.
Both positions allowed her to be active in Berlin's political circles and provided her with connections within military.
Russia rejects the allegations
The Russian ambassador to Berlin, Sergei Nechayev, denied the allegations this week.

"The Russian Embassy has no connection whatsoever to this woman, and even if she happened to cross paths with one of our representatives, perhaps at some reception, that means absolutely nothing," Nechayev told news agency AFP.
Why Berlin remains an espionage hot spot
He also said "he may have seen her himself at an event."
"But she is not a Russian citizen and, as far as we are aware, has no ties to Russia. She is a German and Ukrainian citizen, and, frankly, we do not associate with such individuals here," he said.
The trial is expected to run until May 2027.

articles.title: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling
articles.summary: A landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) convicted Myanmar of genocide against its Rohingya minority.

blocks.text: Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has said in his first public comments since the court decision.
The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.
Myanmar denied committing genocide, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups. It is the first state to have been found in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
Min Aung Hlaing said "the term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation", state media report.

"Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," the country's coup leader-turned-president said at a meeting on Wednesday, according to state media.
The statement did not specify which parts of the ruling the country objects to.
The genocide case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

The ICJ determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.
The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.
The ICJ ordered Myanmar to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure should be determined at a later date.
The court also ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and immediately investigate those suspected of breaking the Convention.
But the ICJ does not have the power to enforce these demands. Instead it has to rely on the UN Security Council and political pressure to make its rulings stick.
While the ruling was largely symbolic, it was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups who have long called attention to the suffering faced by the Rohingya.
More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ICJ ruling, and the UK has announced sanctions on several senior Myanmar military leaders.

Myanmar has been devastated by civil war since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup to oust civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. The move turned Myanmar into an international pariah, and its military regime has faced sweeping international sanctions.
Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to reintegrate Myanmar into the international community, but it remains largely shut out of key diplomatic arenas.

articles.title: UK net migration falls to 77,000, lowest since 1997 excluding Covid pandemic – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Net migration fell in the year ending June 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics

The Liberal Democrats are saying the UK needs a proper plan for immigration. This is from the…

blocks.text: Net migration down to just 77,000 in year ending June 2026, ONS says
Net migration in the year ending June 2026 fell to just 77,000, the Office for National Statistics says.
In its report just out, it says:

double quotation markOur provisional estimates show long-term international net migration stood at 77,000 in year ending (YE) June 2026 and has more than halved compared with YE June 2025 (updated to 204,000). Excluding the coronavirus (Covid-19) pandemic, when international travel restrictions were in place, this is the lowest recorded net migration estimate since 1997 (when we used surveys to measure migration rather than administrative data).

Before the 2010 general election, David Cameron said he wanted to get net migration below 100,000, and successive Tory leaders also repeated that target. Sixteen years later, after a period when annual net migration rose close to one million, the Cameron target has finally been achieved.
Key events

items: 13m agoTories say net migration still too high
16m agoMore Britons leaving UK than coming or returning, ONS figures show
33m agoHow ONS explains steep fall in net migration
46m agoHow net migration ends up at 77,000, according to ONS
51m agoNet migration down to just 77,000 in year ending June 2026, ONS says

blocks.text: The Liberal Democrats are saying the UK needs a proper plan for immigration. This is from the party’s asylum and immigration spokesperson, Paul Kohler.

double quotation markBritain needs to regain control of its immigration system after the chaos of Brexit. Yet sixteen years after David Cameron’s ‘tens of thousands’ pledge, six prime ministers and ten home secretaries have overseen wild swings in immigration numbers with net migration now set to fall below zero. Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services.
Tories say net migration still too high
The Conservatives say net migration is still too high. Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, has issued this statement about today’s figures.

double quotation markThe fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level. British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour’s high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high. British families are left to pay for it with lower wages, longer waits for a GP appointment and homes they cannot afford. Mass low-skilled immigration must end completely as it is bad for our economy and corrosive to our society. Labour’s shameful U-turn on indefinite leave to remain throws open the door to early permanent settlement, benefits, and citizenship for low-skill migrants. Conservatives will take settlement away from those not making a contribution and they will be made to leave – no matter what Labour has promised them.
More Britons leaving UK than coming or returning, ONS figures show
More British nationals are estimated to have left the UK in the year to June 2026 (245,000) than moved to the country (109,000), the Press Association reports. PA says:

double quotation markIt was a similar picture for nationals from “EU-plus countries” – covering the 27 members of the EU plus Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland – with a higher number emigrating from the UK (124,000) than immigrating (79,000), according to the ONS. By contrast, more people from outside the EU moved to the UK in the year to June (550,000) than left (292,000). The number of British nationals leaving the UK is estimated to have fallen slightly in recent years, with 245,000 in the year to June 2026, 251,000 in the year to June 2025 and 257,000 in the year to June 2024.
This is from Sunder Katwala, director of British Future, a thinktank focusing on race and immigration issues, on today’s net migration figures.

double quotation markFigures showing net migration falling to its lowest level since 1997 will come as a surprise to most of the public, who thought immigration was still rising. It must now be time for the political and media debate to catch up and start a new phase of the debate about what happens next. With numbers expected to keep falling, the government needs to ask what a sustainable level of immigration is, and how will they achieve it. Whatever their views on the right level of immigration, any party that is serious about the issue should be able to commit to an annual ‘immigration budget’ process setting out trends, expectations and choices. Andy Burnham’s Labour government could aim for a net migration ceiling of 250,000. But at the level announced today, the UK population is now shrinking – so a medium-term aim should be to stabilise net migration with a floor of 100,000 to avoid population decline. Reform and the Conservatives, who want net emigration, should set out what they would cut and how to manage the impacts.

Katwala is right about the public not realising that immigration is falling. Polling published just yesterday shows that many voters wrongly believe immigration is still rising, and that Reform UK supporters are most likely to think this.
How ONS explains steep fall in net migration

And this is how the ONS explains the fall in net migration in its report. Mainly it is because of a steep fall in the number of non-EU nationals coming to the UK, it says. This is a consequence of visa rules becoming much stricter. The last Conservative government first tightened the rules very significantly, and this crackdown has largely continued under Labour.
Another factor is more Britons, and EU nationals, leaving the UK than entering or returning.
The ONS says:

double quotation markWhile people arriving from outside the EU continued to add to the population, non-EU+ provisional net migration fell to 258,000 in YE [year ending] June 2026, down from 379,000 a year earlier. The fall in the net migration of non-EU+ nationals was the main reason for the latest decrease in overall net migration. It was driven by non-EU+ immigration falling by more than 100,000, while emigration remained broadly stable. Compared with YE June 2025, non-EU+ arrivals for work-related reasons fell by 45,000, asylum-related reasons fell by 19,000 and study-related reasons fell by 33,000. Unlike non-EU+ nationals, more British and EU+ nationals left the UK long term than arrived. Provisional net migration for British nationals remained broadly stable at negative 137,000, while EU+ net migration was negative 45,000 and has been negative since YE June 2022.
And this chart from the ONS report shows how immigration, emigration and net migration figures have changed since 2012.

blocks.text: Government set to publish further documents relating to Peter Mandelson's appointment as ambassador to US

We should get the latest Mandelson documents (see 9.17am) around lunchtime. The Commons authorities have announced there will be two ministerial statements today. At around 11.30pm Polly Billington, an energy minister, will make a statement about the latest price cap announced by Ofgem yesterday. And, about an hour later, Dan Jarvis, the security minister, will make a statement described as an “update on the government response to the Peter Mandelson humble address motion”.
Sam Coates from Sky News has posted this on social media about what the new documents might reveal.

double quotation markIn today’s Mandelson files, I’m expecting a revealing look into the desperate attempts by the civil service to manage the political curveball they’d been thrown by Keir Starmer and Morgan McSweeny. Mandelson was a political appointment, pretty much forced through by No 10 with nobody listening to the warnings. Keir Starmer’s team were not interested in the problems with this appointment. So I believe you’ll see: ⁠ civil service emails about how to manage the conflict of interest with his shares in Global Counsel. Emails to Peter Mandelson as official tried - as was their job - to help him at the height of the crisis. And potentially how Mandelson was helping official figures directly with Global Counsel outside of the watchful eye of the diplomatic service. Mandelson denies wrongdoing
Ministers to publish further details of UK-EU deals, including confirmation of 'Farage penalty' clause if future government scraps agreement
Good morning. On Friday last week Andy Burnham was in Brussels to announce a reset deal with the EU. Today the debate will be revived as we get to read the small print.

We are getting three documents that should help experts assess the merits, or otherwise, of the deal. They are: the text of the legislation implementing the deal, formally known as the European partnership bill, but which ministers are calling the cutting costs bill; the legal text of the deal on food standards, which runs about 200 pages; and the legal text of the deal on emissions trading.

Faisal Islam, the BBC’s economics editor, has more here on what the legal text will show. He says it will confirm that the food deal has “a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal”. Termination clauses like this are not unusual in trade deals, but this one has been dubbed the “Farage clause” because it is partly inspired by the EU’s worry about Reform UK winning the next election and ripping up the deal. It could be called the Badenoch clause too, because the Tories also want to scrap the deal, but Farage is better known in Brussels, where he is considered a more formidable enemy than the Tory leader.

The government says its European partnership bill will “save industry millions by cutting red tape, lifting bans on iconic British exports, and exempting £6.5bn of British exports from EU carbon taxes”.
But the Conservatives are claiming any savings for customers are minimal. Here is an extract from the news release issued overnight.

double quotation markAnalysis by the Conservatives of the government’s own estimates shows that the savings from the sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal will amount to just pennies on everyday essentials, despite Andy Burnham promising the deal would bring down food prices. Beef prices have risen by 27.8 per cent since Labour took office, adding £1.22 to a pack of beef mince. Yet the government’s SPS deal would save shoppers just over 1p on a £5.60 pack. Pork prices have increased by 9.6 per cent, adding 29p to a pack of pork loin steaks, while the deal would cut the price by barely 1p. A six-pack of tomatoes would become just half a penny cheaper, while a head of broccoli would fall by less than a third of a penny. Currently half of all the pickled gherkins Britain imports come from the EU, yet on the government’s figures its EU deal will take just over half a penny off a £1.40 jar of gherkins. However, this would be on top of the government’s generous 4p cut announced at the budget.

If you don’t fancy reading 200 pages of legal text, there might be some more juicy documents coming from the government today when it publishes a fresh tranche of documents required by the humble address on Peter Mandelson. These are the papers relating to his appointment as ambassador to the US. Most documents have already been released but some – particularly those relating to what Mandelson told No 10 when it asked specifically about his links to Jeffrey Epstein – were held back at the request of the police (who are still pondering whether to charge him with misconduct in public office in relation to leaks to Epstein). Now the government is able to release a further tranche. They will come at some point today, but we are not sure when.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.25am: Karin Smyth, the health minister, speaks at the NHS Alliance conference. Sir Jim Mackey, the outgoing NHS England chief executive, is also speaking, at 1.30pm.
9.30am: The Office for National Statistics publishes the latest net immigration figures. At the same time, the Home Office is publishing its latest quarterly asylum figures.
9.30am: The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government publishes its latest homelessness figures.
9.30am: The ONS publishes figures for young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).
Morning: Kemi Badenoch is on a visit in Sidcup.
Morning: Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, is on a visit in Plymouth.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

Around lunchtime: The government is due to publish its European partnership bill, the legislation enacting the three deals with the EU announced last week. The government is also publishing the legal text of two of those deals, the food standards (SPS, or sanitary and phytosanitary) one, and the emissions trading one.
2pm: Friends, relatives and colleagues will attend a memorial service for Ann Widdecombe at Westminster Cathedral.
And at some point today the government is due to release those Mandelson papers.

articles.title: Norse Atlantic Airways suspends all flights as it makes urgent funding plea
articles.summary:
Norwegian airline says its finances are ‘critical’ and it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term backing

Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights and said it will…

blocks.text: Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights and said it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term financing urgently.

The Norwegian airline, which operates long-haul flights around the world including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia, announced it was on the brink on Thursday morning, a day after warning that its finances were “critical”.
The airline, like many worldwide, is reeling from surging jet fuel prices that have sent costs skywards since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, as well as hitting consumer confidence.
In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Norse said: “If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board’s ​intention to file for bankruptcy.”

It said it was still looking at options to secure short-term financing and was in discussion with investors regarding a possible takeover but said: “There can be no assurance that a viable solution will ​be found.”
Norse was founded in 2021 as it sought to step into the space vacated by Norwegian Air, whose attempts to fly budget long-haul were also abandoned as unviable.
Despite that, Norse revived the transatlantic routes, with a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 Dreamliners and ​many former Norwegian staff.

Norse said in the summer it was exploring a potential sale or merger, and set out on a cost-cutting programme called Project Falcon to save $50m (£38m), including axing about 75 jobs. It also moved its headquarters out of Norway to cheaper offices in Latvia, while the founder and chief executive, Bjørn Tore Larsen, left the airline.
It said it “sincerely apologises to its passengers for the inconvenience caused by this situation”.
after newsletter promotion
UK routes affected include London Gatwick to Orlando, Bangkok and Cape Town. A winter service from Manchester to Thailand was due to start operating next month.

articles.title: Hamas political official and wife among eight Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza
articles.summary: The killings are the latest from a series of near daily attacks by Israel against what it says are Hamas targets.

blocks.text: A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.
Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.
A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.
Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.

In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.
In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month.
"No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.

The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.
On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Net migration to UK falls to lowest level since 1997 excluding pandemic
articles.summary: Latest figures show difference between number of people arriving and leaving UK was ⁠77,000 in ​year ‌to ‌June

blocks.text: Net migration across the UK has fallen to its lowest level since 1997 with the exclusion of the years of the Covid pandemic.
Figures released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) and the Home Office show that the difference between people arriving and leaving the UK was ⁠77,000 in ⁠the ​year ‌to ‌June ‌2026.
The ONS figures cover the year ending June 2026, down from the previous estimate of 171,000 for 2025 and a peak of 944,000 in 2023. Annual net migration to the UK in 1997 was 48,000.
The drop has been driven by policies pushed through by Labour and Conservative governments.

Home Office visa data from January to June 2026 shows visa grants to international students fell by 38% (-39,200) and grants to skilled workers including those in the health and care sector and their dependants also dropped by 38% (-26,300) compared with the same period in 2025.

Immigration remains a key political issue, with Labour’s 2024 manifesto promising to reduce net migration, and aiming to “smash the gangs” involved in irregular migration and bringing asylum seekers across the Channel in small boats.

Andy Burnham’s arrival in No 10 has signalled a shift in the way the government views legal migration. Some Labour insiders say that policy is now being driven by economic demands rather than a fear of the rise in Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, which has suffered a dip in the polls.

articles.title: Lacson asks: Why settle unpaid 2024 DSWD guarantee letters in 2027?
articles.summary: Service providers reportedly filed money claims and submitted supporting documents belatedly, which is why the special provision was only proposed in the 2027 budget bill

blocks.text: Service providers reportedly filed money claims and submitted supporting documents belatedly, which is why the special provision was only proposed in the 2027 budget bill

items: Senator Panfilo Lacson raised concerns about a special provision in the House version of the 2027 budget bill that allocates funds to pay off unpaid guarantee letters issued by the DSWD in 2024 for the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations program.
Senator Risa Hontiveros explained that the DSWD was surprised by the late filing of claims by service providers, which led to the need for this special provision.
The DSWD plans to temporarily suspend the issuance of guarantee letters for AICS starting November 30.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Senator Panfilo Lacson flagged the proposed special provision in the House of Representatives’ version of the 2027 budget bill to pay off unpaid guarantee letters (GLs) issued by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) three years ago.
Lacson raised the issue during plenary deliberations on the DSWD’s proposed 2027 budget on Wednesday, November 25.
He pointed out that the House version of the DSWD budget includes a special provision for the “protective services program for individuals and families in difficult circumstances.”

It states that the amount for the program “shall likewise be used for the payment of arrears to accredited and/or partner service providers arising from the issuance of Guarantee Letter (GL) in FY (fiscal year) 2024, subject to the availability of funds and compliance with applicable budgeting, accounting, and auditing laws, rules and regulations.”

The GLs are for the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS) program, which provides financial assistance for medical needs, burial, transportation, education, food, and other support services or needs of a person or family.
Lacson noted that the allotment of over P34 billion for AICS in 2024 was fully obligated.

“So you’re issuing guarantee letters over and beyond what is authorized under GAA (General Appropriations Act) or under the law to spend under AICS. Mahirap maintindihan (This is difficult to understand), Mr. [Senate] President,” Lacson said.

Senator Risa Hontiveros, the DSWD’s budget sponsor, said service providers belatedly filed money claims and submitted supporting documents, which is why the special provision was only proposed in the 2027 budget bill.

“Nagulat din ang department. By the time dumating ‘yong mga GL, wala na pong pondo. Kasi hindi nila ino-obligate pagka-issue ng GL, pagka lamang ginamit na talaga at may billing na mula sa mga ospital,” Hontiveros said.

(The department was also surprised. By the time the GLs arrived, there were no available funds left. The department doesn’t obligate the funds when GLs are issued; only after the GLs are used and hospitals have sent the billing.)
The value of unpaid claims from the guarantee letters was not mentioned.
Asked whether the GLs were issued by lawmakers, Hontiveros clarified that it was the DSWD itself that issued the letters.

“Nagsi-signify ang department na handa sila kung sakaling hindi natin tanggapin na magkaroon ng special provision. Itutuloy ‘yong money claims process. Nga lamang, siyempre matagal ‘yon, at magkakaroon kaagad ng epekto na hindi tatanggapin,” she said.

(The department is signifying that it’s ready just in case the Senate won’t accept the inclusion of a special provision. It’ll just continue with the money claims process. It’s just that the process would be long and the possible effect would be the service providers may not agree with it.)
Learning from the ordeal, Hontiveros said, the DSWD will ensure early liquidation of guarantee letters moving forward, so there would be enough time to settle payments to service providers.

On Monday, November 23, the DSWD said it will temporarily suspend the issuance of guarantee letters for AICS starting November 30. The expected resumption will be on the first working day in January 2027.
This will not affect the availment of outright payment of cash aid to AICS beneficiaries.

“The DSWD will continue to accommodate individuals and families experiencing crisis situations who need immediate financial assistance through its field offices and satellite offices nationwide,” it said in a statement.
Civil society groups criticize the AICS program as “soft pork” being weaponized for political patronage.
During his interpellation, Lacson said he wants to break down the funding for AICS into the DSWD’s sub-programs. He described AICS as “whimsical.”

“Kung sino ‘yong marunong lumapit sa mga politiko, ‘yon ang mga mauuna. Kaya nga minsan naka-hikaw ng ginto eh, hindi talaga nangangailangan, wala talaga sa crisis situations, nakakakuha sila ng biyaya galing sa AICS,” he claimed.

(Only the people who know how to approach politicians are being prioritized. That’s why sometimes those who receive aid from the AICS program are not really needy, not really in crisis situations, or they even wear gold earrings.)
Hontiveros assured Lacson that the DSWD has full control over the decision-making and disbursement of aid under the program.
Under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), AICS was allocated P33.29 billion. The House added P25 billion.
While the DSWD earlier appealed to senators for a P63-billion budget for AICS, the Senate finance committee only recommended P48 billion.

During a committee hearing in October, Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian said restoring the budget to P63 billion, the same level in the 2026 budget, will help them support Filipinos affected by El Niño, inflation, and other crises in 2027.
The Senate panel realigned the AICS budget to augment funding for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation or PhilHealth.
As a whole, the DSWD and its attached agencies have P253.34 billion for proposed general appropriations under the Senate committee report.
That figure is P12 billion higher than the P241.28 billion in the NEP, but P9.42 billion lower than the P262.76 billion in the House budget measure. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 1Password customer data, source code taken in GitHub breach
articles.summary: 1Password says customer vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and unaffected as the platform does not have access to user passwords or secret keys

blocks.text: photo_gonzo/stock.adobe.com
1Password says customer vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and unaffected as the platform does not have access to user passwords or secret keys

items: 1Password reported a security breach where an attacker accessed an employee's GitHub account, stealing customer data and source code.
The stolen data included user names, email addresses, account identifiers, and public keys, but no sensitive user passwords or secret keys were compromised.
In response, 1Password rotated all exposed credentials, tightened security controls, and advised users to be cautious of phishing attempts related to the incident.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Password management software 1Password announced on Wednesday, November 25, that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account, stealing some customer data and copying source code from private repositories.
1Password, in its blog post informing the public about the incident, said it began investigations on November 19 following indications someone had taken over an employee’s GitHub account.

It added, however, that customers’ vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected because 1Password does not have access to user passwords or secret keys.
The attacker downloaded account records of a subset of 1Password’s users.
These records include the following:

items: Names and email addresses
Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times
Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)
Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)
Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery
Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)

blocks.text: 1Password also said the attacker copied source code from private repositories and gained access to a continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment system (CI/CD). The source code contains no customer data or user secrets, while the CI/CD holds “infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work.”

In light of the attack, 1Password has triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed. It disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.

1Password also said it tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, adding new detections for this kind of attack. It also lengthened invitation codes from six to 10 characters as a precaution.
1Password also validated that no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise was done using any exposed account provisioning tokens.
It also asked help from independent cybersecurity experts to validate its containment approaches and remediation efforts.

While 1Password said there was no impact to its services, availability, or product security, it advised users to be wary of “phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.”

The company added, “1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.”
It reminded users to keep their secret keys and passwords safe and invited users to report suspicious activity to support@1password.com. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Excise tax on your coffee? House leader shuts down suggestion
articles.summary: Previously, a group of liquor makers jokingly quipped that lawmakers consider taxing coffee, citing younger consumers’ apparent preference for it over alcohol

blocks.text: Anjo Lapresca
Previously, a group of liquor makers jokingly quipped that lawmakers consider taxing coffee, citing younger consumers’ apparent preference for it over alcohol

MANILA, Philippines – House ways and means chairman Miro Quimbo quickly shut down the idea of imposing an excise tax on coffee, after a group of liquor makers jokingly made the suggestion on Wednesday, November 25.

“The committee will not allow coffee to be taxed,” Quimbo, whose committee handles tax-related bills, said on DZBB Super Radyo on Thursday, November 26. “That (tax on) coffee, that will no longer be discussed.”

During the committee hearing on Wednesday, November 25, Distilled Spirits Association of the Philippines representative Olivia Limpe-Aw quipped that lawmakers might want to consider taxing coffee instead of alcohol.
She cited changing consumer behavior, as younger consumers — particularly Gen Zs — seem to prefer coffee over alcoholic drinks.
“We told Congressman Miro, maybe you would want to tax coffee because the (demand there) is huge, not alcohol. And coffee is expensive,” Limpe-Aw said.
Quimbo diverted the topic in his reply, saying: “Let’s talk about alcohol first. More people might get sleepy if we talk about coffee.”
On Thursday, Quimbo insisted there is no need to impose excise tax on coffee because it is not proven to be harmful.

“Besides, that is very difficult to administer. What kind of coffee? How heavy? With alcohol, you tax it when the alcohol content is higher. How about with coffee? Because it has more caffeine?” Quimbo said. – Rappler.com
