articles.title: Israel ‘officially sanctions’ torture of Palestinian prisoners to extract confessions, report concludes
articles.summary:
Public Committee Against Torture in Israel examined 42 complaints against Shin Bet interrogators over past decade

Israel has institutionalised the use of torture to extract confessions from…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison and Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Israel has institutionalised the use of torture to extract confessions from Palestinian prisoners, sometimes documenting abuse in official records or granting advanced approval for “special measures” in interrogation, according to a report from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI).
This dangerous practice risked leading to irreversible miscarriages of justice, as Israel moved to implement a racist new death penalty law that targets Palestinians, the report said.
PCATI examined 42 cases in which Palestinians filed complaints about the use of torture by Shin Bet interrogators over the last decade.
More than three-quarters said they confessed after the use of “torture or other illegal methods”, and one in 10 provided incriminating statements about other people under torture.

“When it comes to Palestinian detainees, the Israeli legal system officially sanctions torture as a tool for extracting confessions, regardless of whether the content of those confessions is true,” said Sari Bashi, the executive director of PCATI.
“Torture as a tool of interrogation is particularly egregious given initiatives to impose the death penalty in Israel for the first time since 1962.”

Over the years, in hundreds of testimonies, Palestinian detainees have consistently described interrogations employing extreme sleep deprivation, physical violence such as slapping and kicking, threats, sexual violence and being held in stress positions.

Some of this abuse is also laid out in the official records of Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security service. PCATI details the case of a Palestinian lawyer arrested in February 2019 who was subjected to extreme sleep deprivation.

During an interrogation period lasting 27.5 days, or 660 hours, he was questioned for more than 552 hours, an average of 20 hours a day, with one session lasting nearly 48 hours. Some of the remaining 108 hours were spent travelling to and attending detention hearings.

In a 1999 ruling, Israel’s supreme court explicitly prohibited sleep deprivation as a deliberate interrogation method. Despite this, the lawyer was convicted of involvement in shooting attacks based on information extracted during this period.
The state inspector for complaints about Shin Bet interrogations (Mavtan) ruled that the interrogations took place in accordance with procedures, PCATI said.
More than 1,680 torture complaints were filed between 2001 and 2024 with Mavtan. None have led to an indictment.
Other cases are indirectly documented in Israeli judicial records, although judges rarely accept testimony about torture of Palestinians, PCATI said.

In one case, a detainee’s false confession, made under torture, was used as evidence by prosecutors. The man was released after his lawyer presented proof that he was not present at the scene of the crime, PCATI said.
Sleep deprivation was the most frequently used form of torture in complaints examined by PCATI, but more than half included the use of stress positions and other forms of physical violence.

Israel is a signatory to the UN convention against torture, but its legal system has effectively codified the use of violence and abuse where it is deemed “necessary” to extract life-saving information, PCATI said.

In a “necessity interrogation” or “military interrogation”, Shin Bet officials torture detainees “after consulting with their superiors and following an internal procedure for documenting their decisions and conduct”, the report said.

“[A] supposedly narrow exception ballooned and developed into a sprawling system of legal and administrative exceptions that swallowed the so-called rule, enabling the use of violence while maintaining the appearance of prohibition,” it continued.

There is no publicly available information on the scale of “necessity interrogations” inside the Shin Bet, PCATI said. They are an urgent concern as Israel moves to end a de facto moratorium on the death penalty, which had stood since the 1962 execution of the Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann.

“The death penalty is always wrong, because it’s cruel, irreversible and negates the right to life. No one should be executed, particularly not in a system tainted by systematic violence,” Bashi said.
In March, the Knesset passed a racist law allowing the execution of Palestinians convicted of terror charges over deadly attacks, but not Jewish Israelis who commit similar crimes.
In the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians are tried in military courts, execution is now the default punishment for a defendant found guilty of deadly terror attacks.
The legislation drew fierce international criticism, including from the UN’s high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, who warned that it would constitute a war crime if enacted.
A separate law empowers a special tribunal to impose death sentences in cases arising from the 7 October 2023 attacks.
Even in rare cases where courts have excluded confessions obtained under torture, Israeli case law allows prosecutors to use information derived from them as evidence to secure convictions.

PCATI said that as detention conditions worsened after October 2023, rights groups documented a sharp rise in violence by Israeli prison guards and soldiers, including beatings, attacks with dogs, electric shocks, threats and rape.

At least 103 Palestinian detainees have died in Israeli custody since 7 October 2023. Of 10 postmortems reviewed by Physicians for Human Rights Israel, five showed signs of physical assault and six showed evidence of medical neglect.
The Israel Prison Service said “all prisoners are held in accordance with the law”. The Shin Bet and Israel’s justice ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: [READOUT] What businesses can get out of ASEAN 2026
articles.summary: From a landmark digital economy agreement to investment-ready energy projects, here's what businesses can take away from the Philippines' ASEAN hosting

blocks.text: The Philippines hosted the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from November 15 to 17. But aside from bringing world leaders to Manila, ASEAN also drew delegations of businessmen and investors hungry to make deals.
Let’s start with some of the biggest business developments to keep on your radar:

items: Digital economy. All 11 ASEAN countries signed the Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), which seeks to simplify cross-border e-commerce, digital payments, and data transfers across the region. With implementation targeted by May 2027, the Department of Trade and Industry plans to conduct trade shows and information campaigns next year to help entrepreneurs understand the agreement.

Regional power grid. All ASEAN members signed an enhanced agreement on the ASEAN Power Grid that could eventually allow them to buy and sell electricity across borders. While construction remains some ways off, the International Energy Agency estimates that ASEAN will need $27 billion in cross-border power interconnection investments through 2040, on top of more than $300 billion to expand and modernize domestic grids, presenting opportunities for infrastructure developers and financial institutions.

Free trade agreements. Canada concluded negotiations for separate free trade agreements with the Philippines and ASEAN. The Philippine-Canada agreement, targeted for signing in 2027, covers goods, services, investments, and digital trade, opening another avenue for businesses looking to diversify their markets.

US trade relations. US President Donald Trump also flew to Manila for a special summit with ASEAN leaders and a state visit with Marcos, during which he announced what he called the “biggest trade deal” between the Philippines and the US. Although no formal agreement was signed, Trump claimed that the Philippines had agreed to source 100% of its agricultural and energy imports from the US, which Philippine officials have since questioned. Watch how discussions unfold, as even a partial shift toward US suppliers could reshape supply chains and introduce greater competition for local producers.

blocks.text: Beyond the high-level meetings, ASEAN-related forums also brought together an eclectic mix of business leaders and global personalities – from Tessie Sy-Coson, Martha Sazon, and Maria Ressa to Angelina Jolie – for discussions spanning inclusive growth, food and energy security, and artificial intelligence.

Among the businesspeople in the lineup, a recurring theme was how difficult it remains to do business across ASEAN, despite its long-held dream of being a single marketplace. Ayala Corporation chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala lamented differences in regulatory standards and investment approvals, while former CIMB Group chairman Nazir Razak criticized the slow pace of regional economic integration.
Yet ASEAN is still an attractive investment destination, with foreign direct investment reaching a record $246 billion in 2025, up 10%.
And there was no shortage of investment opportunities being pitched.

At the Fourth ASEAN Investment Forum, gathered in one room were Philippine Board of Investments managing head Ceferino Rodolfo, global infrastructure investor I Squared Capital, and representatives of sovereign wealth funds from Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, and of course, the Philippines’ own Maharlika Investment Corporation. Between them, these institutions oversee assets worth well over $100 billion – a dealmaking goldmine.
Here’s a peek at some of the Philippine projects being pitched to investors there, as detailed in an investment booklet distributed during the event and seen by Rappler:

items: Project SAFAL. ALCOM’s proposed $340-million sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) project is seeking $102 million in equity and $238 million in debt financing, with a projected equity internal rate of return (IRR) of 28%.

SPV Clark. SAFAsia’s proposed $226-million facility in New Clark City would convert locally available waste into jet fuel, targeting annual production of 20,000 tons beginning in 2028. The project seeks $67.8 million in equity and $158.2 million in debt financing, with a project IRR of 14% to 17%.

Burgos Solar Power Project. Zenith Renewable’s proposed 64.5-megawatt solar farm in Pangasinan, paired with 51.2 MWh battery storage, seeks $12 million for a 70% equity stake, with a target IRR of 13.4%.
San Pedro Agri-Solar Power Project. Another Zenith project combining agricultural land use with solar power generation seeks $2 million for a 70% equity stake, with a projected IRR of 17%.

blocks.text: However, one investment opportunity conspicuously absent from every ASEAN discussion was the US-led Pax Silica initiative.

As officials had indicated beforehand, no Pax Silica deal was signed during the summit or US President Donald Trump’s subsequent state visit. Given the protests surrounding Trump’s arrival and opposition to Pax Silica itself, the administration had little political incentive to draw even more attention to the controversial project.
We hope this readout helps inform your next strategy or boardroom decision. And as always, feel free to tell us what to tackle next, dear business leader.– Rappler.com

Readout is a new content series from data consultancy The Nerve, bringing you insights that bridge the gap between quick news headlines and dense technical reports. Readout tracks and explains business shifts in different Philippine industries. Crafted from on-the-ground reporting and data-driven analyses, Readout provides a clear read on where market and consumption are headed, what’s shaping demand across different sectors, who the key players are, and why it all matters.

articles.title: Court documents reveal details of Winnipeg man's alleged Bishnoi gang extortion
articles.summary: A man accused of extorting someone on behalf of an Indian organized crime group allegedly used a payphone in Winnipeg's south St. Vital area to demand money from his victim, before mailing a letter…

image.caption: Arshdeep Brar, 36, is accused in a Winnipeg extortion case allegedly involving the India-based Bishnoi gang. (Manitoba Court of King's Bench)

blocks.text: Manitoba

A man accused of extorting someone on behalf of an Indian organized crime group allegedly used a payphone in Winnipeg's south St. Vital area to demand money from his victim, before mailing a letter to the man's home threatening his family.
Letter sent to victim this year says 'mistakes will not be forgiven'

A man accused of extorting someone on behalf of an Indian organized crime group allegedly used a payphone outside a Sobeys in Winnipeg's south St. Vital area to demand money from his victim, before mailing a letter in Hindi to the man's home threatening his family and telling him to leave $150,000 in cash at a site along a highway.

Details about how that case allegedly unfolded earlier this year were revealed in court documents — including an arrest report, affidavit and police narrative — filed in a criminal property forfeiture case against Arshdeep Brar, 36, who was eventually charged for his alleged involvement.
The documents, filed in July, also include a photo of the alleged threat letter and an English translation of its contents.
"Remember I have all the information of your house, your wife, kids and even your brother in India," it said, warning the victim not to contact police or "be clever with me."
"Mistakes will not be forgiven."

The unnamed victim, described only as a person in Winnipeg of South Asian descent, told police he got the first phone call in February from someone who introduced himself as Pardeep Jayani from the international Bishnoi gang, the documents allege. That call was made from outside the Sobeys on Dakota Street.

The criminal organization primarily operates out of India and is run by Lawrence Bishnoi, who has been in a prison in that country since 2015. The gang, which Canada designated a terrorist group in 2025, targets South Asian diaspora communities and is involved with criminal activities such as extortion, contract killings, arson, intimidation, and drug and firearm trafficking.
A photo of the letter allegedly sent to the victim was included in court documents. (Manitoba Court of King's Bench)
Police announced last week that one of the group's top lieutenants, Satinderjeet Singh — also known as Goldy Brar — is wanted alongside another man in a 2023 murder in Winnipeg.
In the recent Winnipeg extortion case, court documents said when the victim got the call asking for money, he panicked "and didn't know what to say or do after he heard [the name] Bishnoi."

items: Man who claimed to be Bishnoi gang member arrested in Manitoba, court document says
Man believed to be top Bishnoi gang lieutenant wanted in 2023 Winnipeg killing

blocks.text: "[Redacted] has no issues with anyone. [Redacted] found it odd that the demand was not made via WhatsApp call as that's the common way Bishnoi gang operates," the documents said.
"[Redacted] knows another [redacted] in Winnipeg who went through the same circumstances. [Redacted] doesn't know how he managed to settle the deal."
The court documents also included this version of the letter, which has English translations of each paragraph. (Manitoba Court of King's Bench)
Brar is accused of calling the victim twice, including a second time from a payphone at Watt Street and Jamison Avenue, in Winnipeg's Elmwood area.
During the phone calls, the victim said the person on the other end told him he would "notify his boss, Aarzoo Bishnoi" and that the victim "would have to face the consequences."

The victim said he also told the person at one point that he "doesn't have that much money and that he is not into illegal things." He said the person replied that he "doesn't care how he arranges the money, but he must do it," the documents allege.

The letter Brar allegedly sent the victim, demanding cash be left in a bag by a yellow gate near a highway rest area outside Portage la Prairie, Man., said "it's not hard to find people to do shootings," for only $5,000 or $6,000.
"If any of my boys get caught, that will be your responsibility," the translated letter said.
Accused 'directed' by gang

Brar ended up being arrested and charged after picking up a package of money police had prepared and delivered to the specified drop-off location, the documents allege. The director of the province's criminal property forfeiture branch is now seeking to seize the truck it says was involved in the crime.
The court documents state Brar and the victim were acquaintances and that both "were working [redacted] in Winnipeg at the time of the incident."
Brar told police he sent the letter to the victim demanding $150,000, but said he "took this action because he was directed to do so by a member of the Bishnoi Gang," the documents allege.

items: Man killed in northwest Winnipeg had long-running feud with rival gangs in India, expert says

blocks.text: In a statement of defence filed by Brar and his wife — whose name the truck is registered in — he denied phoning the victim, being a member of the Bishnoi group or writing the letter.

"In the alternative … Brar pleads that any involvement he had in the transmission or delivery of a letter occurred under compulsion, threat, or coercion from another person who identified themselves as a member of the Bishnoi Gang," the filing said.

Brar's wife said there were no material facts that she participated in or knew about any unlawful activity, and the forfeiture of her interest in the truck would be unjust. The couple's filing seeks to dismiss the forfeiture claim on the vehicle.
Winnipeg case rare: expert

Wade Deisman, an associate professor in the University of the Fraser Valley's criminology school in British Columbia, said because of the pervasive sense of fear that the Bishnoi gang has created in Indian diaspora communities, many people targeted for extortion don't go to police.
That makes the Winnipeg case rare because the person sought help, and because police were able to charge someone, he said.

Deisman also said the suggestion in the case that it was unusual the alleged perpetrator used phone calls and letters instead of WhatsApp "raises the spectre" of whether there are copycat operations happening that aren't actually affiliated with the Bishnoi gang.
But once that deep fear develops in a community, "it becomes kind of immaterial" who's behind a threat like that, said Deisman, who is researching some of the impacts of the Bishnoi gang.

items: Guns, swords and pepper spray: Bishnoi-linked extortionists attacked in apparent retaliation
Inside the world of Lawrence Bishnoi, the Indian gangster Canada says India is using as a proxy

blocks.text: "Sometimes a criminal organization will go after people who kind of get on their coattails," he said. "Sometimes they'll recruit them. Sometimes they'll punish them. Sometimes they won't do anything because it still builds their name and still builds their reputation."
The charges against Brar have not been proven in court, and he is considered innocent unless proven guilty.

articles.title: Philippines requests 6 Chinook helicopters under $2-B US financing
articles.summary: The Philippine government, through the Department of National Defense (DND), has requested the purchase of six CH-47 Chinook helicopters under the $2-billion US Foreign Military Financing, Defense…

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 5:54pm

The Philippines, through the Department of National Defense (DND), has requested the purchase of six CH-47 Chinook helicopters under the $2-billion US Foreign Military Financing, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said on Thursday.

“Nag-request kami sa US government doon sa $2-billion financing ng anim na Chinook. That is the only thing I can disclose out of that package,” Teodoro said after the closing ceremony of the Armed Forces of the Philippines’ Joint Exercise Dagat-Langit-Lupa.
(We made a request to the US government regarding the $2-billion financing for six Chinooks. That is the only thing I can disclose out of that package.)
He said that all six brand-new helicopters could be delivered as early as 2029 if the US agrees to prioritize the Philippine order; otherwise, delivery could take up to six years.
Aside from the acquisition, the request also covers integrated logistics support and crew training.
Teodoro said a Chinook helicopter could carry about four times the load of a Black Hawk, pointing out the time and logistical space it would save.

“A Chinook can carry about 4 times a Black Hawk, so it saves you time, and it saves you logistical space. Kasi hindi minamano-mano ‘yan. Nilo-load na lang ng ano yan, ng lifter, loader,” the Defense chief said.
(A Chinook can carry about four times a Black Hawk, so it saves you time, and it saves you logistical space. Because you don't load that manually—it's loaded using a lifter or loader.)

“So, time is more than a quarter of one-fourth the time na kailangan mong i-load yung Black Hawk. 'Yun lang ang kailangan mo sa Chinook. Kaya mong magbuhat ng malalaking kanyon. Kaya mo magbuhat ng sasakyan na may pasahero pa,” he added.

(So, loading takes less than a quarter of the time you need to load a Black Hawk. That’s all you need for a Chinook. You can carry large artillery pieces, and you can even carry a vehicle with passengers still inside.)
However, Teodoro raised concerns about the helicopters’ maintenance costs, which he sees as a bigger challenge than building basing infrastructure for the aircraft.
“Basing ng anim na Chinook, e kayang-kaya. Maintenance, maintenance problema dun,” he said.
(Basing six Chinooks—we can easily manage that. Maintdenance is the problem there.)

Last week, the White House announced that Manila and Washington had agreed to work toward a foreign military financing loan exceeding $2 billion to supply the Philippines with defense and security capabilities from US suppliers. –Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/NB, GMA News

articles.title: FedEx airplane overruns runway at Miami airport, temporarily closing all but 1 runway
articles.summary: There were no reports of injuries after the plane ran off the runway at about 8:40 p.m. ET, the airport reported. By early Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration was reporting hourslong flight…

image.caption: Investigators and responders work at the site where a FedEx cargo plane overran a runway at the Miami International Airport, Wednesday night in Miami. (Rebecca Blackwell/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

There were no reports of injuries after the plane ran off the runway at about 8:40 p.m. ET, the airport reported. By early Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration was reporting hourslong flight delays.
Incident occurs nearly 3 months after Amazon cargo jet overshot runway in Miami, killing 5 on ground
A FedEx airplane overran a runway at the Miami International Airport on Wednesday night, forcing all but one runway to temporarily close the day before American Thanksgiving, according to officials.

There were no reports of injuries after the plane ran off the runway at about 8:40 p.m. ET, the airport reported. The incident happened almost three months after an Amazon cargo jet overshot another runway in Miami, killing five people on the ground.
By early Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration was reporting hourslong flight delays.
The FAA, which is investigating, said the McDonnell Douglas MD-11 was coming from Memphis.

items: Amazon suspends use of cargo carrier whose plane careened off Miami runway
At least 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane barrels off Miami runway and smashes into cars: police

blocks.text: FedEx said the plane had "an issue upon landing" and that it is coordinating with investigating officials.
"We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries," the company said in a statement.

FedEx had just started flying MD-11s again in May to deliver packages after that type of plane crashed in Kentucky last year as it was taking off. The UPS plane's left engine flew off and three pilots along with 12 people on the ground were killed. The FAA had approved Boeing's proposed fix for the MD-11s "after extensive review."

Responders investigate the cockpit of the cargo plane after it overran a runway at the Miami airport. By early Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration was reporting hourslong flight delays. (Rebecca Blackwell/The Associated Press)
The airport recommended that passengers scheduled to fly Wednesday night should check with their airlines for the latest flight updates before travelling to the airport.
"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," the airport said in a statement.

items: Parts of small plane that crashed in South Florida found as far as 6 km from where it came down
FAA grounds flights across U.S. due to outage affecting air traffic control

blocks.text: The runway this FedEx plane landed on Wednesday is different than the one the Amazon cargo plane overran in September. But three of Miami's runways converge at the west end, so the FedEx plane ended up close to where the Amazon plane careened across a road and struck a van filled with a plane-cleaning crew.

The incident also comes less than two weeks after a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at the Miami airport. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the incident Wednesday. The National Transportation Safety Board said it had no information about the situation.

articles.title: Defense to present VP Sara Duterte's dentist, Cale88 co-owner at impeachment hearing
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team has asked the Senate impeachment court to subpoena her known dentist and a deputy commissioner of the Bureau of Customs for the hearings from December 1 to…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 5:49pm
Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte (front R) leaves court after posting bail in Quezon City, suburban Manila on September 5, 2026.
AFP / Ted Aljibe

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team has asked the Senate impeachment court to subpoena her known dentist and a deputy commissioner of the Bureau of Customs for the hearings from December 1 to 4.
In a manifestation dated November 25, Duterte’s lawyers named Lourdes Tingson-Lebosada and Deputy Commissioner Agaton Uvero in their initial list of witnesses for the week.
Earlier identified as a co-owner of Cale88 Foods Corp., Lebosada will testify on the company’s operations, government registration and financial affairs.
Deputy Commissioner Agaton Teodoro Uvero, meanwhile, will testify on Cale88’s exportation records with the BOC, as well as present a copy of the company’s certificate of registration with the bureau.
Cale88 is a banana chips company owned by Lebosada and Duterte’s husband, Manases “Mans” Carpio.
Its financial records have been flagged for various reasons, including foreign remittances from China and Russia and a lack of supporting documents.
Inconsistencies between the company’s bank inflows and declared sales have also come into question.
Lebosada’s and Uvero’s testimonies are intended to counter allegations against Duterte under the second article of impeachment, which concerns her alleged unexplained wealth.

blocks.text: This is a roundup of the top news stories from Germany on Thursday, November 26, 2026:
November 26, 2026
Parliament continues budget debates
The Bundestag is conducting its concluding debates on the budget for 2027 ahead of a final vote scheduled for Friday.

On Thursday, the focus will initially be on the individual budget for the Interior Ministry led by Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

The government foresees that the ministry, which is responsible for the federal police and the domestic intelligence agency BfV, among other things, will receive some €16.8 billion in 2027 ($18.43 billion), around €1 billion more than this year.

Lawmakers will then go on to debate the individual budgets for the Economics and Energy Ministry, the Ministry for Housing, Urban Development and Building, the Ministry of Food and Agriculture and the Ministry for Education, Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth.

Opening the debates on Wednesday, Merz described the tight budget as an "accurate reflection" of the "difficult situation as a country — geopolitically, technologically, and demographically" — that Germany finds itself in.
"We will no longer be able to afford everything with tax revenue that we have become all too accustomed to for far too long," Merz added.
You can read more about what the planned record-breaking German budget for 2027 includes in this DW article:€561 Billion and Still Not Enough: Germany's 2027 Budget Exposes a Coalition on the Brink

articles.title: News Reflection: President Marcos could not keep his guest waiting
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump received two welcomes in Manila: festivities on the tarmac and protests on the streets.

blocks.text: Although US President Donald Trump almost missed the ASEAN Summit in Manila — he must have had other priorities — Philippine President Bongbong Marcos spared no minute, no time for one more question, to welcome him.

Trump arrived in Manila to the usual festive welcome Filipinos afford guests — on the tarmac. But on the streets near the summit venue, the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City, protesters rallied to express their disagreement with Trump’s policies, specifically his government’s planned establishment of Pax Silica data centers in Central Luzon.

When a reporter tried to ask Marcos about these protests, his press relations chief was quick to point out that he had more important matters to attend to. Both palms raised, he apologized, ending his briefing abruptly — he couldn’t keep the POTUS waiting.
This week’s News Reflection, from Paterno Esmaquel II. – Rappler.com

articles.title: How the Nvidia scandal is testing Singapore’s role in global chip trade
articles.summary: The Nvidia crisis has put Singapore squarely in Washington’s sights amid concerns over its role in China’s access to advanced AI chips. Here’s what’s at stake for the Southeast Asian nation and why…

image.caption: Singapore has come under scrutiny in the wake of the Nvidia scandal for not being vigilant enough in stopping the routing of advanced AI ships subject to U.S. export bans through its territory. Singapore-based Megaspeed, whose office is seen above, is one of the companies accused of facilitating the

blocks.text: World·New

The Nvidia crisis has put Singapore squarely in Washington’s sights amid concerns over its role in China’s access to advanced AI chips. Here’s what’s at stake for the Southeast Asian nation and why it’s stepping up efforts to prevent companies like Megaspeed, which was tied to one of the figures at the heart of the scandal, from circumventing U.S. export controls.
Singapore-based Megaspeed's role in Nvidia crisis has put scrutiny on diversion of chips to China

The Nvidia crisis has put Singapore squarely in Washington's sights amid concerns over its role in China's access to advanced AI chips. Here's what's at stake for the Southeast Asian nation and why it's stepping up efforts to prevent companies from circumventing U.S. export controls by diverting chips through its jurisdiction.

Prior to the emergence of the news that the CEO of chip giant Nvidia had an affair with a former executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed who may have been spying for China, Singapore had positioned itself as a key intermediary in the global AI supply chain.
The city-state benefited from its access to advanced U.S. chips and its established commercial ties with Chinese technology companies.

Singapore accounted for 22 per cent of Nvidia's global revenue last year, according to its financial filings before it stopped disclosing its Singapore sales and revenue. That's despite the fact that the vast majority of the products billed here were shipped elsewhere.
But allegations that Megaspeed diverted advanced AI chips to China have raised a critical question: were businesses here doing enough to verify where the hardware was ultimately going?

Alice Huang, seen in screenshot from a video provided by Taiwanese broadcaster TVBS, is suspected of spying for China while having an affair with Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia. Here, they are seen at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan, in May 2025. (TVBS/The Associated Press)

"That question was never asked: When you do business, would you ask where the thing goes? said Mark Goh, a professor of analytics and operations at the National University of Singapore's business school.
"When the money comes in and nothing is rocking the boat, you say, 'Fine, we'll do it,'"

items: Why Trump's move to get Jensen Huang reinstated won't end the questions
What the Nvidia scandal means for your investments

blocks.text: Now, Singapore is having to rethink its approach. It has launched an investigation into Megaspeed and said it's co-operating with U.S. authorities, who have been looking into the company's alleged diversion of chips to China since 2024 and added it to its trade blacklist earlier this week.
Why Nvidia couldn't afford to lose Jensen Huang | About That
Singapore's access to U.S. tech at risk
What's at stake isn't just its reputation as a trusted global trading hub but its continued access to advanced U.S. technology and its ambitions to become a leading AI hub.

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Singapore was working closely with Washington to improve information sharing and set up a mechanism allowing U.S. authorities to conduct checks and enforce its own export controls.

Singapore's prime minister, Lawrence Wong, seen in Jakarta, Indonesia, in July 2026, said he is co-operating with U.S. authorities in efforts to clamp down on the diversion of AI chips to China through the Southeast Asian country. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images)
But tighter enforcement will require greater visibility over a complex global supply chain.

One of the biggest challenges is tracking what happens to the chips after the initial sale. While suppliers are required to carry out checks on their customers, those customers may subsequently resell the chips to restricted parties.

"From a legal point of view, the selling company is not liable for the onward resale as long as the proper due diligence was carried out," said Goh Puay Guan, an associate professor specialising in supply chain management at NUS business school.
'They can't open every container'
Preventing the diversion of sensitive technology will likely require more stringent checks on end users.
For businesses in Singapore, that could mean higher compliance costs, longer transaction times and greater risks associated with doing business with Chinese technology companies.
The biggest concern for Singapore, perhaps, is losing its appeal as an intermediary between the world's two largest economies.
Shipping containers are seen at the port in Singapore. Local authorities are under pressure to step up monitoring of AI chips being shipped through the city-state. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
"They need to keep the trust with both parties," said Matthias Hendrichs, an independent AI industry adviser.

"They need to step up the investigations and the monitoring they do.... At the same time, there can't be 100 per cent follow-up. They can't open every container that comes into the Singapore harbour."
U.S. moves to restrict cloud computing access
But it's not just the physical movement of chips that Singapore is now under pressure to monitor.

Washington is also moving to close a loophole in its export controls. Until now, Chinese technology companies could access advanced U.S. chips legally by renting computing power from overseas data centres.
That demand has helped fuel Southeast Asia's data-centre boom, with investment in Singapore alone forecast to reach $7 billion US this year, according to research by PwC and Oxford Economics.

items: How China gets around the U.S. ban on Nvidia chips

blocks.text: Under the new U.S. restrictions, data-centre operators serving major Chinese AI customers have until mid-February to secure licences or risk losing access to advanced chips.

Separately, the Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that Nvidia had instructed its manufacturing partners to halt shipments of servers to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.

Malaysian customs officers stand next to a seized server containing advanced AI chips last month. The Financial Times reported Wednesday that Nvidia is halting shipments of servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. (Vincent Thian/The Associated Press)
It is unclear how long the suspension will last, but it adds to the uncertainty facing the region's data-centre industry and risks delaying new projects.

"If projects lose anchor customers or cannot assure lenders that they have a reliable chip supply, financing could be delayed or fall through," said Han-Wei Liu, an associate professor of law at Singapore Management University.

items: Trump administration blacklists Megaspeed
U.S. further restricts China's access to AI chips in wake of Nvidia scandal

blocks.text: "That could slow the expansion of computing capacity across Southeast Asia and make it harder for local firms and researchers to develop AI."
Higher compliance costs could also eat into the profits of existing operators.
For Singapore, it adds to growing uncertainty over its future in the global AI supply chain.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Patrick Fok is director of APAC Strategy and Beijing correspondent for Feature Story News, a global broadcasting agency headquartered in Washington, D.C. A native of Hong Kong, he previously worked for Reuters and Channel NewsAsia in Singapore.

articles.title: Older Australians suffering under Labor’s ‘botched’ aged care at home program, inquiry finds
articles.summary:
The Support at Home system has ‘baffling’ bureaucracy and ‘rations and denies care’, says Greens chair of Senate inquiry

  • Get our

blocks.text: Many older Australians are dying before they can access home support, paying exorbitant fees, and being pushed into hospitals and residential care before they are ready because of a flawed federal government aged care program, a Senate inquiry has found.

The inquiry is examining the impact of the Support at Home program, which launched in November 2025 and has been plagued by complaints of making care harder to access and more expensive. The inquiry was due to finish in November, but has been extended for a further year after receiving almost 300 submissions.
The aged care algorithm, used to assess the home support needs of older people and allocate funding, has been a particular focus of the inquiry.

The inquiry’s interim report, tabled on Thursday, recommended human override of algorithmic assessments be reinstated after evidence that older people are being harmed due to, in many cases, being underassessed and left without adequate support.

The report describes how the algorithm prioritises physical mobility over cognitive decline, meaning people with severe dementia can be classified as “independent” and denied adequate funding. A single point difference on the algorithm’s decision tree can cost an applicant nearly $40,000 a year in funding.

The appeal system can be lengthy and onerous, the inquiry heard, and assessors are barred from overriding any incorrect algorithmic result. It means people are being pushed into residential care homes before they are ready or end up in hospital as their health deteriorates, the inquiry heard.

As of June, more than 106,000 Australians were on the official waiting list for a Support at Home place. In October, the health department reported that 6,436 people had died while waiting for their approved level of funding.
People who are healthy are also left in hospitals for months because they are waiting for a Support at Home assessment, funding allocation, or access to support, the inquiry heard.

The inquiry heard the case of a woman with heart and renal failure who was discharged from hospital as a “medium priority” for Support at Home. She died four months later still waiting for funding to help her eat and administer critical medication.

The Greens senator Penny Allman-Payne, the inquiry chair, said “Labor has clearly botched the implementation of Support at Home and added baffling layers of bureaucracy and complexity, but fundamentally this is a problem of design”.

“Not only are providers jacking up their prices, the system rations and denies care, systematically underassessing need and priority and creating artificial scarcity by withholding packages,” she said.
Algorithm in focus

In September, freedom of information requests by Guardian Australia revealed health officials from several states and the Northern Territory were so alarmed by the impact of the algorithm that they kept a log of hundreds of cases where vulnerable people were severely under-assessed, sending these cases to the federal government.

Days before the algorithm was rolled out in November, the department told aged care assessment organisations that their assessors would be barred from overriding incorrect algorithmic outcomes, despite assurances that they would have the final say.

The government has stopped short of allowing assessors to immediately correct incorrect algorithm decisions, despite growing calls from clinicians, advocacy groups and politicians throughout the inquiry. Instead, the aged care minister, Sam Rae, said in July that assessors would have the option to escalate cases to a system governor.
The government has also announced an independent review of the aged care classification and prioritisation assessment.

“Many of the adjustments to date appear to be reactive in nature, driven by external pressures – including successive inquiries by this committee – rather than robust monitoring and improvement processes put in place by the government,” the interim report found.
after newsletter promotion
High prices and delays

The aged care royal commission, which handed down its final report in 2021, found most older Australians want to remain at home and supporting them to safely do so prevents premature decline and strain on the hospital system.
The Support at Home reforms were supposed to help people stay at home longer and give them greater control over their support, with a focus on human rights.
Instead, aged care assessors have described elements of the reforms as “inhumane”.
The inquiry heard funding is being eaten up by exorbitant prices, with reports of prices for some services, including meals and cleaning, tripling under the system.

The program requires people to make payments for these services, but the inquiry heard that because prices had increased so much and people need to pay up to 80% of the cost, their co-contribution is causing financial distress and forcing older people to cut back on essential support.

An example in the report was crutches, which usually cost about $50, rising to $1,800 since Support at Home began as providers increased prices and administrative hurdles were added, with a three-month wait to obtain them.

There are delays at many points of the program, with the report describing how “older people go without, opt out and die without”. There were 4,812 older Australians approved for Support at Home who died before receiving a single service, the inquiry heard.
“My dad passed away on 29 April, two days short of turning 92, and his package arrived three weeks later in May,” one witness told the inquiry.
The shadow health minister, Anne Ruston, said the committee found many of the problems “were either known, or predicted, prior to the rollout”.
“Older Australians and their families have spent a year telling this government that Support at Home is broken,” she said. “Labor dismissed them, and now a Senate committee has confirmed every word.”

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine war extends to the Baltic and the Mediterranean
articles.summary: By attacking Russian vessels around the world, Kyiv is trying to up the pressure on Moscow and also sending out signals to its Western allies. What is the impact on global maritime trade?

image.caption: The Russian corvette Merkury was attacked by a Ukrainian drone called Sea BabyImage: Security Service of Ukraine/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya. These spectacular Ukrainian operations in regions far from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv have caused a stir. They came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland, not far from where an international military exercise was underway.
Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.
What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?

It is no secret that Russia has long since expanded its operations beyond Ukraine: With military provocation, hybrid operations and acts of sabotage, Moscow has attempted to put pressure on the countries that openly support Ukraine.
And Ukraine has also targeted Russia's military and economy beyond its borders.

Since the summer, attacks by both Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea. Not only have Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships been targeted, but also vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey.

Furthermore, in the past few years, Ukraine has managed to deal significant blows to Russia, deep within Russian territory, thanks to aerial and maritime drones. It has targeted military airfields and other strategic targets such as oil refineries, including one in Omsk, Siberia, as well as military vessels in the eastern Black Sea.

blocks.caption: The Russian cargo vessel Sparta II was attacked off the Finnish coast Image: Finnish Border Guard/Handout/Lehtikuva/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian attacks in Baltic Sea region

Russia has access only to a very narrow strip of the Baltic Sea coast, which is flanked by Finland and Estonia. Even ahead of the attack on the Sparta II, Ukraine had struck in the area multiple times, targeting oil terminals in the region around St. Petersburg, in Ust-Luga and Primorsk.
Russia uses the Baltic Sea to transport supplies to its Kaliningrad exclave and to export oil and other goods to the rest of the world, with the help of its "shadow fleet."

Ukrainian special forces are also said to have carried out operations against Russian military facilities in Syria, well before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They are also reported to have lent support to local Tuareg fighters in Mali who were able to inflict heavy losses on the Malian army and allied Russian mercenaries.
Kyiv is thus attempting to harm Russia's military and economy worldwide, even if in military terms this does not help Ukraine directly.

The Russian corvette that was sunk was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet but because of Turkey's blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, it would not have been allowed to return to the Black Sea. Instead, it was escorting Russian cargo ships in the Mediterranean. Primarily, the attacks send a political message: Russian ships can no longer feel safe — anywhere in the world.
Black Sea drone strikes put key global trade route at risk
Could war become omnipresent?

"We are not speaking about random shadow vessels which simply transport oil above the price cap and as a result bring revenues for the Russian treasury," security expert Elisabeth Braw from the Atlantic Council told DW. Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies.

"Ukraine is showing that it knows exactly, and secondly that it's able to hit them wherever and whatever waters they are in," Braw continued. "And this is something I don't think Ukraine has been able to do at the beginning of the war."

Officially, Kyiv's goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes, but military experts and politicians also see the attacks as a clear political signal to Western allies. They suspect that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is sending a clear message of strength with an eye toward possible future peace negotiations.

In an interview on the German news outlet Tagesschau, security expert Joachim Weber from the University of Bonn suggested that Zelenskyy was paying less attention to the US, out of a sense of disappointment. He said that Ukrainian attacks in distant maritime areas were a sign that there was less inhibition and that Ukraine was ready to expand the conflict geographically to increase pressure on Russia, despite the risks.

Weber warned that war could become omnipresent if there was an increase in attacks on civilian vessels or ships that were considered suspicious in international waters. He said that Russia was providing more military escorts for the ships of its shadow fleet. "The likelihood that an accidental exchange of fire between armed forces, coast guards or anyone could occur is rising."

Braw pointed out that violations of the Law of the Sea were not only rising with regard to the Russia-Ukraine war but also in relation to other conflicts and playing out in "the South China Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea."

She said about 90% of global trade today was conducted via the oceans and she feared that others might conclude it was not "really to their advantage" to follow the rules of international maritime law.
She added that they might find it "beneficial in the short term to violate maritime rules" for short-term gains. "That would make the world's oceans significantly less safe for everybody."
This article was translated from German.
How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy

articles.title: New defence laws could have ‘significant’ implications for human rights, Labor-led inquiry finds
articles.summary:
Anthony Albanese defends laws and calls criticism ‘nonsense’ and ‘conspiracy theories’ from far left and far right

  • Get our

blocks.text: New powers allowing defence officials to use lethal force against suspected trespassers into designated zones could have “significant” human rights implications, a Labor-chaired inquiry has warned.

The committee also raised concerns about a lack of requirements to ensure anyone detained under the new laws had access to fresh drinking water and humane conditions. It noted the broad and extensive changes could capture unwitting members of the public who stumble on to a declared defence security zone that has not been publicised.

The controversial bill, which passed the Senate on Monday, was heavily criticised by civil liberties and pro-democracy groups for granting extraordinary powers to defence officials in the name of national security.
The human rights inquiry’s report, published on Thursday evening, notes a number of issues with the bill, including its proportionality and the extent of the powers without adequate safeguards.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, defended the laws against critics on Thursday, as he decried “nonsense” and “conspiracy theories” from both the “far left” and “far right”.
“What this legislation is about is simply making sure that our defence institutions and infrastructure are kept safe,” Albanese said in question time.

“And, quite frankly, to suggest that a minister would abuse powers in order to designate something that was not associated with defence of this country as somehow needing protection is quite frankly irresponsible, and those spreading that misinformation online should know better.”

But the parliamentary human rights report, led by the committee chair and Labor MP Zaneta Mascarenhas, highlighted concerns raised over transparency, the right to free movement, free expression, privacy, liberty and life.
Among the report’s harshest criticism is a question over powers given to defence officials and law enforcement use of reasonable and necessary force.
Under the laws, such officials have the power to search a person and their devices – with or without consent – and detain them if they have “reasonable suspicion” they are entering a defence zone.
Reasonable and necessary force can be used to prevent serious injury or death, or when a person is fleeing to avoid being detained or to escape from detention.
However, the committee’s report concluded the reasons to use force were broad.

“In light of the low threshold for detention, including detention without arrest or to carry out an inspection or search of a vehicle, vessel or aircraft, the scope of the measure appears broad and the extent of interference with these rights may be significant,” the report said.

It added the inspector general of the Australian defence force could only investigate the use of force after a potential violation had occurred and would therefore “not prevent any violation of the power” in an act against international human rights law.
Detention of a person reasonably suspected of committing an offence was also too vague, the report said.
after newsletter promotion
“The measures do not include requirements for officials to consider and ensure human conditions of detention,” the report said.
These included a lack of clarity over whether a person detained without arrest should have access to fresh drinking water, acceptable and humane temperatures, health care and sanitary practices.
There is also no maximum period of detention specified and it is up to an official’s discretion.
‘Impermissible’ powers

The laws give the minister the ability to make a “capability declaration” which allows declared persons to engage in a “reasonable and proportionate” activity that might otherwise be illegal under federal or state laws.

The report noted the minister isn’t required to notify “affected persons” that the declaration has been made, “meaning that affected persons may be unaware that a declaration exists or that they may be liable for offences in relation to a declaration”.

“The committee considers there is a risk that the proposed defence capability declaration framework may constitute an impermissible limit on a potentially wide range of human rights. However, as the bill has now passed, the committee makes no further comment,” the report said.

Under the laws, the minister can also declare an area of land, sea or airspace to be a “defence area” and classify it as an emergency, temporary or mobile site. This would include conventional defence bases and sites – but could extend to military vehicles, buildings or structures.
A person suspected of entering or taking pictures of such sites could be jailed for up to seven years, or fined $152,880, or both.

The inquiry report said the laws did not clearly outline whether individuals would be notified of declarations, or whether defence zones could include residential or highly populated areas. It added the measures should be “accompanied by strong safeguards to assist proportionality”.

articles.title: Details of two treaties at heart of Andy Burnham’s EU reset to be published
articles.summary: Government also to publish bill that will enact EU deals, as Tories and Reform hit out over 10-year termination clause

blocks.text: Details of two treaties at the heart of Andy Burnham’s post-Brexit reset plans will be published on Thursday alongside the bill that will implement the changes into UK law.

The treaties signed by the UK and the European Union at last week’s summit will have a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party were to end the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, the BBC reported on Thursday.

Any termination clause could bring the longer-term future of the deal into doubt, after the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, described it as a “terrible deal” that she would scrap. Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay, with the Reform UK leader promising to renege on the deal if he were to win power, arguing that Burnham “cannot bind a future British government”.

At a major summit in Brussels last week the UK and EU announced three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK.
But uncertainty around the trio of deals remains, with fears they could be derailed in six months unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.
On Wednesday Burnham indicated that European students would have to pay higher fees than their domestic equivalents at UK universities.

While Burnham has previously stated he would like to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime, he has played down the issue of full integration since the deal was struck, saying it was “not a prelude to anything” and that it would be “unthinkable” for the UK to rejoin the EU without holding another referendum.

Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food and emissions trading deals, alongside the government’s bill to enact the agreement. The government is also expected to publish assessments of the impact on different sectors and regions of the country .

Earlier this year, the Guardian revealed ministers were planning to reshape Britain’s relationship with the EU with legislation that would result in the UK signing up to EU single market rules without a normal parliamentary vote.
after newsletter promotion

The new bill that will bring into force the food and drink trade deal will contain powers enabling the government to dynamically align with Europe on areas where it has already made agreements. It will also allow the UK to quickly implement evolving single market rules if it determines it is in the national interest, without having to face full parliamentary scrutiny each time.

The European affairs minister, Hamish Falconer, said: “The cutting costs bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements. It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier.”

articles.title: Why did Mandaluyong buy 27 cars worth over P1 million each for barangays?
articles.summary: After the backlash, one of the barangays used the car for distributing free lettuce

blocks.text: HYBRID CARS. Vehicles for Mandaluyong barangays.
After the backlash, one of the barangays used the car for distributing free lettuce
Mandaluyong City has a new set of wheels for its barangay officials. These are not the usual vehicles you will see in a barangay hall’s garage.
On Monday, November 23, the city distributed 27 hybrid cars to its 27 barangays.
Mayor Menchie Abalos said that “these cars are long overdue for the barangay captains.”

“Gagamitin nila ‘yung sasakyan na ‘yan pang-service rin. Alam mo naman kapag barangay captain, saan-saan sila nauutusan. Saan-saan din sila nakakapunta. So this one, kinakailangan nila,” Abalos said in an interview during the distribution.

(They will also use that vehicle as a service vehicle. You know how it is when you’re a barangay captain —they get sent on errands all over the place, and they also have to go to various locations. So this one, they really need it.)
Based on photos from the event, the vehicles appear to be Jaecoo J5. According to AutoDeal, the model is priced at around P1.099 million.
The J5 comes with a 13.2-inch touchscreen infotainment system. Oh, and it has a sunroof, too.
The city government said the vehicles would help barangays respond more quickly to residents’ needs and deliver public services more efficiently.
Their primary uses include barangay patrols to maintain peace and order, responding to emergencies, and transporting essential services to residents.
But the purchase did not sit well with people online who raised questions about the need for vehicles costing more than P1 million each.

In response to the criticism, the Mandaluyong City government said in a statement on Wednesday, November 25, that the multipurpose vehicles were intended to serve the entire barangay, not just its captain.

“Pangunahing gamit nito ay ang pagroronda para mapanatili ang kapayapaan at kaayusan, agarang pagtugon sa pangangailangan ng residente o emergencies at paghahatid ng mga pangunahing serbisyo sa mamamayan,” the city government said.
(Its primary uses are patrolling to maintain peace and order, responding immediately to residents’ needs or emergencies, and delivering basic services to citizens.)
The city government maintained that the acquisition followed government procurement processes and regulations.
It said the decision considered the vehicles’ potential to reduce fuel consumption in the long run and lessen their environmental impact.
The city assured residents that it would monitor the use of the vehicles and not allow them to be used for personal purposes.
Barangay Daang Bakal, meanwhile, appeared to have a response to the criticism.
After the backlash, the barangay posted a video showing its new vehicle being used to distribute free lettuce to residents.
“Gamit ang ating bagong Barangay Service Patrol na J5 na pinag-usapan ng madlang people. Basta tama ang gamit, masustansyang buhay ang makakamit!” the barangay wrote in a Facebook post.
(Using our new J5 Barangay Service Patrol that everyone has been talking about. As long as it’s used properly, a healthy life will be achieved!)
Well, at least the new car is already making rounds.
But did barangay operations really require 27 vehicles worth over P1 million each? – Rappler.com

articles.title: Over 1,800 inmate records await review for parole, clemency
articles.summary: In a statement on Thursday, November 26, Catapang disclosed that a total of 1,893 carpetas—or inmate case records—remain pending before the board.

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 5:10pm
The front gate of the New Bilibid Prison in Muntinlupa City.
muntinlupacity.gov.ph

MANILA, Philippines — Nearly 1,900 case records of persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) submitted by the Bureau of Corrections are currently awaiting review by the Board of Pardons and Parole (BPP), BuCor Director General Gregorio Pio Catapang Jr. said.
In a statement on Thursday, November 26, Catapang disclosed that a total of 1,893 carpetas, or inmate case records, remain pending before the board.
Of this number, 1,513 are up for parole consideration, while 380 are being evaluated for executive clemency.
Catapang issued the clarification to dispel misconceptions that the BPP is waiting for BuCor to transmit prison records, noting that the board has the capacity to review up to 500 carpetas per month.

To streamline the evaluation process prior to submission, Catapang said BuCor has established a Management, Screening, and Evaluation Committee across all prisons and penal farms nationwide, each headed by its respective prison superintendent.

To streamline the evaluation process prior to submission, Catapang said BuCor has established a MSEC across all prisons and penal farms nationwide, each headed by its respective prison superintendent.

At the New Bilibid Prison, which holds the largest inmate population among the country's penal colonies, separate MSECs operate within its Minimum, Medium, and Maximum Security Camps, led by their respective camp commanders.

These committees are tasked with screening, evaluating, and recommending PDLs for time allowances, early release, parole, or executive clemency based on their behavior, rehabilitation progress, length of imprisonment, and compliance with existing rules.
From July 2022 to Oct. 15, 2026, 6,491 PDLs have been granted parole, according to the Department of Justice.
In the same period, 2,275 have been recommended for executive clemency, while 150 PDLs have been granted executive clemency.
As of August 2026, the congestion rate in Philippine prisons had decreased to 202%, from 214% in 2025.
From July 2022 to September 2026, 36,175 PDLs have also been released, according to the DOJ.

articles.title: Deadly fire erupts near Cairo killing dozens of people
articles.summary: At least 31 people have died in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo, after a fuel tanker overturned, says Egypt's health ministry.

blocks.text: Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured after a large fire broke out on a busy highway in Cairo.
Footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.
The fire occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, north of the old city centre. Egypt's health ministry said the injured were being treated at hospitals nearby.

Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported that a high-voltage cable fell in front of a fuel tanker, causing the driver to lose control and the tanker to overturn, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.
