articles.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
articles.summary: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.

blocks.text: US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.

Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

articles.title: DAR earmarks P600 million for El Niño response in 2027
articles.summary: The fund will benefit 26,900 agrarian reform beneficiaries, 734 organizations and 579 communities.

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 7:58am
A farmer tends a cracked and parched farmland at a rice field in Barangay Sabang, Naic, Cavite on April 23, 2026
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Agrarian Reform has allocated P600 million from its 2027 budget proposal for a quick response fund in anticipation of the impacts of El Niño.
Sen. Francisco “Kiko” Pangilinan said that the fund forms part of the department’s proposed safeguards against drought conditions brought by the weather pattern.
A separate amount of P949 million under the department’s maintenance and other operating expenses was designated to improve the incomes of agrarian reform beneficiaries.
Roughly P730 million from this bigger allotment will be used for major crop farm productivity enhancement, with the broader aim of boosting crop yields.
The remaining P219 million, meanwhile, will be used for sustainable livelihood support efforts like enterprise development and extension services.
These projects are in addition to existing efforts like solar-powered irrigation systems and the department’s endorsement of climate-resilient crops to beneficiaries.
Pangilinan said that 26,900 agrarian reform beneficiaries stand to benefit from these allocations, as well as 579 communities and 734 agrarian reform beneficiaries’ organizations.
Agricultural losses associated with El Niño have reportedly breached P10 billion, prompting several areas to declare states of calamity.
The province of Isabela alone reported drought-related losses worth P2.88 billion across roughly 125,000 hectares of farmland.
Crop losses can drive up food costs by limiting supply. El Niño is expected to persist until early 2027.

articles.title: Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to weather
articles.summary: The was the first time ever that the iconic celebration - known for its massive balloons floating past the city's skyscrapers - was delayed because of storms.

blocks.text: The potent nor'easter storm is expected to make it too windy and dangerous for the iconic balloons to fly.

Macy's had expected to put 100 inflatables into the sky to mark its 100th parade and feature 10 new balloons, including one depicting the animated dog Bluey wearing a crown and another showing a Minion character riding a banana like a horse.

"While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants and spectators is, and always will be, our top priority," said Will Cross, the parade's executive producer, during a news conference on Wednesday with city officials.
Cross also said the giant balloons would be deflated on Wednesday night and stored at a facility in neighbouring New Jersey until they were reinflated for the parade on Saturday.
Macy's confirmed the new parade date and updated a countdown clock on its website to reflect the Saturday schedule. Meanwhile, broadcaster NBC has said it will show the 2025 parade on Thursday.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who will not attend the parade on Saturday because of a scheduled surgery, said at the news conference that "you have to plan for every possibility" and confirmed that "extreme weather has forced" officials to make the change.

"We know that this is an inconvenience for many who come to visit our city. This decision, however, was made with safety being paramount," he said. "We want to ensure that we're delivering a parade that's not only incredible and spectacular, but one also that doesn't come at the expense of anyone's safety."
Mamdani also said that there would be an expanded police presence along the parade route on Saturday and that there were "no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time".

Cross added that Macy's is working through what costs it could cover as a result of the delay and said the company is in contact with bands, performers and others who travelled to the city for the parade.

articles.title: A renovation to upgrade these Hong Kong homes ended in an inferno that killed 168
articles.summary: A year after one of Hong Kong's deadliest fires, families left behind are still waiting for justice.
articles.byline: Grace Tsoi, Phoebe Kong, Yvette Tan

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
The fire was one of Hong Kong's deadliest in decades
ByGrace TsoiBBC World ServicePhoebe KongBBC Chinese Reporting fromHong Kong and Yvette Tan
It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.
At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.

It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.
"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.
When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.
She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.

Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.
It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Lau Man Kwong took care of his grandson before his death (blurred at source)

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied
Lau Man Kwong took care of his grandson before his death (blurred at source)
"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.
She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.
The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet.
"He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin".
"I would have held onto my husband and died with him.
"He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way."
Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed.
She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park.
"All three of my children adored my husband… He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh."
No way out
In 2024, mandated renovations began in Wang Fuk Court.
In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result.

Like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; £32.4m).

Residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy.
Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere.
The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette.
Watch: Christy says she still sends WhatsApp messages to her husband who died in the blaze

There were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months.
All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding.

The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents".

Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say.
It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself.
ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously".

But for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes.
Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Christy's daughter celebrated her ninth birthday the day before the fire

blocks.text: Image source, Lam Yik / BBC Chinese
Christy's daughter celebrated her ninth birthday the day before the fire

Christy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, says her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off.
She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she says that is at least of some consolation to her.
"My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very least… his suffering was minimal."
Christy says her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it.
Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father.
Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father.
He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family.
"He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression.
Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she says, and channels her emotions through art.
She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight.
Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father.
Bid-rigging and rubber stamps
Wang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began.

The management company hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record.

The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects.

Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added.
Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response.

Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.
Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet.
The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible".

But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum".

One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the event the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year.

On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Homeowners at Wang Fuk Court (pictured) were told their construction company had a clean record

blocks.text: Homeowners at Wang Fuk Court (pictured) were told their construction company had a clean record
A shell of a home
Five months after the fire, Mrs Lau was allowed into her flat for the first time to collect any personal belongings that might have remained.
In her first visit, she was given just three hours to retrieve 40 years' worth of belongings.
Pictures taken from the visit show a home that has been utterly burned out - with every surface blackened and soot covering the floor.
"I almost fainted when I saw what had become of my home. I don't understand how the home I had built, such a warm and beautiful home, could end up like this," said Mrs Lau.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The frame of Mr Lau's wheelchair was one of the few things left in their burnt home

blocks.text: The frame of Mr Lau's wheelchair was one of the few things left in their burnt home

Her children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years.
"Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," said Mrs Lau.
Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a new house.
The government has said it will spend $867m (£663m) to acquire affected flats - but Mrs Lau says it is not nearly enough to buy a similarly sized flat in the area.
Still, her family was in a better position than many others, she said.
"Should I say that we are fortunate?
"I lost my husband but many families lost multiple family members... Babies less than a year old died. "
Stories have emerged of some of the other victims - a six-month-old who died alongside her 68-year-old grandmother when the fire broke out.
The bodies of an Indonesian domestic helper and the elderly person she worked for were found huddled together.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mrs Lau's son has since bought new piggy banks in memory of his father

blocks.text: Image source, BBC Chinese / Phoebe Kong
Mrs Lau's son has since bought new piggy banks in memory of his father
As for Christy, she says she is planning to file a lawsuit against those responsible for the fire - but acknowledges that even if she wins, she "can't [get] my husband's life back".
"I share things that happen in our daily life, as if he still existed," she says. "I often write to him, 'I miss you so much. Are you doing well on the other side?'"
It's a similar story for Mrs Lau, who says she can't go anywhere without seeing her husband.
"Every day, something reminds me of him," she said.
"I still find it very hard to accept that my husband is gone, my home is gone, and so many of my neighbours are gone…. This place was my roots. I never imagined it would also mark an ending for me."

articles.title: Jury selection discussed for trial of Quiboloy co-defendant Felina Salinas
articles.summary: A federal judge and attorneys in Los Angeles discussed jury selection for the trial of Felina Salinas, also known as “Sis Eng Eng,” a Hawaii-based administrator of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC).

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 7:25am

NEW YORK —A federal judge and attorneys in Los Angeles discussed jury selection for the trial of Felina Salinas, also known as “Sis Eng Eng,” a Hawaii-based administrator of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC).

Salinas is a co-defendant of Apollo Quiboloy, founder of the Philippines-based church, in a sex trafficking case in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California. The court calendar listed Salinas as out on bond.

A 2021 superseding indictment charged Salinas with conspiracy to engage in sex trafficking and multiple substantive counts of sex trafficking. Federal prosecutors allege that she helped recruit girls and young women to serve as Quiboloy’s personal assistants, known as “pastorals,” as part of a scheme to coerce them into sexual acts with him.

At the final status conference, the judge and attorneys discussed trial preparations, including voir dire, the process of questioning prospective jurors to determine whether they can decide the case fairly and impartially.

U.S. District Judge Percy Anderson set noon on Nov. 25, 2026, as the deadline for filing a motion in limine seeking a pretrial ruling on whether or how prosecutors may use a particular photograph at trial. The response is due Nov. 30, 2026.
Separate federal case in Hawaii

In June 2020, Salinas pleaded guilty to making a false statement to federal authorities. She had claimed that a cash-filled suitcase aboard a private jet bound for the Philippines was hers. The suitcase reportedly belonged to Quiboloy.

On Feb. 13, 2018, U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers inspected the jet at Honolulu’s Daniel K. Inouye International Airport before its scheduled departure. Salinas declared US$40,000 and 1,000 Philippine pesos.

Officers found about US$40,000 in a red backpack. In a separate carry-on suitcase, they found bundles of cash rolled up inside black socks. The suitcase reportedly contained about US$335,000 and A$9,000.
In October 2020, Salinas was sentenced to 30 days in jail and ordered to pay a $500 fine.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Palestinian journalist killed by Israel in Gaza wins Rory Peck prize
articles.summary:
Mariam Dagga shares award with two of her colleagues from AP for ‘powerful coverage’ of human cost of war

Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in…

blocks.text: Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza in an Israeli strike, has posthumously won the prestigious Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists, the organisers announced on Wednesday.

She shares the award with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press (AP), Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi, “for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war” in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said.
Dagga, who has a teenage son named Ghaith, was killed in August 2025 in an Israeli airstrike on a southern Gaza hospital, which claimed the lives of four other journalists.
The independent photographer and reporter had been working with the AP news agency since the beginning of the current conflict, triggered by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.

Dagga was renowned for her relentless reporting despite the personal losses she suffered throughout the war. She filmed the death of a protester who was shot during the 2018 Great March of Return in Gaza, when Israeli forces shot protesters marching towards the Gaza border fence, killing more than 220 people and wounding more than 9,200. She later discovered that the protester was her brother.
The war correspondent continued her work as a journalist during the war in Gaza over the last 22 months, working as a freelancer with the AP and Independent Arabia.

blocks.caption: Mariam Dagga’s father holds a camera and mobile phone belonging to his daughter after she was killed in August 2025. Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP

blocks.text: The AP’s executive editor, Julie Pace, said: “Journalists play an essential role in documenting events and informing the public, often at enormous personal risk.
“We honour Mariam and all journalists killed during this conflict and other conflicts – and remain committed to seeking answers about their deaths.”
French photographer Robin Tutenges was the recipient of the first Rory Peck award for photojournalism in recognition of his work on the conflict in Ethiopia’s northern Amhara region.

Sudanese freelance photographer and video journalist Ahmed Mohamed Abdalla, who works with Agence France-Presse, was shortlisted for the same award for his coverage of the fall of El Fasher to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Sudan’s civil war.
Abdalla was not allowed to attend the prize-giving ceremony in London as the UK government refused to grant him a visa.

In a recorded video message shared during the ceremony, he told of how the capital of the North Darfur region’s besieged inhabitants had to eat livestock feed to survive amid the daily deluge of missiles.
The prize has been awarded since 1995 in memory of Northern Irish video journalist Rory Peck, who was killed in Moscow in 1993, to celebrate the work of freelance video journalists.

articles.title: Record-breaking California tides cause major flooding of roads and businesses
articles.summary:
Beaches close as Los Angeles and La Jolla see all-time high tides and big waves batter landmark pier in Pacifica

Super El Niño weather brought record-breaking high tides up and down the…

blocks.text: Super El Niño weather brought record-breaking high tides up and down the California coast on Wednesday, sending seawater rushing into beachside communities and flooding roads and businesses.

As big waves battered the coast, the tip of a landmark pier in Pacifica, south of San Francisco, was slammed into the sea, local news outlets reported. The pier, which had once housed a favorite local cafe, had previously suffered structural damage and had been closed to the public, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.

Los Angeles and Santa Barbara tied or broke all-time high tide records on Wednesday, at 8.19 and 8.21ft, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). La Jolla, California, just north of San Diego, also set an all-time high tide record of 8.11ft (2.5 meters), according to the National Weather Service, while preliminary data suggested that tides in Monterey, south of San Francisco, might also have set an all-time record at 8.03ft.
The city of Monterey closed multiple beaches to the public over safety concerns, with closures lasting until Friday.
“That sun may be out, but the beach and surf zone remain dangerous,” NWS San Francisco warned, citing waves around the San Francisco Bay area as high as 24ft.

blocks.caption: Waves crash while a king tide and a series of storms begin to hit the Pacific north-west in Pacifica, California. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters

blocks.text: In Pacifica, local video and live streams showed giant crashing waves, tide waters sweeping over beaches and piers, and flooded coastal roads. Tide waters flooded areas of including Highway 1, including near the famous local landmark Taco Bell Cantina, America’s poshest Taco Bell, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.
Low-lying coastal roads around the Bay Area saw flooding, including a stretch of road near the Golden Gate Bridge, which was temporarily closed, the Chronicle reported.
Wednesday’s blue skies and early reports suggested that most of the state is on track to avoid the worst-case scenario – coastal flooding amplified by intense winter rainstorms.

“We’re past high tide, and San Francisco has made it through the worst of this round of king tides,” mayor Daniel Lurie said in a social media statement just after noon local time, saying officials were “only aware of minimal impacts across the city”.

Local officials had been preparing for weeks for the risk that flooding would disrupt travel during Thanksgiving week, one of the busiest times of the year. Experts warn that flooding risk will only worsen in the next two months.

Flooding risk at San Francisco international airport, a major transit hub situated on low-lying coastal land, had been of particular concern. At least three airlines offered free trip changes to travelers whose journeys took them through San Francisco on Wednesday, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.
But the airport announced at noon that “We’re in the clear,” and said it was deactivating its emergency operations center after avoiding any impact from the high tides on Tuesday and Wednesday.

On the north coast, the National Weather Service reported that Humboldt Bay saw its second highest tide on record, and advised residents to prepare for major coastal flooding in low lying areas. The county sheriff warned the public to stay away from beaches during the storm.

A local news outlet in Oregon shared a video on Tuesday that illustrated the risk of the west coast’s high-tide surf, showing a man and his dog almost getting swept away by unexpectedly high waves during the king tides in Cannon Beach, Oregon. Both man and dog escaped without injury, police told KVAL News.

blocks.caption: A  flooded neighborhood during a king tide event in Pacifica, California. Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Citing Wednesday’s forecast, some cities on California’s central coast, including Santa Cruz, Monterey and Carmel-by-the-Sea, announced they would be closing beaches starting on Tuesday evening because of the potential dangers, KSBW Action News reported.

“California took early action to prepare for El Niño, and we’re continuing that work by strengthening flood defenses, positioning emergency supplies, and coordinating with local emergency crews to reduce risks to communities,” California governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement on Tuesday, warning residents to take extra caution when preparing for holiday travel.

The California governor’s office of emergency services deployed crews and equipment around the state to assist with storm response. In the Bay Area, crews could be seen preparing sandbags to help protect buildings from flooding.

California’s flooding risk this week is the result of a combination of factors, some of them driven by this year’s super El Niño weather, including the lingering effects of the massive Kelvin wave that traveled up California’s coast. The overlap of unusually high Pacific coast water levels this year with the seasonal high tides called “king tides” has sparked alarm from weather experts, who have warned that the most dangerous flooding is likely to occur if a strong winter storm with heavy wind and rain hits areas of the coast at the same time as the high tide’s peak.

So far, it seems like California has avoided the worst of that risk during the November king tide period. But the amplified king tides will return twice more, around late December and then in late January, in periods where big winter storms remain likely.
Dani Anguiano contributed reporting

articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65
articles.summary: The band had numerous hits in the 1980s including "Girls on Film" and "Hungry Like The Wolf."

image.caption: Andy Taylor fought 'a long and courageous battle' with prostate cancer, his family saidImage: IPA/ABACA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer," his family announced on Wednesday. He was 65.
Taylor was responsible for 1980s new wave hits like "Girls on Film," "Hungry Like The Wolf" and "Rio."

"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music," the band said in a statement.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."
More to follow...

articles.title: Andy Taylor, guitarist of new wave icons Duran Duran, dead at 65
articles.summary: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, has died. He was 65.

image.caption: Andy Taylor of Duran Duran performs on stage in April 2004 during a celebration of the band's 25th anniversary. Taylor died this week at the age of 65, his family and bandmates said in a statement posted on social media Wednesday. (Jo Hale/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, has died. He was 65.
Taylor brought 'indelible fire and swagger to our music', band says in statement
Taylor's death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran's website.
"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music," the band said.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."
On the night he was inducted in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.

items: Duran Duran still 'preaching to the unconverted' 38 years later

blocks.text: "I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band," he wrote. "You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one's own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible."
The band's huge pop hits include Hungry Like the Wolf, The Reflex and Rio and whose rise up the charts was inextricably linked to the launch of MTV.

The two-time Grammy Award winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the UK and 18 in the U.S. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.
Andy Taylor, second from right, poses with his bandmates of British pop group Duran Duran in 1983. (Express Newspapers/Getty Images)
Fashion, synthesizers and glam-pop

The band's imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as Girls on Film and Union of the Snake and the moody ballads The Chauffeur and Save a Prayer. Other hits in the coming years included The Wild Boys, New Moon on Monday and Come Undone.
Their popularity was cemented when they recorded the James Bond theme song A View to a Kill and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.

Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesizers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band were all over radio and young people's walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heartthrobs and the band being labelled part of the New Romantics. Princess Diana was known to be a fan, which meant a lot to the band.
The band's success was in large part to their videos, including their Antigua-set song Rio, which featured shots of the band in pastel suits sailing confidently on a yacht.
From the archives: Duran Duran plays Calgary at the height of their fame

For the album Rio, they shot three music videos in Sri Lanka — including Save a Prayer, for which bass guitarist John Taylor was sprayed by an elephant — and two in Antigua, feeding MTV's need to have a stream of visuals, something classic rock didn't have.
"A lot of the success of the album is down to the power of the videos and the way it made the band omnipresent around the globe," Le Bon told the Daily Beast in 2012.
Andy Taylor agreed: "I don't think we could have done it without MTV."

articles.title: At least 30 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
articles.summary:
Blaze on ring road surrounding Egyptian capital injures at least 25 people and leaves cars and motorcycles charred

A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway…

blocks.text: A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 30 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 25 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, the public prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
The stretch of the highway where the crash occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, according to the health ministry.

blocks.caption: Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb, where charred vehicles remained after the blaze. Photograph: Amr Abdallah Dalsh/Reuters

blocks.text: At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.
The Egyptian president, Abdel-Fattah al-Sissi, expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The public prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were under way to identify the victims.

The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further.

Deadly traffic incidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.
In January, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

articles.title: Egypt: At least 31 dead after fuel truck overturns on highway
articles.summary: The accident occurred on the packed Ring Road in Giza near Cairo. Dozens of ambulances are responding to the crash, and Egyptian health authorities say the death toll could rise.

image.caption: Rescue workers rushed to the scene and pulled people out of burning cars Image: Mohammed Salah/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A fuel truck overturned on a packed highway in Giza, Egypt, on Wednesday, killing 31 people and injuring 21 more, according to Egyptian authorities.
What do we know so far?
The fuel tanker crash ignited a massive blaze on Ring Road in Giza's Waraq district. The Ring Road encircles the greater Cairo metropolitan area.

Egyptian Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured were transported to nearby hospitals and added that the death toll could rise further. He said 39 ambulances are responding to the accident.

blocks.caption: Cars were seen burned out after the accidentImage: Mahmoud el-Khawas/AFP

blocks.text: A massive fire broke out after the accident, with rescue workers pulling people from their vehicles. A large crowd gathered in the densely populated Waraq neighborhood amid the rescue efforts.
An investigation has been launched into the crash, according to Egypt's public prosecutor. DNA tests are being carried out to identify badly burned victims of the blaze.
El-Sissi expresses condolences to the victims

Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his deepest condolences and sympathy to the victims and directed relevant authorities to provide necessary support to the families of the victims and the injured.

Italian Foreign Affairs Minister Antonio Tajani said he extended his "deepest solidarity to the victims' families," Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty "and to the Egyptian people, whom I count as friends, at this tragic time."
Car accidents are frequent in Egypt due to poor road conditions, reckless driving and lax enforcement of safety rules.

articles.title: At least 30 killed in massive fire as fuel truck crashes on Cairo highway
articles.summary: Another 19 are injured after the tanker reportedly overturns on a busy ring road in the Egyptian capital.

blocks.text: At least 30 people have been killed and 19 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.

Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.
Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.
Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the fuel truck had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.
The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.

The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.
It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.

Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.
Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.

articles.title: B.C.'s new premier outlines 3 immediate priorities after first cabinet meeting
articles.summary: B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson says he's taking immediate action on three top priorities after his first cabinet meeting. They include posting a notice of intent for a design of a bridge option to…

image.caption: B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson speaks at a news conference on Wednesday. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson says he's taking immediate action on three top priorities after his first cabinet meeting. They include posting a notice of intent for a design of a bridge option to replace the George Massey Tunnel, taking SOGI 123 materials off government websites, and starting a return-to-office plan for the B.C. Public Service.
Lorne Doerkson's top 3 to-dos: George Massey replacement, removing SOGI materials, return-to-office
B.C. Premier Lorne Doerkson has announced he's taking immediate action on three top priorities after his first cabinet meeting.
Doerkson listed his first priority as posting a notice of intent for a design of a bridge option to replace the George Massey Tunnel between Richmond and Delta.
He said at a news conference Wednesday afternoon the notice would be posted later in the day and will ask the current contractor to do the work.
He said cabinet would review the numbers before making a final decision to ensure the project is the most cost-effective.
"Our responsibility is to ensure taxpayers get the best value for their money," Doerkson said.
He said British Columbians want access over the river, and he wants the space to understand the project.
"I am, obviously, very big on 'bridge' right now, but I do want to understand a few things just before that final decision happens, and I hope that to happen before Christmas."
The previous B.C. NDP government had planned to replace the tunnel, rather than build a bridge.

items: Here are 5 promises the B.C. Conservative government could get started on right away
B.C. Premier Doerkson's mandate letters call for health-care guarantee, reforming carbon pricing

blocks.text: Secondly, Doerkson said SOGI 123 materials will be taken off government websites "as of today."

SOGI (which stands for sexual orientation and gender identity) 123 has been a resource teachers and educators can turn to to make schools safer and more inclusive for students of all gender identities and orientations, according to its website.
Doerkson said the Ministry of Education will work with school districts to take SOGI 123 materials out of schools.
"We are starting that work right now."
He said parents should have a say in how and when "sensitive topics" are introduced in schools.
"We want our schools to be safe and welcoming places, of course, for every student, with a strong focus on reading, writing, arithmetic and on teaching kids to think for themselves," Doerkson said.

items: Can the B.C. Conservatives actually repeal SOGI 123 in schools? What you need to know

blocks.text: He said he wants to "better understand how our schools were not safe prior to SOGI" and "how we will make sure that our student body is safe."
He added: "SOGI, of course, has been conflated with so much now — I'm not certain that I've even been able to get a good explanation from ministry staff or from teachers, frankly, on this topic."
Doerkson responded to a reporter's question on what would happen if teachers continue to use the SOGI resource.
"We've asked for it to be removed from the rooms, so it's not just that they'll get pushback from parents, but they'll get pushback from me as well."
Return-to-office planned for public servants
Doerkson's third priority is for B.C. Public Service workers to return to the office in a phased plan.
Those who can work from the office "will be back at it, five days a week," Doerkson said.
He said he's written to the head of the public service to start planning for the return-to-office policy.
He said thousands of public servants, such as nurses, teachers, correctional workers and those providing frontline services, have never had the choice to work remotely.
"I think it's reasonable to ask for people in our offices to do the same," Doerkson said, adding people collaborate better in the same room.
With files from Akshay Kulkarni

articles.title: Nigeria detains 5 Mexicans, confiscates over $220 million of meth
articles.summary: Nigeria's anti-drug agency said Mexican experts were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national to run a meth laboratory in the southeastern state of Enugu.

image.caption: At least 10 Mexicans are now in Nigerian custody, including five from an earlier raidImage: NDLEA/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLA) said Wednesday it had arrested five Mexicans and confiscated over $220 million (around €200 million) in methamphetamine as part of a significant drug bust.
What do we know about the drug bust?
The agency said the Mexican experts were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national to run a meth laboratory in the southeastern Nigerian state of Enugu.

"A total of 1,512 kilograms of methamphetamine, finished and in production, with an estimated value of $226.8 million was recovered from the clandestine factory," NDLA spokesperson Femi Babafemi said.

Nigeria first rejected the entry of the Mexicans into the country in August. They later entered Nigeria again in September via neighboring Benin using forged passports, with authorities then putting them under surveillance.
On November 11, the Mexicans were taken into custody at the Enugu lab after their movements were tracked by the Nigerian government. A Nigerian was also arrested in a nearby hotel.

blocks.caption: Nigerian authorities inspected the Enugu facility and seized industrial equipment along with chemicalsImage: NDLEA/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: The latest drug bust comes after Nigerian authorities in May also detained 10 people in a anti-meth operation in the southwest, including three Mexicans.
Why do Mexican cartels find African countries desirable for drug production?

The arrests raise concern that Mexican cartels are getting a foothold in Africa for international drug trafficking. In addition to Nigeria, South Africa is another country where Mexicans have been arrested for being involved in a meth lab.

According to Vanda Felbab-Brown, an expert at the Washington DC-based Brookings Institution, Mexican cartels such as the Sinaloa Cartel and the Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generation (CJNG) have expanded their operations into other continents such as Africa.
How drug cartels expand their reach across West Africa

In a June testimony to the US Senate Caucus on International Narcotics Control, Felbab-Brown said the cartels find "desirable partners" for production in countries such as South Africa and Kenya due to factors such as "limited law enforcement capacities and entrenched criminal and corrupt networks."
According to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime,criminal networks often take advantage of porous borders in the West and Central Africa region to carry out activities such as illicit drug trafficking.

"Many countries in the region have vast territory and borders are located either in very remote or densely populated areas, thus making law enforcement activities particularly difficult to conduct in an efficient manner," the office said. "The porous nature of the borders in West and Central Africa is a major factor of insecurity: the borders are neither demarcated or sufficiently controlled."

articles.title: Australian politics live: federal Liberal senator Leah Blyth defects to One Nation
articles.summary: • Get our breaking news email, free app or

blocks.text: Federal Liberal senator Leah Blyth defects to One Nation
Leah Blyth, federal Liberal senator for South Australia, is defecting to One Nation and will become the party’s first upper-house member for the state, according to The Australian.
The move will cause recriminations in Coalition ranks because Blyth is a member of Angus Taylor’s shadow cabinet.
But she told the paper she no longer felt the Coalition was capable of opposing the Albanese government, which was “running the country into the ground”.
She said:

double quotation markI can no longer in good conscience tell Australians that the Liberal party can save this country. Australia is a country worth fighting for … I want our children to grow up proud of their country, with the freedom and opportunity to build a better life. One Nation has never shied away from confronting the uncomfortable truths facing our nation. They are the only party with the bold ideas needed to turn this country around.
Key events

items: 12m agoBlyth ‘wasn’t a big contributor to the party room’: Jane Hume
31m agoBlyth defection ‘smacks of self-interest’, Nationals leader says
44m agoFederal Liberal senator Leah Blyth defects to One Nation
46m agoEnergy minister says geopolitical tension ‘infected’ Cop31 talks

blocks.text: Blyth defection shows disunity in Liberal party: Cabinet minister

Labor will get a good kick out of this story today, particularly after securing a few legislative wins with the help of the Greens this week. (Although I would say the wins were bigger for the Greens who got massive concessions out of the government on the digital duty of care, trusts, and private health insurance bills.)
Cabinet minister, Pat Conroy, doesn’t want to stick the knife in too hard though this morning, deferring the question to the Coalition.
But he says regardless of who defects where, the Liberals and One Nation “can’t govern without each other”.
He tells ABC News Breakfast:

double quotation markWe are facing at the next election clearly a Coalition and Liberals and One Nation with all the baggage that each of these parties brings to the table. They’re all anti-worker, they’re all extreme … this demonstrates, I think, more disunity in the Liberal Party under Angus Taylor.
Blyth ‘wasn’t a big contributor to the party room’: Jane Hume
The claws are OUT this morning.
The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, has been stopped by journos on her way into Parliament House, and is clearly incensed by her Senate colleague Leah Blyth’s defection.
She, like Matt Canavan, says it’s a “disappointing decision”.

double quotation markThe fact that she feels that the Liberal party doesn’t reflect her views any more is a surprise to all of us. It’s certainly not something that she ever mentioned in the party room – but she wasn’t a big contributor to the party room.
Ouch.
Asked what her highlight of the year is, Hume says “unity” in the Liberal and National parties (notwithstanding the last 24 hours).

blocks.caption: Jane Hume in the Coalition party room on Tuesday. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images

blocks.text: ‘Turncoat town’: Canavan takes a crack at Blyth and One Nation
Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, is pretty salty this morning – taking another crack at Leah Blyth over her defection from the Liberal party to One Nation.
He calls One Nation “turncoat town” by hoovering up defectors from other parties.
Speaking to journos in the press gallery corridor after his RN Breakfast interview, he doesn’t hold back:

double quotation markI think people see that as a defection, as a turncoat, and One Nation is becoming turncoat town right now, where they seem to be much more focused on taking people away from other political parties than changing the government, and therefore changing the policy and changing the direction of this country. I don’t buy Leah’s explanation that this is some grand policy principle. It instead just smacks of self-interest.

blocks.caption: Krishani Dhanji

blocks.text: Krishani Dhanji
Good morning
Krishani Dhanji here with you for the final sitting day of the year, thanks to Martin Farrer.
Just when I thought this week couldn’t get any busier, Leah Blyth said “hold my beer”.
It’s going to be a cracker today – let’s get stuck in!
Blyth defection ‘smacks of self-interest’, Nationals leader says
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, has called Leah Blyth’s defection to One Nation “disappointing on a number of levels”.
Speaking to Radio National, Canavan said he thought he was friends with Blyth but that he had received no warning of her move.

double quotation markI always find it disappointing when someone leaves the party [that] they were elected under, particularly in the Senate, because I know as a senator, you’re not really elected in your own name, you’re elected as a party … And so it’s right that people feel a bit let down when someone[who is] elected by them ticking a party box changes parties after the election.
Speaking to Blyth’s reasoning that her values aligned more closely with One Nation, Canavan said the move “smacks of self-interest to me”.

double quotation markGood luck to her. Leah went to the election last year supporting net zero. She didn’t oppose the hate speech laws earlier this year, like we did – the Nationals. To turn around now a few months later and say … “my principles and policies are more aligned with One Nation,” I mean, give me a break.

blocks.caption: Matt Canavan. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP

blocks.text: Energy minister says geopolitical tension ‘infected’ Cop31 talks

blocks.caption: Catie McLeod

blocks.text: Catie McLeod
The energy minister, Chris Bowen, has said the failed Cop31 negotiations he presided over were more strained than previous years.

Bowen, who served as president of negotiations at the talks in Turkey, was interviewed on the ABC’s 7.30 program last night about the conference, which did not result in consensus among the countries over a proposed “cover decision”, or an overarching agreement, for the conference.
Bowen told the ABC it was not unusual that the negotiations were difficult, but:

double quotation markThe difference this year was countries were a lot harder to budge from their position and frankly I felt a lot of geopolitical tension in the room on other issues infecting the conversation and making it so much harder to negotiate. I’ve been to five Cops, seen plenty of argy-bargy, but there was a lot more rigidness to the negotiations this year. We [Australia] have always supported transition away from fossil fuels. This year I had a slightly different job. Normally we go – I go – to Cops and argue for what should be in. This year my job, running the negotiation – was to find ... the strongest outcome that I could get 195 countries from Tuvalu to Saudi Arabia to agree [on].
As Guardian Australia previously reported, the biggest sticking point was whether the agreement would mention the need for the world to transition away from fossil fuels.

blocks.caption: Tess Ikonomou

blocks.text: Tess Ikonomou
Labor and Coalition on cusp of gas deal
A federal scheme requiring Australia’s largest gas exporters to keep up to a fifth of their product for domestic use is likely to be announced, with Labor and the Coalition on the cusp of a deal.
The Albanese government and the opposition have been locked in negotiations to reach an agreement before parliament breaks for the year after Thursday.
Labor agreed to a carve-out from the policy for Western Australia, as the mining state already has its own reservation scheme.
But the Coalition has held out over a provision that will require gas companies to oversupply the market by 10%, arguing it will affect future investment.
The opposition has remained the government’s partner of choice for this policy, as the Greens demanded a 25% tax on gas exports in return for their support.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

articles.title: Moment Nasa spacecraft hit asteroid - and what happened next
articles.summary: The crash was 'like something out of a disaster movie,' the BBC's science editor Rebecca Morelle says.

blocks.text: The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.
Video released by Nasa showed the moment of impact in 2022, while new images show the extent of the damage done to the asteroid.
Dimorphos, the asteroid, posed no threat to Earth, but the crash was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.
Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.
The BBC's science editor Rebecca Morelle explains.

articles.title: Lululemon founder stuns Canadian women’s leadership conference with sexist comments
articles.summary:
Chip Wilson said men importing brides from Thailand was due to women waiting too long to have children

The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in

blocks.text: The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in Canada are having too few children and this could lead some men to bring in brides from Thailand, in remarks that stunned audience members at a women’s leadership conference.

Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. The organization says it aims to create space for “candid conversations about the barriers women face both in business and society”.

Wilson’s talk on 23 November, titled “Little Black Stretchy Pants” after his memoir, was billed as an “intimate, fireside chat” offering insight into the “mind and instincts of the man himself”. It was moderated by Nuvyn Peters, CEO of Axis Connects.

There is no publicly available video of the event, but the Guardian spoke with people who attended it and reviewed social media posts from those present. Outrage over the event was first reported by the Globe and Mail.

According to people who were there, Wilson told the audience that companies would be reluctant to hire a 22-year-old woman because she might become pregnant at 23 and take maternity leave. He went on to suggest that women were waiting too long to have children, prompting men to import brides from Thailand.
“There were audible gasps in the room and everyone was clearly uncomfortable. It was a mix of disengaging, walking out and also just complete shock of what was being said on stage,” one person said.

“I am floored that Axis gave this man a platform. We all were saying before the event it was surprising he was there – and it’s clear that [Wilson] runs in the organizer’s circles after she opened with the fact that they go on walks [at a Vancouver mountain] together.”
The event, which was supposed to run for an hour, was cut short at 45 minutes.

The remarks are not the first time Wilson has attracted criticism for his comments about women and their bodies. He stepped down as chair of Lululemon’s board in 2013 after the company’s signature black yoga pants were criticized for being see-through and Wilson blamed the problem on the body types of some customers.
On Monday, he reportedly told the group that those prior comments about body types had been “misconstrued” and said he was referring to women who wear sizes that are too small.
Wilson, who is believed to be worth more than C$6bn, has not had a leadership role at Lululemon for several years but remains a major shareholder.
He also reportedly told the audience that poverty had largely been eradicated, and that he was looking forward to going to space with Elon Musk.

Audience members also said Wilson suggested that men were better suited to helm clothing companies that catered to women, because they knew what looked good on women’s bodies. He said the same was true of women who lead companies focused on men’s fashion.

“We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the Leadership Forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects,” Peters said in a statement. “We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community. His comments also underscore an uncomfortable reality: attitudes and assumptions that hold women back in the workplace and in leadership have not disappeared. Challenging those attitudes is central to the work and ethos of Axis Connects.”

Wilson’s spokesperson pointed to the work the Lululemon founder has done to mentor and “empower” women in leadership roles over the years and said his efforts “speak for themselves”. A number of women who were early employees of the company and worked closely with Wilson became millionaires when the company went public, he has previously noted in his memoir, and have gone on to found their own businesses.

More than 700 women attended the conference, many representing organizations they worked for. One person said the experience left her “irate”, adding that it was also indicative of what women continued to tolerate.
“It’s just sad that this is what women still have to deal with, in a forum literally for women.”

articles.title: Health Canada issues warning on rare risk of vision loss with semaglutide GLP-1 drugs
articles.summary: A safety review from Health Canada has found a possible link between semaglutide GLP-1 drugs and a rare form of vision loss.

image.caption: Health Canada has issued a public warning about the 'very rare but serious' risk of vision loss tied to semaglutide GLP-1 drugs. (CBC)

blocks.text: Health·Breaking
A safety review from Health Canada has found a possible link between semaglutide GLP-1 drugs and a rare form of vision loss.
Federal team's safety review found possible link between use of drugs and 'very rare' eye condition
Health Canada has issued a public warning about the "very rare but serious" risk of vision loss tied to semaglutide GLP-1 drugs, known by brand names such as Ozempic, Rybelsus, and Wegovy.

On the heels of similar warnings in the U.S. and Europe, the federal department announced on Wednesday that it had completed its own safety review which found a possible link between prescription semaglutide drugs and the risk of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).
Described by Health Canada as "very rare," the eye condition causes sudden, painless blindness or vision changes due to reduced blood flow to the optic nerve.
The condition has no known treatment.
More to come.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Lauren Pelley is a senior health and medical reporter for CBC News. She's a two-time RNAO Media Award winner for in-depth health reporting in 2020 and 2022, a silver medallist for best editorial newsletter at the 2024 Digital Publishing Awards, and a 2024 Covering Climate Now award winner in the health category. Contact her at: lauren.pelley@cbc.ca.
