Hong Kong will host the 94th Interpol general assembly between 30 November and 3 December, attracting police chiefs from its 196 member countries to set global policing policy, approve budgets and activities, and pass binding resolutions.

Keith said that hosting the assembly offered an opportunity for China to “reputation wash”, arguing that Beijing ran a sophisticated public relations machine to hide the high proportion of red notice and extradition requests that were politically motivated.

The red notice system is used by China to target those sought under the state campaigns launched under President Xi Jinping to track down fugitives overseas and recover illicit funds, known as Operations Fox Hunt and Sky Net, it is claimed.

A new report, The Red Notice Trap, by Ben Keith and Rhys Davies of the legal firm IHR Advisors, draws on court judgments, Interpol records and Chinese-language official documents, to show how red notices fit into Beijing’s campaign to silence critics and bring them home for persecution.

It notes under a 2025 revision of the implementing regulations for the People’s Repubilc of China’s supervision law that red notice requests sit with extradition, judicial assistance, law enforcement cooperation, prosecution abroad, asset seizure and ‘ideological education’, as tools for the recovery of people.

blocks.caption: Yidiresi Aishan, AKA Idris Hassan, a Uyghur activist, was detained after a red notice was issued by Interpol at China’s request.  Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Among the cases cited in the IHR Advisors report is that of Yidiresi Aishan – a Uyghur activist who is also known as Idris Hassan – who was arrested in July 2021, when arriving at Casablanca airport on a flight from Turkey, where he had been living.

He was detained on the basis of a red notice issued by Interpol at China’s request “for belonging to a terrorist organisation”. Within two weeks, Interpol suspended the notice as it breached its rules and it was later cancelled.
The Moroccan extradition proceedings carried on regardless and in December 2021 the country’s court of cassation approved Hasan’s surrender to China.

The UN committee against torture found that Hasan’s extradition would breach article 3 of the convention against torture and Morocco did not carry out the extradition But Hasan remained in detention until 12 February 2025 after spending nearly four years in prison on the basis of an Interpol red notice.
“His case shows the central weakness this report returns to: Interpol can correct its own data, but it cannot undo what national authorities have already set in motion”, the authors write.
Hasan, who now lives in Canada, said he no longer travelled and that his life had been thrown “upside down”.
“Four years of life have gone, just spent in prison, I could not be with my children,” he told the Guardian. “Everything has changed. I cannot describe this. But I trust Canada.”
Hasan added: “I don’t understand how this kind of the big organisation like Interpol how they took my name down without evidence, without nothing. Just put my name out.”
Interpol and the Chinese embassy have been approached for comment.

articles.title: Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: ‘I still have a right to my beliefs’
articles.summary:
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, at center of legal fight, says he ‘should not be unjustly accused’ because of leftwing views

James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor…

blocks.text: James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is “not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I’m a jerk – but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them”.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
The complaint also includes riot and conspiracy to riot charges stemming from 2023 protests against New England branches of Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit.

Chambers was speaking from his Madrid apartment in his first in-depth interview after a Spanish appeals court ordered his provisional release on bail on Friday. That release was due to issues with the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported by the Guardian.
“Support for my case doesn’t imply support of me, or my ideas,” Chambers said. “It’s about my right to have those ideas – and not be falsely accused of things.”
Chambers, whose case has gained attention across the world, had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.

The order granting Chambers’s provisional release asserted that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”. Spanish judges had previously denied bail three times.

The wealthy heir to at least $250mn from his family’s business – Atlanta–based Cox Enterprises – was in the middle of his first visit without being separated by glass with his mother, Lauren Hamilton, when he was summoned to receive the “good news” on Friday, Chambers told the Guardian.

Minutes later, he returned to tell his mother he was being released. “She freaked out crying. We went nuts for about five minutes. Then we got to contacting my lawyer and getting my kids on a plane to Spain.”
On Monday, Chambers’s five-year-old son with actor and activist Stella Schnabel could be heard in the background. The tableau was in stark contrast to his months in prison.

“I tried to build a cocoon to deal with the immense unknown, the immense fear,” he said of his time in Aranjuez prison. “I would pray a lot. The only idea I could hold onto was, my home is the truth. The truth of who loves you. The truth of my own innocence. And the truth of what is happening in Palestine and all the things connected to what is happening in Palestine – other wars, gas prices. No one can take that away from you.”

blocks.caption: Stella Schnabel, Chambers’s wife, and lawyer Baltasar Garzon speak to the media in Madrid in September. Photograph: Eduardo Parra/Europa Press/Getty Images

blocks.text: Chambers has been supported by his mother throughout his case, and has reconnected with his father, James Cox Chambers – who owns an estimated 17% stake in Cox Enterprises but does not play an active role in the company – for the first time in five years.
“Speaking with my parents has provided emotional stability – and intelligent, adult minds to help make decisions,” Chambers said.

Although he has had political disagreements with his father, a donor to the Democratic party, Chambers said his father “sees this situation as totally unthinkable and out of step with anything resembling a just society”.
He also invoked his grandfather, the ACLU civil rights lawyer James Cox Hamilton, who died in 2014. “He would’ve turned in his grave over this,” Chambers said.

While locked up, Chambers, a US citizen, received hundreds of letters of support from friends, family and strangers, postmarked from Atlanta to Barcelona – including, he said, “from a guy who had been imprisoned under [Spanish dictator Francisco] Franco, who painted the ‘key of return’ [a symbol of homes lost in the 1948 Nakba] on the Palestinian flag”.

Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
after newsletter promotion

His release followed a separate decision on Thursday by a three-judge panel at Spain’s high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.

The US admitted to making several of the changes, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent”. These and dozens of other changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian last week.

It was also recently revealed that there is no indictment behind the complaint, meaning the federal government has not had a grand jury evaluate evidence against Chambers, and instead is seeking his extradition based on the affidavit of a single FBI agent, the core of the sealed criminal complaint.

During his time in prison, Chambers also began the process of applying for political asylum in Spain. He cannot be extradited until the asylum case runs its course, and also cannot be extradited if he is granted asylum. His legal team has notified the government office evaluating his asylum petition of the altered translations.

Chambers was arrested 10 July as he and Schnabel pulled into the driveway of a school they were visiting to see about enrolling their five-year-old, part of plans to move to Spain. They had been staying in Ireland, where Schnabel was working on a film.

Although the arrest came as a surprise – “I was confused! Did I speed?” he thought – Chambers revealed to the Guardian that a car had been following him around Dublin only days before, and that someone had broken into their car parked outside their house at night, without taking anything of value.
“I noticed signs of surveillance,” he said. Months later, last Wednesday, Irish police raided the same house, acting on a request from US authorities.
With his immediate future uncertain, Chambers said he was “looking forward to sharing a couple of nice dinners with my family this week”.
As for the past, he said the millions he has donated to an estimated 100 projects in about 20 countries is “the most important thing I’ve done”.

“Somebody with the political orientation I have and with resources, no matter how good of an activist I am, it’s not gonna be as effective as medical aid or feeding children in Gaza, supporting independent media that wouldn’t otherwise exist, or paying people’s bail who have been arrested for protesting.
“I’m giving a lot of money to things that other people aren’t giving money to.”
Chambers also said he was “grateful for the way Spanish courts have dealt with this – just focusing on the facts. It shouldn’t matter that I’ve made some emotional statements.”

articles.title: Climate loss and damage fund exists, but the money doesn't
articles.summary: Climate-vulnerable countries fought for years to create a loss and damage fund. Four years on, demand far outstrips funding, pledges are scarce, and disaster-hit nations are still waiting for support.

image.caption: Nepal in the aftermath of August flash floods that killed more than 1,500 people, with thousands more missingImage: Arun Sankar/AFP

blocks.text: On the sandbars and river islands of Bangladesh's Brahmaputra and its branches, families have little to fall back on when the water rises.
"The floodwater swallows everything," said 16-year-old Rasel Babu who had traveled to Antalya, Turkey to speak to delegates at the UN climate conference.

Created after years of pressure from vulnerable nations, the loss and damage fund was designed to help countries recover from climate disasters and irreversible climate impacts. This includes extreme weather events such as floods, heat waves and wildfires as well as slow onset impacts such as sea level rise, desertification and damage to infrastructure and crops.
But the fund is already struggling to meet demand. It received $2.8 billion (€2.56 billion) in urgent requests in a first call for funding, with only $342 million available at the time.
Even the money promised has not fully arrived. Only about half of the money currently pledged had been received by this summer.

While the European Commission signed a €25 million ($27 million) contribution agreement to the fund on the margins of COP31, formalizing an earlier pledge made at COP28, and Spain pledged an additional €15 million, other contributions to loss and damage remained scarce.
First payout will go to Nepal after glacier collapse

The fund's first emergency response is going to be paid out to Nepal. The board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage had provisionally set aside $21.6 million following the catastrophic glacier collapse that triggered flash floods in August, killing more than 1,500 people with 5,600 more missing.
But the money has not moved yet. Nepal must first submit a funding request setting out how it will be spent.

"It's asking for a country that is dealing with the climate emergency to work on a proposal," Nepali climate finance expert Bibek Raj Kandel said, adding a layer of bureaucracy inefficient to address the urgency.
UN warns climate change could force millions to move

Nepal is already waiting on another request, filed after floods in Kathmandu and landslides in the eastern hills. "There's already one pending proposal sitting on the table," Kandel said. Unless the fund speeds up, he warned, it's "going to disappoint many, many countries."
Pakistan which led the push for the fund in 2022 after floods affected 33 million people and killed more than 1,730, also hasn't seen any of the money yet.

"Pakistan was one of the countries which really spoke up and managed to get the loss and damage fund on the climate agenda. But it takes a long time," Pakistan's Minister of State for Climate Change, Shezra Mansab Ali Khan Kharal, told DW.

blocks.caption: In 2022, monsoon and floods killed more than 1,730 people in Pakistan, with 33 million people affectedImage: Akhtar Soomro/REUTERS

blocks.text: "We have still not really got anything. We haven't seen anything on the ground at all as yet," Kharal said. Pakistan has submitted two projects and was told the cap is $200 million.
Other forms of aid often come in the form of loans.

"These promises, they are hollow promises," said Abid Qaiyum Suleri, Executive Director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI) in Islamabad, adding that for a heavily indebted country, the form of the money matters as much as the amount.
"We do not want that a climate disaster in Pakistan should translate into further debt for Pakistan," Kharal said, calling for grants rather than loans.

articles.title: Germany's women's football team take stand against domestic violence
articles.summary: Germany's women's football team are to wear UN Women badges in games against Argentina and Peru, as domestic violence hits a record high in Germany.

image.caption: Germany's women have been strong supporters of the campaign, as the orange logo of 'stop violence agianst women' reveals on Lea Schüller's sleeveImage: imago images/Beautiful Sports

blocks.text: Domestic violence has reached a record high in Germany, with 16 women subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors each hour.

UN Women Germany is one of 13 UN Women national committees worldwide, each an independent, non-profit, non-governmental organization committed to gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls.

Their current campaign "Orange The World" runs from the start of International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women on November 25 to December 10, International Human Rights Day. It is designed to raise awareness around violence against women in the country and worldwide. The 2026 campaign's focus is particularly on men's responsibility in ending gender-based violence.

"In these 16 days of activism, we can deliver a lot of information. Survivors of gender-based violence can find out where to get support and be reminded that they are not at fault," UN Women Germany chair, politician and long-standing campaigner for women's rights Elke Ferner told DW. "The debate helps and it's a chance to change consciousness about the topic."

Germany captain Giulia Gwinn said in a statement via the German Football Association (DFB): "Violence against women and girls affects us all and must have no place in our society. As the women's national team, we therefore want to once again use our reach to create awareness for this important issue and jointly set a visible sign against violence."
The campaign with the women's team is not new. Two years ago, the team joined the campaign, delivering a moving video that saw players reveal the truth of statements by crossing out words.

During Germany's upcoming South America tour — part of their preparations for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil — they are to wear special UN Women Germany badges on their sleeves in their games against Argentina and Peru.
Role models pivotal for the campaign

Ferner believes the work with role models is pivotal and that the campaign is powerful, especially in a football context. A 2022 study from Warwick Business School in the UK revealed alcohol-related domestic abuse rises by nearly 50% after England's men's football team win a World Cup game, never mind lose.

Currently, there is no data on domestic abuse during Germany games, however during the 2026 World Cup last summer, Berlin police recorded a 31% increase in domestic violence compared to the week before.

Ferner is encouraged that sport has understood the importance of the issue, and that the German Olympic Committee (DOSB) and other sports clubs and organizations are helping move the conversation forward.

In sport, this is particularly important given the problematic nature of dependency relationships that so often exist in high-performance environments. But violence against women is really a societal issue that is not specific to class, origin, religion or societal space, such as sport.

"Violence against women has structural origins and to change that you need to change the structures," Ferner said. "You just need to do it. I always say, this isn't about a lack of knowledge but rather a lack of action."
Performance is an integral part of sport, but a multi-dimensional understanding of it might help shift perspective in a country that remains driven by a performance culture.

"What is performance? Higher, faster, further? Or is it managing to look after a family of three?" Ferner asked. "Why do people who repair washing machines earn more than those looking after your kids in nursery? This is about changing business culture, but also awareness around the role men play at home and in the family.

"The picture boys and young men get of girls and women in school is a problem that needs addressing. We can't wait for generational change. This is about saving lives. We need to change societal structures."
Male power structures a problem

Sports structures are also in need of reform. Non-profit organization Safe Sport provides independent support for people affected by sexual, physical and psychological violence in both amateur and professional sport in Germany.

They are the only organization with a specific focus on violence in grassroots sports in Germany, and one of only two in professional sport in the country. They also have to contend with structures, in a sporting context, that make spaces less safe for women.

"Gender roles have become more fluid in the last few years, but in associations and clubs management positions are still occupied by men, regardless of the sport," Safe Sport manager Ina Lambert told DW.
"In professional sport, there are a lot fewer women involved in training and so the space remains male dominated, and, as a result, so do the power structures.

"We have people in search of advice, men included, who see the problems and want to enforce change, and we offer them support so they are not alone," Lambert said. "But whether in a big association or a small club, perpetrators are frequently protected, incidents are ignored and so the people who want to enforce change are often prevented from doing so."

Safe Sport, which provides free psychological and legal support, has only been in action since July 2023, but in that time the number of support requests they have received continues to grow. Psychological violence in sport in Germany is the most common case they are faced with, but sexual violence is also a major problem.
"There is finally recognition of the problem and there is a seriousness about tackling it," Lambert said.

"There is a lot of good work being done in the right direction, with many good concepts for prevention, intervention and processing violence, as well as more education, holistic training and focus on women's menstrual cycles."

blocks.caption: Germany is backing UN efforts to highlight that more must be done to tackle violence against womenImage: imago images/Lucca Fundel

blocks.text: Comprehensive support on the way

Germany's Interior Ministry is leading the process with participants from the country's states, organized sport, affected parties and academia to create a central hub. The center for safe sport was founded in July 2026, but investigative and sanctioning work is expected to begin in the spring of 2027.
Support from leading figures clearly makes a huge difference, but it's also clear that more data is needed. Addressing the underlying issues, such as social norms and gender stereotyping, is a must.

After all, as UN Women Executive Director Sima Bahous said: "No country has yet eliminated violence against women. Ending it requires transformative action — greater investment, innovation, and unwavering political will."
This article was originally published on November 28, 2024, and updated on November 25, 2026.
Behind domestic violence: Causes, patterns and solutions

articles.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, says president
articles.summary:
Operation in which one hostage-taker was killed ends daylong siege in Cartegena shopping centre, where 30 people were initially held

Colombian security forces have stormed a supermarket in…

blocks.text: Colombian security forces have stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena, ending a daylong hostage siege, with the president saying all those held had been rescued and one hostage-taker killed.
Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 people were believed to be being held by armed men.
President Abelardo de la Espriella, said: “In an extraordinary joint operation between the national police and the armed forces, all the hostages were rescued.”

Shortly after midnight on Wednesday, a police helicopter was hovering low over the shopping centre as security forces massed outside the supermarket. Explosions then echoed around the complex as tactical teams moved in.
Ten of an estimated 30 people that were initially held had already been released during the 17-hour standoff, including several elderly women.
Moments later, soldiers could be seen inside the Éxito supermarket as security forces secured the building.

De la Espriella, who appeared at the scene wearing fatigues and carrying a sidearm and a walkie-talkie, described the operation as a success. He said: “We gave them the opportunity to surrender and free the hostages. They rejected that opportunity and we acted decisively.”
Cartagena’s mayor said all the hostages were “safe and sound” and would be reunited with their families before undergoing medical checks.
The siege gripped Cartagena, a Caribbean port famed for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship tourism. Supermarket employees had been among those feared trapped inside.

blocks.caption: Hostages inside the supermarket. Photograph: Sergio Jimenez Ciro/EPA

blocks.text: “My son is there,” Jacob Pérez, the father of one of the workers, said earlier in the standoff. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him.”
Images broadcast by Colombian media and shared online appeared to show masked gunmen in tactical gear alongside zip-tied hostages inside the store.

De la Espriella was quick to rule out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups. “It’s not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping – no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people,” he said.
Authorities said the siege began after an attempted robbery on an armoured vehicle at the shopping centre.

According to local media, the hostage-takers were demanding nearly US$2m (£1.5m), two armoured vehicles and safe passage to the city of Barranquilla, about 80 miles (130km) north-east of Cartagena. AFP could not independently verify those reports.

The siege began on the 10th anniversary of Colombia’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas amid a series of attacks across the country. Despite the deal to end the region’s largest insurgency, dissident guerrilla groups and criminal organisations still fight for control of parts of the country.
On Monday, authorities blamed a dissident Farc faction for a car bomb attack in the city of Villavicencio that wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.

Separately, the presidency said a “terrorist attack” on electrical infrastructure had disrupted power supplies in several south-western departments and prompted additional measures to protect energy facilities.

articles.title: After 18-year-old’s online exploitation and death, mom wonders why police didn’t search devices right away

image.caption: A mother in Newfoundland is fighting for justice for her teen who died by suicide in April after years of being exploited online. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC)

blocks.text: WARNING: This story contains references to suicide, abuse and graphic material that may be upsetting to some readers.

A grieving mother in St. John's says she and her family were left to find their own evidence after police didn't investigate signs her teen was being exploited by a sadistic online network, despite RCMP in the province being the first police force in Canada to warn parents about the threat more than two years ago.

The family — who CBC News is not identifying for fear of retaliation by online predators — reached out to the fifth estate earlier this year after seeing the program's investigative documentary about 764 — an online network of violent extremists that targets vulnerable minors. It also tries to coerce them into sending sexually explicit messages and images, doing self-harm — including carving their predators' names into their skin as a sign of devotion — and even killing themselves.
The mother says her teen, who we are referring to by the initial J, was being exploited in a similar manner and died by suicide in April at the age of 18.
J was an 18-year-old in Newfoundland who loved sunrises, sunsets, their family and their dog. They died by suicide in April. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Since their death, J's mother says she has been left to scour her child's devices and journals and has found evidence of multiple usernames exploiting her child, utilizing similar tactics used by members of 764, including sexual exploitation and pressure to self-harm.
While police were aware of J's victimization after J attempted suicide in June 2025, J's mother says police did not take J's devices for analysis then or after J died by suicide this past April.
Mom says police ‘asked for nothing’ after teen’s death, online exploitation

Following an interview with the fifth estate, Sgt. Brent Perry, who runs the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary's integrated internet child exploitation unit, reached out to J's mother. He apologized for not "properly" communicating the force's "offer/ability to further this investigation" and has since taken the devices for review.
An inner world of exploitation
J's mother is speaking out now, she says, to find justice for J.
"I feel like this is my role now as J's mom … so the world can see what happens online because a lot of us are blinded to it and J's not here to tell the story themselves."
J left behind multiple phones and journals for their family in which they outline the extent of their online exploitation. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

J's vulnerability can be seen in journal entries, drawings and videos they left behind. In one recording, when J was 15, J speaks about their struggles with mental health, suicidal ideation and self-harm.
J's journal entries also reveal a window into a sadistic online world where J's vulnerability left them targeted and trapped.

According to their mother, J — who loved sunrises, their family and their dog deeply — was struggling with their gender identity during the pandemic and began to spend more time isolated in their room on their phone.

It was only after a suicide attempt in June 2025 that J ended up in hospital and disclosed they had been exploited online by several individuals who had pushed them to record and share images of them self-harming and attempting suicide.
J's mother said she was shocked by what her child shared.
"J explicitly said: ‘They told me to do this, they told to kill myself, they told me to cut myself. They told me, you know, they made me do it. I had no choice. They knew where we lived.'"
For what would have been J's 19th birthday in August, the family placed a purple bench in memory of the teen, at a spot where they enjoyed watching the sunset. (Submitted by J's family)

J's mom called Canada's national tipline, Cybertip.ca, which alerted police. An officer from the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary's integrated internet child exploitation unit came to the hospital and interviewed J.
But according to their mother, a few months later, an officer informed the family that without more information, the investigation was stalled.
Previous police warning

Just a year before, Newfoundland and Labrador RCMP was the first police department in Canada to warn the public about violent online networks that went by names like 764 or CVLT — groups targeting vulnerable children as young as eight on popular social media, gaming and streaming platforms.

At the time, police warned caregivers about how members of the group often invite minors to private chatrooms where they sexually exploit and groom them — for the main purpose of gaining clout within the group.
Since that advisory, the unit has been investigating at least half a dozen cases in the last year. In June, the unit held a news conference to alert the public of another 764 victim in the province.

items: RNC warns parents after youth targeted by extortion group through Roblox

blocks.text: Despite the growing awareness, and J's case bearing the hallmarks of 764's exploitation, J's mother says her child's online abuse was not flagged as another potential case.
J's mother says she can't understand why her child's case wasn't examined more closely given the RCMP had issued the 764 alert just a year before police became aware of J's exploitation.

"When it came to the 764 and knowing that my child was only a year after that and nothing was done — like it was basically dismissed and said: ‘This is it, there's nothing we can do….' Like, why didn't they take this more seriously? Why didn't they ask to see [the] devices?"
Instead, the family says after J's death, an officer told them to reach out if they found any evidence themselves.
J had several devices and in a note left behind included passwords and pointed to where the family could find phones, computers and journals documenting the abuse they endured.

With the help of family members, J's mother spent weeks poring through J's journals, combing through accounts and chats as well as images and videos and found evidence of multiple individuals exploiting her child.
"Why do I, as a parent who just lost my child, have to go through all of this looking for that explicit content? You know, like it's, to me that's torture."
J's mother has kept a number of J's personal belongings close, including the teen's baby blanket. (Roxanna Woloshyn/CBC)

When asked why a family in that situation would be left to gather evidence of their dead child's exploitation, Perry said he could not speak about individual cases. But he acknowledged his empathy for the family.
"I'm a father myself and that issue is very much alive to me," Perry told the fifth estate.
"I'll reiterate that if a family has information that they believe would be of interest to the police to investigate, our door is always open to investigate and hear what information they have."
764 offshoots continue to evolve

Understanding how to tackle the larger problem of 764 and its offshoots is still in its infancy, says Marc-André Argentino, an extremism expert with Public Safety Canada who has been tracking 764 and affiliate groups since 2022.
Argentino says 764 and its offshoots continue to evolve from a loose network urging minors to self-harm to pressuring members to commit acts of public violence.
"This is not fictitious. And it is as bad as we are saying. And actually it is worse."
764 and its related groups draw inspiration from a satanic neo-Nazi movement called the Order of Nine Angles (O9A). (CBC)
Argentino has spent much of his time in the last year training thousands of front-line workers around the world, including 2,000 police officers in Canada, to recognize signs of 764.

"We have a challenge talking about 764 and the network simply because of the type of harms and criminal acts that are perpetrated, the extreme nature of these acts," he said, adding that the fact youths are often behind the violence is hard for many to comprehend.
As the threat escalated, Canada was the first country in the world to designate 764 a terrorist threat in December 2025.

items: Canada becomes 1st country to list extremist network 764 as terrorists

blocks.text: Since then, police have made multiple 764-related arrests across the country, including in Quebec City, New Brunswick and Saskatchewan, as well as identifying several victims in British Columbia.
In an email, a spokesperson for the RCMP said while it cannot share how many 764 cases are being investigated, the "threat is evolving and increasingly involves young people."
Calls for legislation

At a recent event in Ottawa, parents, young people and advocacy groups called on the federal government to implement its online harms legislation, the Safe Social Media Act (Bill C-34), which was tabled in June 2026.

The bill is designed to implement age-appropriate protections and safeguards for younger users, including safer design features and measures to reduce children's exposure to harmful material and high-risk online interactions. The bill is expected to become law next year.
J's mother says the legislation can't come soon enough.
She has spent hours going down dark online corners hoping to hold someone accountable and find justice for her child.
Police apologize, take devices
In the email to J's mother that was sent a day after the fifth estate interviewed Perry, he offered to support her analysis of J's devices "to further her search for answers."
Sgt. Brent Perry is in charge of the RCMP-Royal Newfoundland Constabulary’s integrated internet child exploitation unit. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Perry added that "it has recently come to my attention that our offer/ability to further this investigation was not communicated properly and for that I offer my sincere apology."

The email, sent in June, was the first significant development since J's death in April. In that time, J's mother had found evidence to share, including images of who J claimed was their main predator and messages offering money in exchange for J to carve a name into J's skin.
The RCMP has since asked J's mother to bring in everything she found — including J's devices.
"I provided whatever information I possibly could," she said.
Her voice breaking, she added that she could feel J working through her "to keep me going, to push further and to keep searching. I so badly want justice."
Police have since copied most of the devices and told her the investigation could take months.

articles.title: ‘They don’t believe in freedom’: Yemenis plan their escape as Houthis advance on Aden
articles.summary:
With Iran’s proxy fighters encircling the temporary capital, residents and NGOs prepare to evacuate

Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far…
articles.byline: A reporter in southern Yemen and William Christou in Beirut

blocks.text: Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far south as he could to the port city of Aden, where there was a measure of safety.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government had made the city its temporary capital; the hundreds of kilometres between it and the Houthis were well fortified.

Today, Hussein is once again considering the painful decision of leaving home. In September, the Iran-aligned Houthis swept aside Yemeni government forces, and now have set their sights on Aden. Houthi fighters are amassing to the north and east of the city, and have begun encircling the government-controlled territory.

blocks.caption: People displaced by war on the Red Sea coastline receive aid near Aden, Yemen. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: “I fled my home in Sana’a and came here. I don’t think the Houthis plan to take over Aden right now, but if they get closer, I will have no choice but to flee again to Marib or Hadhramaut,” said Hussein, who was speaking under a pseudonym.

Hussein works as a schoolteacher and was formerly a member of the Islah party, an Islamist political party aligned with Saudi Arabia that is in opposition to the Houthi movement. He fears that if the Houthis take control of Aden he could face persecution for his former affiliation.
“The Houthis don’t believe in freedom, they just want to hear one voice, the one they like,” he said.

Hussein is one of many residents and organisations nervously watching the Houthi advance. The militia is still about 50 miles (80km) north of Aden, but local people fear government forces may not be able to resist another Houthi assault, having seen the dramatic collapse of government forces and allied militias in September.

blocks.caption: Houthi forces take over from Dhubab to Bab el-Mandeb, Taiz governorate, Yemen, after Saudi-backed forces withdraw from the area, 16 November 2026. Photograph: Houthi Military Media/Reuters

blocks.text: Aden has been the seat of the Saudi-backed government of Yemen since 2015. If the Houthis took the city, it would be a huge blow for the government, and a massive failure for the Saudi-led coalition which has for years fought against the Houthis.
The 12-year-long civil war would tilt dramatically in the Houthis’ favour and be a boon for Iran, which has long invested military and political support in the insurgent movement.

The Yemeni government has pulled back many of its fighters to help defend Aden and the surrounding areas, announcing last week that fighters were redeployed from areas along the south-western coast towards the port city.

Saudi Arabia has tried to halt the Houthi advance with a renewed bombing campaign, carrying out hundreds of airstrikes in Yemen since September, killing and wounding 822 civilians, including 181 children, according to statistics from the independent Yemen Data Project.
Houthi authorities have alleged that Saudi Arabia has carried out 5,500 air and missile attacks since July.

blocks.caption: A rescuer walks through the debris of a destroyed building belonging to Yemen’s Public Telecommunications Corporation following a Saudi strike in the port city of Hodeida. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Houthis have not announced any intention to take Aden, but have instead been amassing troops north of Kirish, and in al-Bayda, areas which, if taken, would cut off the northern and eastern roads to Aden.
“The buildups in al-Bayda could threaten Aden’s eastern road links through Abyan and Saudi supply lines into the city,” said Mohammed al-Basha, the founder of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report.

“The Houthis appear to be testing how well Aden’s defences will hold. If they collapse, the Houthis could try to seize the city. If government forces hold, the Houthis could try to lay siege to it,” al-Basha added.

blocks.caption: Members of the National Security Forces at a checkpoint as security is tightened in Aden. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Houthi forces have begun striking Aden and its surrounding areas, rupturing the relative safety the city has offered for years. Residents have watched anxiously as explosions grow nearer, and displaced people from surrounding areas have started to arrive in greater numbers.
“Since last week, we’ve started following the news every hour. When I get busy, I tell my daughter to follow it and update me,” said Rami, a resident of Aden who spoke under a pseudonym.

The 53-year-old bitterly recalled his experience during the four-month battle for Aden in 2015, when he was stuck in the crossfire between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces. He, like other people in Aden, is trying to make his own calculation of when, or if, the Houthis will arrive.
International organisations are also making contingency plans in case of a Houthi takeover of the city.

blocks.caption: A displaced woman carries an aid box at the al-Fardous displacement camp in Ras Imran, on the outskirts of Aden. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: “We were informed by management that they are issuing termination notices to all staff this week. If the Houthis don’t reach Aden, they will continue operations and renew our contracts; otherwise this is the end of the road,” an aid worker with an international NGO said.
Already, several NGOs were forced to shut down in the city of Taiz after sweeping Houthi gains.

Not all NGOs would leave in the case of a Houthi takeover, but some are unable to work in Houthi-controlled areas either due to fears for the safety of aid workers, or because the US Treasury designated the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation in 2025.
Yemen has for years faced a severe humanitarian crisis, with about 18.7 million people facing acute food insecurity.

blocks.caption: Displaced Yemenis from the west coast wait to receive medical care at Prince Mohammed bin Salman hospital in Aden. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: Fighting has only exacerbated conditions, severing transport routes, pushing up the prices of goods and worsening the country’s displacement crisis – including more than 350,000 people displaced since August.

“I earn daily wages, and when there is no work, my six family members don’t get enough food,” said Ahmed, a restaurant worker in his 50s. “I don’t care about politics or wars, and I’m not involved in any of it. I’m just like millions of Yemenis struggling to provide basic necessities for their families.”
For many of Aden’s residents, the prospect of a Houthi takeover has shattered the sense of safety that they sought by coming to the government stronghold in the first place.

“I’m not stocking up on food because I won’t stay in Aden and wait for the battles to reach the city. It isn’t only me; my family is also ready to flee at any time … staying at home won’t be safe and we might get trapped,” Rami said.

articles.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, man at center of Trump deportation battle, leaving US
articles.summary:
Salvadorian man, who was deported in March 2025 and returned to US after supreme court ruling, leaving of own volition for Spain

Kilmar Ábrego García is leaving the United States of his own…
articles.byline: Cris Seda Chabrier in New York

blocks.text: Kilmar Ábrego García is leaving the United States of his own volition, his lawyers confirmed on Tuesday.
Ábrego is leaving the US for Spain on Tuesday evening.

The Salvadorian immigrant was at the center of a months-long legal battle since he was deported to El Salvador in March 2025 by the Trump administration, in defiance of a court’s protection. He was held in Cecot, a notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison.

He was ultimately returned to the US following a decision by the supreme court three months later. Since then, Ábrego has been fighting a second deportation to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials.
The Washington Post reported earlier on Tuesday that he negotiated a deal with federal authorities to depart the US voluntarily in order to avoid being forcibly removed.

In a statement, the US senator Chris Van Hollen, who has advocated for Maryland resident Ábrego and who met with him in El Salvador last year, described him as a “free man” and referenced Ábrego’s agreement with the Trump administration.

“While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said. “I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution.”

The 31-year-old has an American wife and child and has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the US illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, but he was not given residency status.

He was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadorian prison in what an official later called an “administrative error”. Facing public pressure and a court order, the Trump administration brought him back in June 2025, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the justice department’s pursuit of criminal charges was designed to punish Ábrego García for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.
The Trump administration vowed to deport him to a third country, threatening to send him to Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia.

“We will always admire his remarkable courage in staring down and defeating a vindictive prosecution instigated by the highest reaches of the Justice Department,” one of Ábrego García’s attorneys, Sean Hecker, said in a statement provided to the Washington Post. “He, in turn, is grateful to those who stood by him.”
The Associated Press contributed

articles.title: Canada says it ‘does not report to the US’ after Pentagon criticizes military spending
articles.summary:
Scathing US document memo supposedly ‘atrophied’ defence capabilities of its northern neighbour

Canada is a “sovereign nation” that does not “report” to the United States, the country’s…

blocks.text: Canada is a “sovereign nation” that does not “report” to the United States, the country’s defense minister said after the Pentagon released a scathing memo that criticized the supposedly “atrophied” defence capabilities of its northern neighbour.

The document, released on Tuesday, said Canada had “yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs” necessary to meet previous defence spending pledges and become a “credible partner in the defense of our shared continent”.

The Pentagon memo said it took Canada nearly two decades to finally reach spending promises made in 2006 “despite Canada’s role as a major G7 economy as well as one of the largest and wealthiest members of the NATO alliance”.

Historically, Nato members have fallen short of meeting the security organization’s funding goals. When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, only three Nato members – the US, the UK and Greece – were meeting the alliance’s guideline of spending 2% of GDP on defence. By 2025, all 31 members with armed forces, including Canada, had reached the goal.

The document also suggested Canada faces significant operational hurdles in its air, land and sea operations, blaming political leaders for pursuing “parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization”.

The Pentagon document said the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military, suggesting American taxpayers had been “footing the bill for its defense” for decades.
The defense minister, David McGuinty, told reporters he could not “divine” the thinking behind the Pentagon’s decision to criticise Canada’s defence spending now.

“The amount of cooperation we are pushing under Norad [North American Aerospace Defense Command] has not changed. What we’re doing together at Nato has not changed. Our military-to-military cooperation has not changed. Our work on integrated air missile defence has not changed,” he said.
McGuinty also bristled at the suggestion from a reporter that the memo implied Canada required approval from the US when it came to its spending plans.
“Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States,” he said.
The memo came as a Canadian official travelled to Europe to pitch a new defence bank championed by the prime minister, Mark Carney.

Isabelle Hudon, Canada’s lead negotiator for establishing the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, is looking to cajole more countries into joining a global initiative that would lend to governments and contractors at low cost to support defense projects.

Ten countries have pledged their support but no others from the G7 have done so yet, with both the UK and Germany so far declining to join. Hudon says the €4bn in commitments secured so far is enough to start the bank up but she is aiming for up to €100bn.

Carney has made significantly increased spending commitments in defence. The country spent $63.4bn on national defence in 2025, meeting its Nato pledge to spend 2% of gross domestic product for the first time.
Last year, Nato members agreed to raise the goal to the equivalent of 5% of GDP by 2035.

Canada’s federal budget this month laid out a plan to spend about 4% of Canada’s GDP on defence and security annually by the end of the decade, and 5% by 2035, including the purchase of submarines and early warning aircraft.

Canada’s air power is a key point of friction with Washington. Carney’s government has yet to make a final decision on its order of F-35 fighter jets from the US firm Lockheed Martin and is weighing the possibility of purchasing Swedish-made Gripen aircraft instead. The multibillion-dollar purchase has been the subject of a political review for more than a year. The Pentagon memo warned that operating a “mixed fleet” of aircraft would “compound existing personnel shortfalls”.

articles.title: Armed men take 25 hostages at supermarket in one of Colombia’s top tourist destinations
articles.summary:
Police say group seized store in city of Cartagena and local media showed footage of snipers on nearby buildings

A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the

blocks.text: A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding 25 people hostage, the president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said on Tuesday.
De la Espriella, said the men were “common criminals” who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
Military and police forces have been deployed to the hostage site, Colombian police said.

Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the Exito supermarket in Cartagena’s La Castellana neighborhood, while local media have shown footage of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff between the armed men and police.

“Thirty people were kidnapped, five ​of whom have already been released. They are older women,” said de la Espriella from the city of ​Villavicencio, where he traveled after an overnight bombing ​there.

Cartagena is one of Colombia’s main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well-preserved 18th-century architecture, and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.

The Rafael Núñez airport in Cartagena temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday after the incident, as the armed forces used one of the runways in ​connection with ​the incident. It later said operations were slowly returning to normal and landings were reopened about 45 minutes after the suspension.
Local media reported the hostages are ​being her at the Castellana location of ​the ⁠Éxito supermarket chain.
More details soon …

articles.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
articles.summary:
Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa

When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the…
articles.byline: Pjotr Sauer, Michael Goodier, Harriet Agerholm and Philip McMahon

blocks.text: When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.

“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”

The Kremlin-controlled forces and their Malian allies were facing a coordinated surprise assault by the al-Qaida-linked JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), whose fighters used suicide car bombs and drones to break through the city’s defences.

blocks.caption: The view from a helicopter flying over a convoy of tankers heading towards Mali’s capital, Bamako, in May 2026, posted on the X account of the Africa Corps. Photograph: Africa Corps/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Leaked Russian state records suggest the losses were heavy that day. Death certificates of Russian fighters killed in Mali, held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, were obtained by the hacker groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow and analysed by the Guardian.

The records show that 43 Russians died in Mali on 25 April, including six in Kidal and one in nearby Aguelhok. Others were recorded as dying in the capital, Bamako, and in Gao, where rebels shot down a Russian military helicopter that day.

By the following morning, the Russians had abandoned Kidal, which Russian mercenaries had helped capture in November 2023 and which Moscow had since held up as a showcase of its growing influence in Africa.
In all, the records list 349 Russian deaths in Mali between September 2023 and September 2026, most of which the Guardian was able to link to known battles with rebel groups.

blocks.caption: A billboard in Bamako carrying birthday wishes for Vladimir Putin, October 2024. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The figures offer a previously unseen glimpse into the human cost of Moscow’s efforts to prop up Mali’s military junta, in what has become Russia’s largest military deployment in Africa.
Two western officials who have travelled to Mali and were shown the data said the death toll was higher than previously estimated.
“That’s over 10% of Russia’s forces killed in action,” said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.
Moscow does not publish its losses in Africa, and its foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The Wagner private military group, led by the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin, first arrived in Mali in late 2021, a year after a military coup had toppled President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. French forces were ordered to leave the country as relations with the junta deteriorated, bringing an end to France’s decade-long counter-terrorism operation and leaving Russia as the regime’s main foreign protector.

blocks.caption: Three Russian mercenaries operating in northern Mali, January 2022 Photograph: French army/AP

blocks.text: Wagner handed over its operations in Mali to the Africa Corps in June 2025, two years after Prigozhin led a failed mutiny on Moscow that discredited the group in the eyes of the Kremlin. By that summer, British intelligence estimated that about 2,000 Africa Corps personnel were deployed in the country.

The Africa Corps, closely overseen by Russian military intelligence, currently provides backing to several African governments in return for payment or lucrative contracts granting access to natural resources.

Despite the Russian presence, Mali’s security situation has continued to deteriorate. In late July 2024, Russian and Malian forces fought Tuareg separatists for several days near Tinzaouaten, on the Algerian border.
Wagner at the time issued a rare statement admitting losses, including the death of a commander, but gave no figure. Estimates from Russian sources ranged from about 20 to more than 80 dead.

blocks.caption: Graves of Wagner fighters in a cemetery near the village of Bakinskaya, in Russia’s Krasnodar region, January 2023. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: The Rosstat records list 70 Russians who died on 27 July 2024, all but one of them in the Kidal region. The figures make the battle of Tinzaouaten the deadliest single day for Russian forces in Africa since Wagner mercenaries first deployed to the continent in 2017.

The toll in Mali may have been driven up by Ukraine, which has extended its war against Russia to the Sahel. Kyiv has been assisting Tuareg rebels there, according to two people with knowledge of the operations. CNN has reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were deployed to Mali to help local rebel forces fighting Russian troops.

The records are probably an undercount. Registration often lags, and no Russian deaths in Mali are recorded for March 2026 although at least three Africa Corps fighters were reported killed in an ambush near Nampala that month.

The leaked data also sheds light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa. Central African Republic, where Wagner fighters guard the president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, accounts for 30 deaths. While not all could be linked to known incidents, three men died on the night drones struck Wagner camps in Kaga-Bandoro in December 2023.

In Libya, where Russian forces back the eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and use his airbases as a supply route to their deployments in the Sahel, some of the recorded deaths were probably linked to a helicopter crash at the Maaten al-Sarra base in February 2026. On Sunday, Ukrainian drones sunk a Russian warship off the coast of Libya; it is unclear whether there were any casualties.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Niger’s ruling junta hold up a Russian flag in Niamey, August 2023.  Photograph: Sam Mednick/AP

blocks.text: In Niger, where Russia’s Africa Corps moved in after the military junta expelled French and US troops, a Russian fighter died two days after Islamic State militants attacked Niamey airport in January, a previously unreported casualty.

Moscow has in recent months stepped up its effort to show it is back in control in Mali. On 6 October, Malian troops and the Africa Corps recaptured Kidal after what the army called an air and ground campaign.

A report this month by the US-based Conflict Insights Group (CIG) found that the Africa Corps had sharply increased its use of drones in Mali, including Lancet suicide drones, amid an intensifying air campaign.

The group wrote that the drone campaign had also targeted civilians, boostering support for the rebels. “Civilian deaths in the intensified air campaign, which the Africa Corps leads, are likely to aid insurgent recruitment,” it said.

blocks.caption: Vladimir Putin and the Malian junta leader, Assimi Goita, at the Kremlin in June 2025. Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A western diplomat who works in the region said the attacks in late April had punctured the image of Russian military invincibility that Moscow and the junta had cultivated among Malians.
“Russia still wields considerable influence in Mali, but patience with its military performance is wearing thin.”

articles.title: World Chess Championship 2026 Game 1: Gukesh Dommaraju v Javokhir Sindarov – live
articles.summary:
• Youngest title match in chess history starts Tuesday

  • Sindarov, Gukesh open with Berlin defense of Ruy Lopez

blocks.text: Everything you need to know about the World Chess Championship

India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is defending the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov in the youngest title match in the competition’s 140-year history. The best-of-14-games contest is scheduled to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer outside Geneva, with an overall prize fund of $2.5m (£1.9m).

items: Game 1 starts at 3pm in Geneva, 2pm in London, 9am in New York and 7.30pm in India
Sindarov will have the white pieces for Game 1 and make the first move
Gukesh and Sindarov are both 20 years old, making this the youngest matchup in world championship’s 140-year history
Read the Guardian’s comprehensive watch guide for the Gukesh v Sindarov showdown
Go move by move through 22 of the most famous games in world championship history

blocks.text: Key events

items: 1h agoGame 1 is under way!
2h agoHow do Gukesh and Sindarov match up?
2h agoThe format
2h agoPreamble
3h agoEverything you need to know about the World Chess Championship

blocks.text: And finally Gukesh makes his move! After a think of more than 15 minutes, the world champion has opted for 13 ... Bd7, bringing his last minor piece into play. The bishop also shields the black king from a potential check along the d-file, giving Gukesh greater flexibility in repositioning his king and coordinating his rooks. He’s more than 35 minutes behind the challenger on time, though.
Gukesh is in another deep think as Javokhir leaves the board for the nearby lounge chair inside the cramped playing hall.

“Now I understand what Javokhir was playing for,” English grandmaster David Howell says on the Chess.com broadcast. “I would have expected this opening from two older players, not maybe two 20-year-olds. But now I understand he’s trying to bait Gukesh. He’s trying to tempt him into some line where he has a deep, deep idea. Yeah, it’s very provocative.”

blocks.caption: Sindarov looks on as Gukesh ponders his response to 13 Ne4. Photograph: Chess.com

blocks.text: Gukesh has developed his dark-squared bishop and Sindarov has centralized his queenside knight (12 ... Be7 13 Ne4). The pace of play has slowed considerably as the players begin to grapple with the strategic subtleties of the Berlin. Both Stockfish and the Sesse supercomputer assess the position as dead even (0.00).

blocks.caption: Gukesh studies the position during Tuesday’s opening game of the world chess championship. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters

blocks.text: An email from the always welcome Gary Naylor, who sees parallels between the world chess championship and another of Europe’s great endurance events:

double quotation markGiven the location, the schedule, the fact that each leader has a team supporting him and, more than anything, the stamina required, this feels like the Tour de France. I suppose players have the ability to make stages – games – hard or easy by their strategies too. Any sign of lycra?

No lycra to report, Gary, but there’s certainly something to the analogy. The ability to conserve energy over a three-week campaign, knowing when to attack and when to settle for a quiet day, is an underrated component of world championship matchplay.
Gukesh has been mulling his response to 12 Be3 for more than 10 minutes, after spending about eight minutes on his previous move.

“He still knows the position, but he is taking time to make sure he makes the right moves,” Russian grandmaster Peter Svidler says on the official Fide broadcast. “But Gukesh is already down almost 18 minutes on the clock. Considering he’s playing one of the most topical openings of the past 25 years, that’s some time expenditure.”
Gukesh has brought his knight to g6, putting pressure on the advanced white pawn on e5, and Sindarov has continued his development by bringing his bishop into play (11 ... Ng6 12 Be3).

Gukesh has returned his king to its original square and rerouted his knight (9 Rd1+ Ke8 10 Nc3 Ne7 11 h3). Sindarov’s last move prevents black’s light-squared bishop from coming to g4 and pinning the knight on f3, while giving his own king some breathing room.

“I think it’s important to highlight for our viewers that black is not playing for a draw,” the Hungarian grandmaster Judit Polgár says on Chess.com’s broadcast. “Black is just deciding to go into an endgame or a middlegame without queens, where it seems like only white has a slight edge. Black has doubled pawns on c6 and c7, black has the bishop pair, but basically black can go b6, develop the pieces properly.”

blocks.caption: The position after 10 Nc3. Photograph: Fide

blocks.text: We’re heading straight into the famous Berlin endgame (4 O-O Nxe4 5 d4 Nd6 6 Bxc6 dxc6 7 dxe5 Nf5 8 Qxd8+ Kxd8). The queens are off the board after only eight moves, leaving white with a kingside pawn majority and black with the bishop pair but doubled c-pawns and a king that has forfeited the right to castle.

Don’t mistake the early exchange of queens for a lack of ambition. The resulting position is deceptively rich in strategic possibilities and has been the subject of decades of analysis at the highest level. Gukesh has continued with 9 Rd1+, and both players are still moving quickly.
Game 1 is under way!
The players have shaken hands and we’re off! We have a Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez (1 e4 e5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 Bb5 Nf6), one of the most thoroughly analyzed openings in modern chess.

The Berlin famously helped Vladimir Kramnik dethrone Garry Kasparov in their 2000 world title match in London and has been a staple of elite chess ever since, earning a reputation as one of black’s most reliable weapons against 1 e4.

We’re eight minutes to the scheduled first move, but American grandmaster Maurice Ashley has started with his introduction of the players to the playing hall. Gukesh enters first and takes his seat behind the black pieces. Sindarov, playing as white after Sunday’s drawing of lots, enters second.

blocks.caption: Fide president Timur Turlov makes the ceremonial first move for white in Tuesday’s opening game of the world chess championship between Javokhir Sindarov and Gukesh Dommaraju near Geneva. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters

blocks.text: If you’re looking for some pre-match reading, the Guardian spoke exclusively with Javokhir Sindarov on Sunday about his meteoric rise, his love of Lionel Messi, his plans to play GTA VI once the match is over and why chess’s happy warrior believes there’s more to life than the game. A taste:

double quotation mark“I’m the guy who can’t play games just for fun,” Sindarov tells the Guardian less than 48 hours before Tuesday’s world championship opener in Geneva, smiling at the absurdity of it. “If I play something, I always try to learn, trying to become better.” That means poring over Counter-Strike tactics and watching YouTube tutorials before joining in with his mates. There is, it appears, no such thing as a casual game in Sindarov’s world, much less a friendly. “I always like to beat my friends,” he says. “I watch some video lessons and then come and beat them after some tournaments. I think the best thing is to beat your friends in some game.” It is a revealing admission from a young man who has acquired a reputation for being uncommonly relaxed at the chess board. While many of the world’s elite players seem to carry the weight of every position on their shoulders – the viral clip of Sergey Karjakin agonizing for 25 minutes over a move during the 2016 world title match remains a cult classic in chess circles – Sindarov frequently gives off the impression of someone who is simply enjoying himself. The easygoing mien of the sport’s happy warrior is a quality that has caught his opponent’s attention. “One thing I learned from Sindarov is that he seems to be so happy while playing chess,” Gukesh Dommaraju, the reigning world champion, said in an interview published last week.

We’ve gone through the 140-year history of the world championship and chosen 22 of the most memorable games. You can go move by move through each of them here. It’s the perfect timesuck in the final run-up to today’s first move.

double quotation markFrom the middle of the 16th century, there have come down to us the names of chess players who have been widely regarded as the strongest of their time. The earliest of these was the Spanish priest Ruy López de Segura, after whom one of the most popular openings of modern times is named. Others who followed include the Calabrese Gioachino Greco, François-André Danican Philidor, Louis-Charles Mahé de La Bourdonnais, Alexander McDonnell, Howard Staunton, Adolf Anderssen, Mikhail Chigorin and Paul Morphy, each of whom are lionized for their contributions to the development of theory and strategy as well as their dominance over their board during their respective eras. But not until Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort sat down in a small room at 80 Fifth Avenue in New York City on the afternoon of 11 January 1886 did a formal competition to determine the best player on the planet come to pass. Their first-to-10-wins encounter was held in three US cities over the next 78 days for a prize fund of $4,000. Since then, the world chess championship has provided the stage for countless unforgettable contests showcasing the precision, imagination and brilliance of the royal game at the highest level.

The legitimacy of the world championship, of course, remains a subject of lively debate. The absence of Magnus Carlsen continues to cast a long shadow over the sport’s showcase event. The 35-year-old Norwegian has held the world No 1 ranking for more than 15 consecutive years and was widely regarded as the game’s strongest player even before he defeated Vishy Anand for the world title in 2013. He only strengthened his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021, when he crushed Ian Nepomniachtchi in Dubai in his fourth successful defense of the crown.

But Carlsen declined to defend his title for a fifth time in 2023, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long grind of preparation that championship matches demand. Only twice before had the chain of succession that stretches back to Wilhelm Steinitz in 1886 been broken: when Alexander Alekhine died as champion in 1946 and when Bobby Fischer forfeited the title in 1975.

blocks.caption: Norway’s Magnus Carlsen has held the world No 1 ranking for more than 15 consecutive years. Photograph: Yu Chun Christopher Wong/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ding Liren went on to defeat Nepomniachtchi for the vacant title before losing it to Gukesh Dommaraju in Singapore the following year. Now Gukesh faces Sindarov in a match between two 20-year-olds ranked No 26 and No 4 in the world respectively, while the planet’s top-ranked player remains on the sidelines – at a time when his No 1 ranking is looking more vulnerable than any time in anyone’s memory. The generational stakes are undeniable, but the question that has dogged the championship since Carlsen walked away remains unresolved: can the winner truly claim to be the best chess player in the world?
How do Gukesh and Sindarov match up?

For two elite players born in the same general part of the world barely six months apart, their competitive history is remarkably sparse: just three encounters in classical chess. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. Sindarov also holds a 2-1 edge in their three rapid and blitz contests this year.
Allow content provided by a third party?

This article includes content hosted on lichess.org. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Gukesh’s form has largely gone off the rails since reaching the summit 23 months ago in Singapore. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad.

Many of the world’s top grandmasters have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently. “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.”

Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September. “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.”

blocks.caption: Javokhir Sindarov, left, and Gukesh Dommaraju stand on the podium during Sunday’s world chess championship opening ceremony at the United Nations’ European headquarters in Geneva. Photograph: Salvatore Di Nolfi/EPA

blocks.text: The format

Here’s a review of the format for the world championship match. Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played).

The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours, testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter.

If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023.
The complete official regulations can be found here.

blocks.caption: Gukesh Dommaraju speaks with chess presenter Charlize van Zyl during Sunday’s media day at the United Nations’ European headquarters in Geneva. Photograph: Michał Walusza/Fide

blocks.text: Preamble

Hello and welcome to Geneva for day one of the World Chess Championship. Over the next three weeks, India’s defending champion Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan will compete in a scheduled best-of-14-games match for the sport’s most prestigious title and a share of a $2.5m prize fund. The setting is the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, an affluent suburb overlooking Lake Geneva, where the two 20-year-olds will make history as the youngest pairing ever to contest a world championship match in the competition’s 140-year history.

Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world chess champion in history when he defeated China’s Ding Liren in Singapore in December 2024, aged just 18, shattering the record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in 1985. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai-born grandmaster has struggled badly for form since winning the crown, sliding from a career-high No 3 to No 26 in the world rankings and raising questions over his chances of retaining the title in his first defense.

blocks.caption: A tram bearing promotional artwork for the world chess championship in Geneva. Photograph: Maurizio Giuliani/Fide

blocks.text: Sindarov, meanwhile, has emerged as one of the most formidable talents of a new generation of Uzbek grandmasters. Born in Tashkent, he became a grandmaster at 12 years and 10 months, the second-youngest in history at the time, and secured his place in Geneva by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament earlier this year. A fearless, resourceful player in a rich vein of form, he enters his first world championship match ranked fourth in the world, up from No 25 last year and a remarkable 22 places above the reigning champion, and with a favorable head-to-head record against Gukesh in classical chess.

We’re roughly 80 minutes away from the ceremonial opening moves. Fide president Timur Turlov will do the honors for white, with five-time world champion and Fide deputy president Viswanathan Anand moving for black. Plenty more to come between now and then.
